MRI is preferred and expedited for atypical, rapid, focal, or early-onset presentations.

options.t: APOE genotyping — an APOE ε4 allele would confirm Alzheimer disease and guide management.

trap.name: Genetic confirmation
trap.note: APOE status informs population-level risk but does not diagnose AD and is not part of the standard workup — reversible causes must be excluded first.

qb_cog_009.why: Jump to autoimmune and Genetic confirmation both skip the foundational step. The reversible-cause panel — B12/folate, TSH, CMP, and when indicated RPR/HIV — must precede neurodegenerative labeling because these conditions are treatable and clinically indistinguishable at presentation. APOE genotyping is not a diagnostic standard. Structural imaging is part of the same initial workup rather than a later step, but it is not the laboratory screen this stem asks for, and it does not require gadolinium.
qb_cog_009.pearl: Every new cognitive diagnosis gets both halves of the reversible screen: the panel (B12/folate, TSH, CMP, ± RPR/HIV) and structural imaging — labs cannot exclude NPH or a chronic subdural.
qb_cog_009.evidence: t_neurocog.md 'Initial workup' — Labs to catch reversible causes: CBC, CMP, TSH, B12/folate, and — when indicated — HIV and RPR/treponemal testing. Neuroimaging (CT or MRI) as part of the initial workup of any new cognitive diagnosis — it is the only way the NPH and chronic subdural hematoma on the reversible list above get found — with MRI preferred, and expedited for atypical, rapid, focal, or early-onset presentations.

qb_cog_010.stem: A 78-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment is admitted for worsening confusion and agitation over the past week. She recently started diphenhydramine nightly for insomnia and oxybutynin for urge incontinence. The student reviews her medication list. Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.t: Add risperidone for the agitation — it is the most evidence-based pharmacotherapy for behavioral symptoms in cognitive impairment.

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Adding a dopamine blocker before addressing the obvious medication-related drivers is pharmacologically backwards and potentially harmful.

options.t: Order a 24-hour EEG — medication-induced encephalopathy can produce seizure patterns that explain cognitive worsening.

trap.name: Jump to testing
trap.note: Costly procedural workup before deprescribing the medications most likely causing the problem is a diagnostic error of omission.

options.t: Flag diphenhydramine and oxybutynin as high-risk anticholinergic agents for the team, escalate for deprescribing, and recommend non-pharmacologic sleep and bladder strategies.
Reassure the family that mild cognitive impairment commonly worsens under medical stress and will recover once she is discharged.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: Dismissing a potentially reversible pharmacologic cause without addressing identifiable high-risk medications is a clinical error of omission.

qb_cog_010.why: Agitation = antipsychotic and Face-value reassurance both bypass the diagnosis. Anticholinergic burden is a recognized, reversible driver of cognitive worsening in older adults — diphenhydramine and oxybutynin are among the Beers Criteria's most flagged agents. Jump to testing substitutes cost for the straightforward clinical action. The geriatric psychiatry principle: the drug list is often the diagnosis; deprescribing is active treatment.
qb_cog_010.pearl: In older adults with cognitive change, the medication list is often the diagnosis — assess anticholinergic burden and deprescribe before adding anything.
qb_cog_010.evidence: t_geri.md 'Acute inpatient management' — Apply the Beers Criteria and assess cumulative anticholinergic burden, then actively deprescribe deliriogenic and high-risk agents. 'High-yield pearls' — The drug list is often the diagnosis — deprescribing is active treatment.

tier2.q: Why do anticholinergic medications disproportionately impair cognition in older adults?

options.t: Older adults have reduced hepatic metabolism, causing higher serum drug levels than predicted for a given dose.
Older adults have reduced cholinergic reserve due to aging and often concurrent dementia — blocking acetylcholine impairs attention and memory in a system already depleted.
Anticholinergic agents cause orthostatic hypotension, reducing cerebral perfusion and producing cognitive symptoms.
The mechanism is peripheral: urinary retention and constipation trigger systemic inflammation that secondarily impairs cognition.

tier2.why: It is a pharmacodynamic-reserve problem, not primarily pharmacokinetic. Acetylcholine is essential for attention and memory; older adults — especially those with early Alzheimer or MCI — have fewer cholinergic neurons. Blocking the remaining ones with an anticholinergic produces an outsized, often rapid cognitive effect that clinically mimics dementia progression. This is why cholinesterase inhibitors (which increase acetylcholine) treat AD, and anticholinergics are its pharmacologic enemy.

qb_cog_011.stem: A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife, who reports an 18-month history of increasingly disinhibited behavior — making inappropriate sexual comments to strangers, hoarding food, and neglecting hygiene. He has no memory complaints, names and recognizes objects normally, and denies mood symptoms. Neuropsychological testing shows prominent executive dysfunction with intact episodic memory. Most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Bipolar disorder — new-onset mania presents with disinhibition, impulsivity, and executive dysfunction in midlife.

trap.name: Bipolar by default
trap.note: Mania is episodic and includes mood elevation and increased energy — a progressive 18-month course of isolated behavioral change without mood symptoms indicates a neurodegenerative process, not a mood disorder.

options.t: Behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia — early disinhibition, socially inappropriate behavior, and executive dysfunction with relative sparing of episodic memory in a younger adult is the classic bvFTD presentation.
Early-onset Alzheimer disease — insidious behavioral change in a 58-year-old is most commonly early-onset AD.

trap.name: Most common = correct
trap.note: Alzheimer typically begins with episodic memory loss — prominent early behavioral disinhibition with intact episodic memory is the FTD signature, not Alzheimer.

options.t: Personality disorder — disinhibition, impulsivity, and boundary violations reflect a longstanding personality pattern rather than a new neurological process.

trap.name: Personality disorder by default
trap.note: A progressive 18-month course representing a clear change from baseline is a neurodegenerative process — personality disorders are stable and longstanding, not new-onset in the sixth decade.

qb_cog_011.why: Bipolar by default, Most common = correct, and Personality disorder by default are three forms of the same error: assigning a functional psychiatric diagnosis before considering neurodegeneration. FTD is the dementia of younger adults, presenting with behavior and personality change or progressive language, while sparing episodic memory early — the exact opposite of Alzheimer.
qb_cog_011.pearl: Frontotemporal dementia: younger onset, behavioral disinhibition or progressive language first, episodic memory spared early — the signature that separates it from Alzheimer.
qb_cog_011.evidence: t_neurocog.md — Frontotemporal — younger onset with early personality/behavior change or progressive aphasia; memory relatively spared early.

qb_cog_012.stem: A 74-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history is brought to the emergency department by her family. She has developed, over the past month, a fixed belief that her neighbors are poisoning her food and has stopped eating. She is alert, coherent, and oriented. There is no mood disturbance. Which is the most important next step?

options.t: Diagnose late-onset schizophrenia — paranoid delusions in late life unexplained by a mood disorder represent a primary psychotic illness.

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: First-episode psychosis in a 74-year-old has an extensive organic differential — labeling it late-onset schizophrenia without a medical workup is premature diagnostic closure.

options.t: Start an antipsychotic immediately — the refusal to eat constitutes an acute safety emergency requiring empirical treatment.

trap.name: Treat before diagnosis
trap.note: The safety concern is real but empirical antipsychotic treatment without an organic workup can mask a reversible medical or neurological cause.

options.t: Reassure the family that paranoid ideation is a normal variant of cognitive aging.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: Paranoid ideation is not a normal aging variant — in an older adult with no prior psychiatric history, it is a medical red flag requiring evaluation.

options.t: Conduct a medical workup to exclude organic causes of new-onset psychosis — including delirium, medication effect, CNS lesion, metabolic derangement, and autoimmune encephalitis — before establishing a primary psychiatric diagnosis.

qb_cog_012.why: Psychosis = schizophrenia, Treat before diagnosis, and Face-value reassurance all skip the foundational step. New-onset psychosis in an older adult without a prior psychiatric history is a medical emergency until proven otherwise. The differential includes delirium, CNS lesion, metabolic cause, autoimmune encephalitis, and medication-induced psychosis — all requiring workup before a primary psychotic diagnosis is made.
qb_cog_012.pearl: New psychosis in an older adult is a medical emergency until proven otherwise — work up before labeling or treating.
qb_cog_012.evidence: t_geri.md 'High-yield pearls' — New psychosis in an older adult is delirium or a medical cause until proven otherwise.

qb_cog_013.stem: A 35-year-old man with bipolar disorder screens positive for catatonia on the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale — he is mute, maintains awkward arm postures for extended periods, and stares past the examiner. The team has appropriately held the antipsychotic. What is the indicated next step?

options.t: Administer a lorazepam challenge (IV or IM) — meaningful improvement in catatonic signs after benzodiazepines supports the diagnosis and begins treatment; benzodiazepines are first-line for catatonia.
Initiate a clozapine trial — persistent psychiatric symptoms after stopping the antipsychotic indicate a need for a clozapine evaluation.

trap.name: Clozapine for catatonia
trap.note: Clozapine is not the next step after a positive catatonia screen — first-line treatment is benzodiazepines (lorazepam challenge); ECT is reserved for benzodiazepine-refractory or malignant catatonia.

options.t: Restart the antipsychotic at a lower dose — catatonic symptoms worsen without dopamine blockade and the patient needs partial antipsychotic coverage.

trap.name: Restart antipsychotic
trap.note: Antipsychotics must be avoided until catatonia is treated — they can precipitate or worsen NMS and malignant catatonia; the first step is a lorazepam challenge, not partial antipsychotic re-exposure.

options.t: Apply soft restraints and obtain an urgent head CT to rule out structural causes before proceeding with any treatment.

trap.name: Restraint before treatment
trap.note: Catatonia is a treatable psychiatric syndrome — the next step after a positive screen is the lorazepam challenge; neuroimaging may help exclude organic causes but should not delay the diagnostic-therapeutic lorazepam trial.

qb_cog_013.why: Clozapine for catatonia, Restart antipsychotic, and Restraint before treatment all defer or undermine first-line treatment. The catatonia source states: 'A test dose of lorazepam is both a diagnostic maneuver and the start of treatment — a meaningful, often rapid improvement supports the diagnosis and predicts response.' Benzodiazepines are first-line; ECT is for benzodiazepine-refractory or malignant catatonia.
qb_cog_013.pearl: After positive catatonia screen + holding the antipsychotic → lorazepam challenge next: both diagnostic and therapeutic.
qb_cog_013.evidence: catatonia.md 'The lorazepam challenge' — A test dose of lorazepam (IV or IM) is both a diagnostic maneuver and the start of treatment; meaningful improvement after the challenge supports the diagnosis and predicts benzodiazepine response. Benzodiazepines are first-line; ECT is for benzodiazepine-refractory or malignant catatonia.

qb_cog_014.stem: A 29-year-old woman with schizophrenia has been mute and posturing for 2 days. Today she is found febrile to 39.6°C, diaphoretic, hypotensive, with lead-pipe rigidity and a markedly elevated CK. Her antipsychotic was increased yesterday. Best next step?

options.t: Administer additional lorazepam challenge doses and observe on the psychiatric unit — the rigidity suggests catatonic stupor responding to benzodiazepines.

trap.name: Underestimate the emergency
trap.note: Autonomic instability + hyperthermia + rigidity + elevated CK after antipsychotic escalation is a medical emergency requiring transfer, not continued psychiatric unit observation.

options.t: Increase the antipsychotic — this is a catatonic variant of treatment-resistant psychosis requiring more aggressive dopamine blockade.

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: In a febrile patient with elevated CK and rigidity after an antipsychotic was escalated, this is NMS/malignant catatonia — increasing the dopamine blocker accelerates the emergency.

options.t: Stop all antipsychotics, move to a medical unit for monitoring, continue lorazepam, and arrange ECT if there is no rapid improvement.
Treat empirically for sepsis — fever, hypotension, and elevated CK indicate bacterial infection requiring antibiotics.

trap.name: Sepsis first
trap.note: Sepsis is on the differential but the timing (antipsychotic escalated yesterday), catatonic signs on exam, and the specific combination of lead-pipe rigidity + fever + elevated CK after a dopamine blocker constitute NMS/malignant catatonia until proven otherwise.

qb_cog_014.why: Underestimate the emergency and Agitation = antipsychotic are the two clinical catastrophes. This is NMS/malignant catatonia: fever, autonomic instability, lead-pipe rigidity, elevated CK after antipsychotic escalation. The correct sequence is stop all antipsychotics, transfer to a medical unit for hemodynamic monitoring, continue lorazepam — benzodiazepines remain first-line pharmacotherapy for malignant catatonia while ECT is arranged — and pursue ECT emergently if the patient does not rapidly improve; the error in option A is observation on the psychiatric unit, not the lorazepam, and certainly not more antipsychotic. Obtain urgent psychiatry and neurology consultation.
qb_cog_014.pearl: Malignant catatonia overlaps with NMS: fever + rigidity + elevated CK + autonomic instability after antipsychotic exposure — stop antipsychotics, transfer to medical, continue lorazepam, and consider ECT urgently.
qb_cog_014.evidence: catatonia.md — The emergency you must never miss is malignant catatonia: autonomic instability, hyperthermia, and rigidity that clinically overlaps with neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). ECT is the treatment for severe, malignant, or benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia and should not be delayed when the patient is deteriorating.

tier2.q: Why does ECT have a role in malignant catatonia when benzodiazepines have not been effective?

options.t: ECT provides dopamine agonism that directly counteracts antipsychotic receptor blockade.
ECT is used because it avoids all pharmacologic agents, preventing further receptor blockade.

ECT directly treats the catatonic syndrome regardless of etiology — it is the definitive treatment for malignant or benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia and it can work before the antipsychotic has fully cleared (the antipsychotic is still stopped).
ECT is a last resort used only after a second antipsychotic trial has failed in treatment-resistant psychosis.

tier2.why: ECT acts directly on the motor and autonomic systems driving catatonia — its mechanism bypasses the pharmacologic state that triggered the syndrome. The BAP 2023 catatonia guideline endorses ECT for severe, refractory, or malignant catatonia as a treatment that should not be delayed when the patient is deteriorating. The example here illustrates this: benzodiazepines alone may be insufficient for malignant presentations, so ECT should not be delayed if lorazepam does not produce rapid improvement — the antipsychotic is still stopped, and ECT can be lifesaving before it has fully cleared.

qb_cog_015.stem: An 82-year-old man with moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease is currently on donepezil 10 mg daily. His neurologist asks the student to identify what pharmacotherapy optimization is supported by evidence for this stage of disease.

options.t: Increase donepezil to the maximum tolerated dose — dose escalation of cholinesterase inhibitors alone is the evidence-based approach for moderate-to-severe disease.

trap.name: Dose escalation alone
trap.note: Dose escalation of a cholinesterase inhibitor alone is not the evidence-based approach for moderate-to-severe AD — memantine should be added.

options.t: Add memantine — combination of a cholinesterase inhibitor and memantine (NMDA antagonist) is the evidence-based pharmacotherapy for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease.
Switch to a rivastigmine patch — transdermal delivery is more effective than oral donepezil in advanced disease.

trap.name: Newer = better
trap.note: Formulation does not determine efficacy — donepezil is appropriate; the treatment gap is the absence of memantine, not the delivery route.

options.t: Start a monoclonal anti-amyloid antibody — these agents are now standard of care for all stages of Alzheimer.

trap.name: Newer = better
trap.note: Anti-amyloid antibodies modestly slow early Alzheimer progression and require amyloid confirmation and specialized monitoring; they are not standard of care for all stages and are not started on an inpatient psychiatry unit.

qb_cog_015.why: Dose escalation alone and Newer = better in two forms. For mild-to-moderate AD, cholinesterase inhibitors alone are the standard. For moderate-to-severe AD, adding memantine is the evidence-based optimization. Anti-amyloid antibodies are specialist-initiated, amyloid-confirmed, and restricted to early disease.
qb_cog_015.pearl: Cholinesterase inhibitors for mild-to-moderate AD; add memantine for moderate-to-severe disease.
qb_cog_015.evidence: t_neurocog.md 'Acute inpatient management' — Cognitive symptoms: cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) for mild–moderate Alzheimer/Lewy body disease; add memantine (NMDA antagonist) for moderate–severe disease.

qb_cog_016.stem: A 73-year-old woman with recurrent major depression (last treated 5 years ago) is referred for cognitive evaluation after 3 months of 'memory problems.' On formal cognitive testing she scores in the impaired range on delayed recall but consistently answers 'I don't know' rather than confabulating; she is slow to initiate answers and appears effortfully disengaged. She remains alert and attentive, and scores 22 on the PHQ-9. Most appropriate next step?

options.t: Diagnose major neurocognitive disorder — the cognitive test scores confirm a dementia syndrome independent of mood.

trap.name: Scores = diagnosis
trap.note: Cognitive test performance in the context of active major depression does not establish dementia — scores may normalize with successful mood treatment in pseudodementia.

options.t: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor — the episodic memory impairment indicates Alzheimer-spectrum disease requiring pharmacotherapy.

trap.name: Treat the number, not the patient
trap.note: Cholinesterase inhibitors are not indicated until reversible causes, including depression, are excluded — treating the score without treating the depression is the error.

options.t: Order an amyloid PET scan — direct amyloid visualization definitively distinguishes depression-associated cognitive impairment from Alzheimer disease.

trap.name: Jump to advanced imaging
trap.note: Amyloid PET is a research and specialist tool, not a first-line workup step — the well-established clinical approach is to treat the depression and reassess cognition.

options.t: Prioritize treatment of the depressive episode and reassess cognitive function after remission — the pattern of 'I don't know' responses, effortful disengagement, and a PHQ-9 of 22 is consistent with pseudodementia that may resolve with antidepressant treatment.

qb_cog_016.why: Scores = diagnosis, Treat the number not the patient, and Jump to advanced imaging all bypass the pseudodementia maneuver. 'I don't know' responses with effortful disengagement and preserved alertness — rather than confabulation and unawareness — is the clinical signature of depression-associated cognitive impairment (Caine 1981). The correct next step is antidepressant treatment and follow-up cognitive assessment.
qb_cog_016.pearl: Pseudodementia: 'I don't know' with effortful disengagement and preserved alertness — treat the depression first and reassess cognition; scores may fully normalize.
qb_cog_016.evidence: t_geri.md — Depression can masquerade as cognitive impairment — the pseudodementia presentation (Caine 1981), where patients say 'I don't know' rather than confabulate, show effortful disengagement, and improve cognitively when mood is treated.

qb_saf_003.stem: A 22-year-old man is admitted following a suicide attempt by acetaminophen overdose. When the student asks about means restriction, he asks only: 'Do you have access to anything dangerous at home?' The patient answers 'no.' The attending asks what a complete means safety assessment requires. Which response is best?

options.t: Ask the patient if he feels safe returning home — a verbal assurance of safety constitutes adequate means restriction documentation.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: A general feeling-of-safety answer is not a means safety assessment — specific items must be asked about explicitly and the plan for restriction must be named.

options.t: Ask specifically about firearms, stockpiled medications, sharps and ligatures, and who will remove or secure each item — then ask how it will be confirmed before discharge.
Have the patient and family sign a no-harm contract — a signed document constitutes the means safety plan.

trap.name: Safety plan = discharge permission slip
trap.note: No-harm contracts are not evidence-based as a risk-reduction measure and do not substitute for specific, actionable means restriction counseling.

options.t: Document 'means safety discussed' in the note — documenting the discussion fulfills the clinical obligation.

trap.name: Document and continue
trap.note: 'Means safety discussed' without specifying the items addressed and the restriction plan is weak documentation that does not fulfill the clinical obligation.

qb_saf_003.why: Face-value reassurance and Document and continue are both documentation traps. Means safety requires asking by item — firearms, stockpiled medications, sharps, ligatures, and the patient-specific methods the presentation revealed — and confirming who will secure them and how the team will know it happened. A general safety question or a no-harm contract does not accomplish this.
qb_saf_003.pearl: Means safety = ask by item (firearms, medications, sharps), name who will secure them, and confirm how the team will know.
qb_saf_003.evidence: pg_suicide.md 'Means Safety' — Ask specifically. Do not say only 'we discussed safety.' Include: Firearms. Stockpiled medication. Sharps or ligatures when relevant. Who will remove/secure means. How it will be confirmed.

qb_saf_004.stem: A 45-year-old man with schizophrenia and two prior suicide attempts is admitted for worsening command hallucinations telling him to jump. He is calm on exam; he reports the voices are 'quieter today' and denies current intent. Which statement best reflects how to frame his suicide risk?

options.t: His current denial of suicidal intent indicates low acute risk — patient self-report is the most reliable indicator of imminent safety.

trap.name: Denies SI = low risk
trap.note: Denial of intent in the context of active command hallucinations and prior attempts is not sufficient to conclude low acute risk — command hallucinations are an explicit acute risk factor.

options.t: His prior attempts are the most important factor and define his overall risk level — chronic factors drive the primary assessment.

trap.name: Denies SI = low risk
trap.note: Chronic factors establish the floor but acute factors — active command hallucinations — are the focus for this admission; relying on chronic factors alone misses the immediate targets.

options.t: His schizophrenia diagnosis independently elevates his risk to high — a psychiatric diagnosis drives the risk classification.

trap.name: Diagnosis = high risk
trap.note: A psychiatric diagnosis is a chronic risk factor, not a standalone determination of the acute risk level — the formulation must address both tiers separately.

options.t: Separate chronic risk (prior attempts, schizophrenia — the floor) from acute risk (active command hallucinations — the current target); the formulation must address both tiers and identify the modifiable acute drivers.

qb_saf_004.why: Denies SI = low risk in two forms and Diagnosis = high risk all produce single-tier formulations that miss the key structure. Risk formulation separates the chronic floor (prior attempts, schizophrenia) from the acute drivers (command hallucinations, current voices) that are the admission's targets. Command hallucinations are explicitly listed as an acute risk factor; denial of intent does not neutralize them.
qb_saf_004.pearl: Separate chronic and acute risk — prior attempts and a psychiatric diagnosis set the floor; command hallucinations and current intent are the acute targets.
qb_saf_004.evidence: pg_suicide.md 'Separate Chronic And Acute Risk' — Acute risk: current intent or plan; psychosis or command hallucinations. Chronic risk: prior attempts; chronic psychiatric illness.

qb_saf_005.stem: A 38-year-old woman is admitted after a near-lethal suicide attempt. She has three young children and is an ICU nurse. A student notes 'strong family ties and professional identity' as protective factors and proposes these substantially mitigate her acute risk. The attending asks the student to refine this reasoning. Which statement is most accurate?

options.t: The number of protective factors is inversely proportional to acute risk — more factors reliably indicate lower risk.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: The number of protective factors does not reliably predict acute risk — their credibility and availability during the risk window are what matter, not the count.

options.t: Protective factors reduce risk only if they are credible and available during the risk window — family who cannot be reached does not help in a crisis.
Professional status significantly reduces suicide risk — healthcare workers have lower suicide death rates than the general population.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: Healthcare workers do not have lower suicide death rates — female nurses die by suicide at about twice the rate of women in the general population (Davis, JAMA Psychiatry 2021), and professional identity may create barriers to seeking help rather than functioning as a protective factor.

options.t: Protective factors and acute risk factors can be numerically compared — strong protective factors offset recent preparatory behavior in the calculation.

trap.name: Safety plan = discharge permission slip
trap.note: Protective factors and acute risk factors are not numerically additive — protective factors must be evaluated for real-time credibility, and preparatory behavior is a hard escalation indicator.

qb_saf_005.why: Face-value reassurance appears throughout. Protective factors are not protective if they are geographically distant, unavailable, or theoretically present but non-operative during the crisis. Healthcare worker status does not protect against suicide. The page states explicitly: 'Protective factors are not magic. They matter only if they are credible and available during the risk window.'
qb_saf_005.pearl: Protective factors matter only if they are credible and available during the risk window — not as a list, but as real-time assets.
qb_saf_005.evidence: pg_suicide.md — Protective factors are not magic. They matter only if they are credible and available during the risk window.

qb_saf_006.stem: A student is asked to draft the safety note for a patient admitted with active suicidal ideation, a stated plan, and unsecured firearm access. Which of the following best illustrates strong safety documentation?

options.t: "Patient endorses suicidal ideation. Reviewed the risks, benefits, and alternatives of hospitalization with the patient at length; patient verbalizes understanding of the plan and agrees to continued treatment on the inpatient unit."

trap.name: Document and continue
trap.note: Consent documentation does not substitute for a safety formulation — reviewing risks and benefits of hospitalization does not record chronic factors, acute drivers, protective factor limits, or modifiable targets.

options.t: "Denies SI/HI. No acute safety concerns."

trap.name: Denies SI = low risk
trap.note: This is the prototypical weak documentation: it records a denial without any formulation, omits the known risk factors, and provides no reasoning for the safety decision.

options.t: "Acute suicide risk elevated: active plan, persistent insomnia, escalating alcohol use, unsecured firearms. Chronic risk: prior attempt, family history. Targets: means restriction, substance stabilization. Continue inpatient care."
"Patient stated: 'I want to die and I have a gun at home.' Verbatim suicidal statement documented per policy."

trap.name: Quotes = documentation
trap.note: Verbatim quotes capture content but do not constitute a risk formulation — the clinician's reasoning about severity, modifying factors, and the safety plan is absent; a defensible note requires formulation, not just transcription.

qb_saf_006.why: Document and continue, Denies SI = low risk, and Quotes = documentation all replace formulation with something easier to write. Strong safety documentation names chronic factors, acute drivers, protective factors with limits (omitted in the keyed example for brevity — add them), modifiable targets, and the current plan. 'Denies SI/HI. No acute safety concerns.' is the example the page uses for the weakest possible documentation.
qb_saf_006.pearl: Strong safety documentation = chronic factors + acute drivers + protective factors with limits + modifiable targets + current plan — not 'denies SI/HI.'
qb_saf_006.evidence: pg_suicide.md 'Documentation Sentence' — Strong: [detailed formulation with acute risk factors, chronic risk, means safety status, and plan]. Weak: 'Denies SI/HI. No acute safety concerns.'

qb_saf_007.stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the inpatient unit after a self-reported suicide attempt. On arrival she is visibly intoxicated with alcohol. The student is attempting to complete an initial risk assessment. Which of the following best describes the correct approach?

options.t: Escalate to the attending immediately — intoxication is an explicit escalation trigger; a reliable risk assessment cannot be completed while she is intoxicated, and medical monitoring is required.
Complete the risk assessment now — gathering history while the patient can still speak is more important than waiting for sobriety.

trap.name: Assess before escalate
trap.note: A meaningful risk assessment cannot be conducted while the patient is intoxicated — the acute safety priority is medical monitoring and attending notification, not history-taking.

options.t: Document 'unable to assess due to intoxication' and defer further evaluation to the morning team.

trap.name: Document and continue
trap.note: Deferring without escalating creates an unmonitored safety gap — intoxication is an escalation trigger requiring immediate attending notification, not a deferred entry.

options.t: Reassure the patient that alcohol often exaggerates suicidal statements and that a full assessment in the morning will clarify her actual risk level.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: Alcohol is an acute risk factor that amplifies risk, not a minimizer — intoxication during a period of expressed suicidal intent requires immediate escalation, not reassurance.

qb_saf_007.why: Assess before escalate and Face-value reassurance both produce the same error: treating an escalation trigger as a reason to delay action. Intoxication is explicitly listed on the card as 'what to escalate immediately.' Document and continue creates an unmonitored gap. The correct approach is immediate attending notification, with the formal risk assessment deferred to sobriety.
qb_saf_007.pearl: Intoxication during active suicidal ideation is an escalation trigger — notify the attending now; complete the formal risk assessment after sobriety.
qb_saf_007.evidence: pg_suicide.md 'What To Escalate Immediately' — Intoxication or withdrawal.

qb_saf_008.stem: A medical student is alone with a patient who says: 'I feel so much better — can you put in a good word with the team about going home today?' The student has not been briefed on this patient's risk. Which response is most appropriate?

options.t: Affirm to the patient that she appears improved and will relay this to the team, then complete a brief suicide screen to provide the team with an update.

trap.name: Student clears patient
trap.note: Affirming improvement to the patient and conducting an independent assessment crosses the student role boundary — the student cannot produce or communicate a dispositive safety determination.

options.t: Explain that discharge is the team's decision, then complete and document a formal suicide risk assessment in the medical record based on this conversation.

trap.name: Student clears patient
trap.note: Independently completing and documenting a formal risk assessment in the chart is well outside the student role — the student's job is to gather and relay the patient's report to the team, not to produce a signed clinical assessment.

options.t: Reassure the patient that the team is working toward discharge and provide the hospital's crisis line number.

trap.name: Reassure and defer
trap.note: Providing a crisis line to an admitted patient implies discharge is coming; the student is implying endorsement of a decision the team hasn't made, without any supervisory loop.

options.t: Tell the patient that discharge is the team's decision and that you will let the attending know she wants to discuss it — then inform the team promptly.

qb_saf_008.why: Student clears patient in two forms — direct affirmation and independent documentation — both cross the role boundary. The student's role is to ask, observe, and report to the team — not to clear a patient for discharge or to produce an independent safety assessment. Reassure and defer leaves the student in a limbo of implied endorsement without any supervisory loop.
qb_saf_008.pearl: Students can ask, observe, and report to the team — they cannot independently clear a patient for discharge or conduct a solo risk assessment.
qb_saf_008.evidence: pg_suicide.md 'Student Role' — You cannot: Clear a patient for discharge independently.

qb_saf_009.stem: A patient placed in physical restraints 4 hours ago following an agitation episode is now calm, cooperative, and asking to be released. His nurse pages the on-call student. Which of the following best reflects the correct management principle?

options.t: Continue the restraints through the end of the shift to ensure safety is maintained across the nursing team handoff.

trap.name: Restraint as stability
trap.note: Restraints are not a shift-duration safety measure — they must be discontinued the moment the patient is safe, regardless of shift timing.

options.t: Notify the attending immediately — the patient's calm state and request to be released require prompt reassessment; restraints must be discontinued as soon as the patient is safe, not held to shift end.
Ask the patient to demonstrate he can remain calm for 30 minutes, then release him and document the trial.

trap.name: Restraint as stability
trap.note: Imposing a time-contingent test before release inverts the standard — the principle is discontinue as soon as safe, not apply additional criteria.

options.t: Since the original physician order is still active, no action is needed until the order expires.

trap.name: Order = permission to continue
trap.note: A restraint order requires continuous time-limited review — a patient who is calm and requesting release must be reassessed immediately, not held to order expiration.

qb_saf_009.why: Restraint as stability in two forms and Order = permission both treat the order as a static permission. Restraint is a time-limited safety measure requiring a physician order, continuous monitoring, and discontinuation the moment the patient is safe — the page explicitly states 'not the end of a shift.' The student's correct action is immediate attending notification so the reassessment can happen.
qb_saf_009.pearl: Restraints require time-limited orders, continuous monitoring, and discontinuation as soon as the patient is safe — not the end of a shift.
qb_saf_009.evidence: agitation.md 'Restraint and seclusion' — They require a time-limited physician order, close and continuous monitoring, and discontinuation the moment the patient is safe — not the end of a shift.

qb_saf_010.stem: A team is debriefing after a physical restraint episode involving a Black patient on the inpatient unit. A student asks what the published evidence shows about racial disparities in restraint use in inpatient psychiatry. Which statement correctly reflects the data?

options.t: Black patients are restrained at similar rates to White patients after adjusting for clinical acuity — the apparent disparity is explained by severity of presentation and does not belong in the post-restraint debrief.

trap.name: No disparity exists
trap.note: The disparity persists after adjustment for measured clinical factors — adjustment cannot rule out every residual confounder, but a disparity that survives it is treated as a quality-of-care issue.

options.t: Black patients are more likely to receive verbal de-escalation before physical restraint — the data show greater resource deployment, not disparity.

trap.name: No disparity exists
trap.note: The evidence shows the opposite — Black patients face higher adjusted odds of physical restraint, not more de-escalation.

options.t: Black patients faced roughly 1.85× the adjusted odds of a restraint event in a large inpatient psychiatric sample — a disparity that persists after adjustment and should be treated as a quality-of-care issue.
Joint Commission non-discrimination standards adopted in 2015 have eliminated racial disparities in restraint use.

trap.name: No disparity exists
trap.note: The disparity is ongoing and documented — regulatory standards have not eliminated it.

qb_saf_010.why: No disparity exists in three forms. The page explicitly states: 'Black patients face roughly 1.85× the adjusted odds of a restraint event on inpatient psychiatric units (Singal et al., Psychiatric Services 2024), and higher adjusted odds of physical and chemical restraint during emergency psychiatric evaluation in the ED as well (aOR ~1.35; Smith et al., Psychiatric Services 2022) — that disparity is a quality-of-care issue, not a footnote.' Singal et al. is one health system's retrospective chart review (adolescents and adults), so adjustment cannot exclude residual confounding by acuity: the defensible claim is a disparity that persists after adjustment, and the page frames it as belonging in a post-restraint debrief.
qb_saf_010.pearl: In a large inpatient psychiatric sample, Black patients faced ~1.85× the adjusted odds of a restraint event — a disparity that persists after adjustment and belongs in every post-restraint debrief.
qb_saf_010.evidence: agitation.md 'Restraint and seclusion' — Black patients face roughly 1.85× the adjusted odds of a restraint event on inpatient psychiatric units (Singal et al., Psychiatric Services 2024), and higher adjusted odds of physical and chemical restraint during emergency psychiatric evaluation in the ED as well (aOR ~1.35; Smith et al., Psychiatric Services 2022) — that disparity is a quality-of-care issue, not a footnote.

qb_saf_011.stem: A patient with mania is pacing loudly in the hallway, slamming cabinet doors, and making hostile comments toward staff. He has not made a direct threat or moved toward anyone. You are the student and the first person to encounter him. Which response is best?

options.t: Signal a nearby staff member that you are approaching, then step calmly into the hallway — not blocking his exit — introduce yourself and acknowledge his frustration: 'I can see you're really upset right now. What's going on?' Then offer a choice of where to speak.
Return to the nursing station and request an involuntary IM medication order before approaching, so the team is ready to intervene.

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Medication is not the default first step when verbal de-escalation has not been attempted and no imminent threat exists — the framework starts with presence and listening.

options.t: Stand in the doorway and firmly instruct him to return to his room or further action will be taken.

trap.name: Commands over choices
trap.note: Issuing a command removes the patient's sense of control — the de-escalation framework centers offering choices, not issuing directives.

options.t: Alert the restraint team and position staff at the hallway exits in case the patient escalates.

trap.name: Restraint first
trap.note: Preemptively positioning the restraint team before de-escalation has been attempted violates least-restrictive principle when no imminent threat has occurred.

qb_saf_011.why: Agitation = antipsychotic, Commands over choices, and Restraint first are three forms of reaching for escalation before de-escalation. The Project BETA framework starts with calm presence, acknowledgment, genuine choices, and listening. The student also needs to stay near the exit and never block the patient's — personal safety and de-escalation are not competing goals. A student encountering an agitated patient should signal a staff member before engaging — personal safety and de-escalation are complementary, not competing goals.
qb_saf_011.pearl: Calm presence + acknowledging distress + offering choices = the first move in de-escalation; stay near your exit and never block the patient's.
qb_saf_011.evidence: agitation.md 'Verbal de-escalation, first' — The Project BETA de-escalation framework (Richmond et al. 2012) centers respect, simple boundaries, listening, and offering choices rather than issuing commands.

qb_saf_012.stem: A 67-year-old man with no psychiatric history, admitted for pneumonia, begins shouting at night and pulling at his oxygen tubing. He is combative with staff. The on-call resident asks the student how to approach this. What is the most appropriate first frame?

options.t: Start an antipsychotic immediately and then search for the cause — treating the agitation reduces the risk of self-harm while the workup proceeds.

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Reaching for the antipsychotic before identifying the driver is the error — non-pharmacologic and cause-directed management comes first even in hyperactive presentations.

options.t: Initiate a CIWA-Ar protocol — nighttime agitation in an older admitted patient is most likely alcohol withdrawal.

trap.name: It's just withdrawal
trap.note: Alcohol withdrawal is on the differential but imposing a specific protocol before the actual driver is identified may apply the wrong treatment to the wrong cause.

options.t: Apply soft restraints and then assess — the agitation puts both the patient and staff at immediate risk.

trap.name: Restraint first
trap.note: Restraints are the last resort after lesser measures have failed or are clearly inadequate — applying them before cause-finding and de-escalation bypasses the entire ladder.

options.t: Name the question: 'What is driving this agitation?' — systematic evaluation for delirium, substance withdrawal, medication effects (akathisia, steroids), pain, hypoxia, urinary retention, and fear must precede any pharmacologic decision.

qb_saf_012.why: Agitation = antipsychotic, It's just withdrawal, and Restraint first all skip cause-finding. Agitation is a symptom. The standard is to name the driver — delirium, withdrawal, akathisia, pain, hypoxia, retention, fear — before selecting an intervention. Pharmacotherapy, if needed, then matches the cause.
qb_saf_012.pearl: Agitation is always a symptom — name the driver before selecting the intervention; the treatment should match the cause.
qb_saf_012.evidence: agitation.md 'Find the driver' — Before you decide what to do, ask what is producing this. The usual drivers are delirium, intoxication or withdrawal, an acute psychotic or manic process, akathisia, unrelieved pain, and a fear or trauma response. 'High-yield pearls' — Agitation is a symptom — always ask 'what is driving this?' before 'what do we give?'

tier2.q: Why does matching the treatment to the agitation driver matter so much in an older medical patient?

options.t: Older patients cannot metabolize antipsychotics — any dose will cause over-sedation regardless of indication.

Benzodiazepines are preferred over antipsychotics in older adults when a calming agent is needed — their rapid onset and lower risk of EPS make them the safer pharmacologic choice after non-pharmacologic measures fail.

trap.name: Benzodiazepines preferred in older adults
trap.note: Benzodiazepines are appropriate for alcohol or sedative withdrawal, but deepen most other causes of delirium in older adults — using them when the driver is unknown or medical risks worsening the underlying cause, not treating it.

options.t: The wrong treatment can worsen the driver: benzodiazepines deepen most delirium; antipsychotics can precipitate NMS in unexcluded catatonia; treating withdrawal incorrectly can cause seizures — mismatching agent to cause produces iatrogenic harm.
Pharmacotherapy is inappropriate in all older patients — verbal de-escalation is the only evidence-based approach regardless of driver.

tier2.why: It is a drug–driver matching principle. Benzodiazepines are correct for alcohol/sedative withdrawal and dangerous in most other delirium. Antipsychotics are appropriate for dangerous agitation in non-catatonic, non-LBD states and dangerous if catatonia or LBD is present. Analgesics resolve pain-driven agitation that no psychotropic would touch. The wrong drug in the wrong patient makes the agitation worse — the paradigm case being benzodiazepines deepening delirium in a delirious elder.

qb_sud_003.stem: A 57-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder is admitted through the ED with altered mental status. The nurse establishes IV access and is preparing to infuse D5W. He appears malnourished and confused. Which step must occur before the glucose infusion is started?

options.t: Start a CIWA-Ar protocol — the altered mental status indicates active alcohol withdrawal requiring immediate benzodiazepine dosing.

trap.name: It's just withdrawal
trap.note: Starting symptom-triggered withdrawal treatment is appropriate, but thiamine should go in before or with the glucose — carbohydrate loading in a thiamine-depleted patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.

options.t: Obtain a CT head to exclude intracranial pathology before administering any fluids.

trap.name: Imaging before treatment
trap.note: Imaging may be appropriate if there are focal deficits, but the immediate priority is empiric treatment — thiamine before or with the glucose — which cannot wait for CT.

options.t: Administer IV thiamine before or together with the glucose-containing fluids — carbohydrate loading in a thiamine-depleted patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.
Confirm blood alcohol level — management depends on whether the AMS is from intoxication or withdrawal.

trap.name: Labs before treatment
trap.note: A BAL may guide management but does not change the immediate thiamine requirement — carbohydrate loading without thiamine in a depleted patient is what precipitates Wernicke.

qb_sud_003.why: It's just withdrawal and Imaging before treatment both bypass the cheap, time-critical intervention: thiamine given before or together with the glucose. Wernicke encephalopathy — confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia — can be precipitated when carbohydrate is infused into a thiamine-depleted nervous system. Here the D5W is routine maintenance and nothing is lost by giving thiamine with it. Read the rule correctly, though: in symptomatic hypoglycemia the dextrose goes in immediately and the thiamine goes in with it, because delayed correction of hypoglycemia causes its own neuronal injury.
qb_sud_003.pearl: Thiamine before or with glucose in any malnourished or alcohol-dependent patient — but never delay emergent dextrose for documented hypoglycemia; give thiamine alongside.
qb_sud_003.evidence: t_sud.md — Give thiamine before or with glucose; administering carbohydrate to a thiamine-depleted patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy, and the sequencing never justifies withholding emergency dextrose.

qb_sud_004.stem: A 46-year-old woman is admitted for alcohol detoxification. Her CIWA-Ar score is 16 on admission. A nurse asks how benzodiazepines should be dosed for alcohol withdrawal management on this unit. Which approach is correct?

options.t: Symptom-triggered dosing guided by serial CIWA-Ar scores — administer benzodiazepines when the score crosses a threshold and escalate monitoring for seizure or delirium tremens risk.
A fixed-schedule taper starting at maximum dose for 5 days regardless of symptoms — scheduled dosing prevents breakthrough withdrawal.

trap.name: Scheduled over symptom-triggered
trap.note: Fixed-schedule dosing tends to over-sedate patients with mild withdrawal and is not the guideline-recommended approach; symptom-triggered CIWA-Ar dosing is preferred.

options.t: Administer benzodiazepines only if a seizure occurs — prophylactic dosing is not supported by evidence.

trap.name: Underestimate the emergency
trap.note: A CIWA-Ar of 16 indicates moderate withdrawal; waiting for a seizure before treating is dangerous — seizure prevention is the goal.

options.t: Use a non-benzodiazepine anticonvulsant such as phenobarbital as first-line — benzodiazepines are contraindicated in alcohol withdrawal due to cross-tolerance.

trap.name: Contraindication confusion
trap.note: Benzodiazepines are the first-line treatment for alcohol withdrawal precisely because of GABAergic cross-tolerance — cross-tolerance is the therapeutic mechanism, not a contraindication.

qb_sud_004.why: Scheduled over symptom-triggered, Underestimate the emergency, and Contraindication confusion are all active. Symptom-triggered CIWA-Ar–guided benzodiazepine dosing is the standard for alcohol withdrawal — it provides treatment when needed, avoids over-sedation, and maintains vigilance for the lethal end of the spectrum (seizures, delirium tremens).
qb_sud_004.pearl: Alcohol withdrawal: CIWA-Ar–driven, symptom-triggered benzodiazepines — escalate monitoring for seizure and DT risk.
qb_sud_004.evidence: t_sud.md — For alcohol withdrawal, score serially with the CIWA-Ar and treat symptom-driven with benzodiazepines, escalating vigilance for seizures and delirium tremens in high-risk patients.

qb_sud_005.stem: A 28-year-old man with opioid use disorder requests buprenorphine. He last used heroin 5 hours ago and reports mild cramping but looks comfortable. His COWS score is 5. He says, 'I'm ready to start — please give it now.' What is the most appropriate response?

options.t: Start buprenorphine now — early induction prevents relapse and meeting the patient's readiness is clinically more important than withdrawal scoring.

trap.name: Comfort-first induction
trap.note: Starting buprenorphine before objective withdrawal is present risks precipitated withdrawal — buprenorphine displaces residual full agonist from receptors and can precipitate severe withdrawal if opioids are still present.

options.t: Wait for objective withdrawal (COWS roughly ≥8–12) before standard induction — starting now risks precipitated withdrawal.
Administer a test dose of buprenorphine 0.5 mg and observe for 30 minutes — a small test dose avoids precipitated withdrawal.

trap.name: Comfort-first induction
trap.note: Any buprenorphine dose before adequate objective withdrawal risks precipitated withdrawal — the scoring threshold is the safety check, not a half-dose adjustment.

options.t: Refuse buprenorphine and offer clonidine instead — clonidine is safer in the early withdrawal window.

trap.name: Non-MOUD for OUD
trap.note: Clonidine addresses symptoms but has no evidence for reducing overdose risk or supporting recovery — MOUD (buprenorphine or methadone) is the goal; the issue is timing, not substitution.

qb_sud_005.why: Comfort-first induction in two forms is the central trap. Buprenorphine is a partial agonist with high receptor affinity — it displaces full agonists. If taken before sufficient withdrawal, it precipitates sudden, severe withdrawal. The COWS threshold (≥8–12) makes it likely that residual full agonist has cleared enough receptors for induction to be tolerated — though with fentanyl, precipitated withdrawal can still occur at these scores. Low-dose initiation is a separate, structured multi-day protocol — not a single test dose.
qb_sud_005.pearl: COWS ≥8–12 before buprenorphine induction — the scoring threshold prevents precipitated withdrawal, not patient readiness.
qb_sud_005.evidence: t_sud.md — Begin buprenorphine induction only once objective withdrawal is present (roughly COWS ≥8 to 12) to avoid precipitated withdrawal from displacing residual full agonist too early.

qb_sud_006.stem: A 34-year-old woman with cocaine use disorder presents with elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, and grandiosity beginning 2 days after she used cocaine heavily. The team wants to document a diagnosis of bipolar I disorder. Which statement best characterizes the diagnostic approach?

options.t: Bipolar I disorder should be diagnosed — the clinical picture is classic and the cocaine use is a separate comorbidity.

trap.name: Diagnose through intoxication
trap.note: Co-occurring psychiatric illness cannot be reliably diagnosed while the patient is within the acute intoxication or withdrawal window.

options.t: Stimulant-induced mood disorder is the only possible diagnosis — patients with SUD cannot be diagnosed with primary bipolar disorder.

trap.name: SUD excludes comorbidity
trap.note: Co-occurring bipolar disorder is common in SUD; the issue is timing — the acute window is not the right time to establish primary diagnosis, not that it is permanently excluded.

options.t: The decreased sleep alone confirms a manic episode distinct from stimulant effects.

trap.name: Single criterion = diagnosis
trap.note: Stimulant intoxication produces virtually identical symptoms to mania — a single criterion does not differentiate them.

options.t: A primary psychiatric diagnosis cannot be reliably established while the patient is within the acute intoxication or withdrawal window — stabilize medically, allow clearance, then reassess.

qb_sud_006.why: Diagnose through intoxication and SUD excludes comorbidity are the two opposing errors. The standard is clear: co-occurring psychiatric illness is the rule in SUD, but you cannot reliably diagnose a primary mood or psychotic disorder while the patient is acutely intoxicated or withdrawing — the symptoms are indistinguishable. Stabilize first, then reassess.
qb_sud_006.pearl: No primary psychiatric diagnosis while acutely intoxicated or withdrawing — stabilize first, then reassess.
qb_sud_006.evidence: t_sud.md — You cannot reliably diagnose a primary mood or psychotic disorder while the patient is acutely intoxicated or withdrawing.

qb_sud_008.stem: A 31-year-old man with opioid use disorder is being discharged after a brief admission for opioid intoxication. He declines to start buprenorphine during the admission. Which discharge intervention has the strongest direct evidence for preventing death in the weeks following discharge?

options.t: Refer to a residential rehabilitation program — structured environments eliminate the post-discharge overdose window.

trap.name: Referral without bridge
trap.note: Referral alone without immediate naloxone and MOUD linkage leaves the highest-risk window unaddressed — residential programs have wait times and the risk is immediate.

options.t: Prescribe clonidine for autonomic withdrawal symptoms — addressing physiological discomfort reduces relapse.

trap.name: Non-MOUD for OUD
trap.note: Clonidine addresses symptoms only and has no evidence for reducing overdose mortality — naloxone and MOUD linkage are the life-saving interventions.

options.t: Provide naloxone with overdose-prevention education and arrange linkage to medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD) before discharge.
Schedule a routine outpatient psychiatric follow-up in 4–6 weeks — continuity of care addresses the root causes of relapse.

trap.name: Routine follow-up adequate
trap.note: Routine follow-up in 4–6 weeks does not address the immediate post-discharge overdose window — naloxone and MOUD linkage are needed before the patient walks out.

qb_sud_008.why: Referral without bridge, Non-MOUD for OUD, and Routine follow-up adequate all fail to address the acute post-discharge window. Tolerance drops during admission; returning to a pre-admission dose now carries high overdose risk. Naloxone plus MOUD linkage before discharge is the concrete, evidence-based life-saving intervention named on the page.
qb_sud_008.pearl: Naloxone + MOUD linkage at discharge for every patient with opioid use disorder — the post-discharge window is the highest-risk period.
qb_sud_008.evidence: t_sud.md — Provide naloxone and overdose-prevention education to any patient at opioid risk and to their family. Arrange linkage to MOUD before the patient leaves, since the post-discharge window carries elevated overdose risk.

qb_sud_009.stem: A 52-year-old woman completes medically supervised alcohol detoxification and wants pharmacotherapy to support sobriety. She has normal renal and hepatic function and no contraindications. Which agents are FDA-approved, evidence-based first-line options for alcohol use disorder maintenance?

options.t: Naltrexone or acamprosate — both are FDA-approved pharmacotherapies with evidence for reducing relapse and supporting sobriety in alcohol use disorder.
A long-term benzodiazepine — GABAergic agents reduce alcohol craving through the same receptor mechanism as alcohol.

trap.name: The reflexive benzodiazepine
trap.note: Benzodiazepines are for acute withdrawal management, not maintenance sobriety — chronic use produces dependence and does not treat alcohol use disorder.

options.t: An SSRI — the anxiety and dysphoria underlying alcohol use are the primary drivers, and antidepressants address them.

trap.name: Treat the symptom not the disorder
trap.note: SSRIs are not first-line pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder; they may be appropriate for a co-occurring mood or anxiety disorder but do not replace naltrexone or acamprosate.

options.t: Valproate — mood stabilization reduces the emotional dysregulation and impulsivity that drive relapse.

trap.name: Off-label equals evidence-based
trap.note: Valproate is not FDA-approved for alcohol use disorder maintenance and is not the standard; naltrexone and acamprosate have the evidence base.

qb_sud_009.why: The reflexive benzodiazepine, Treat the symptom not the disorder, and Off-label equals evidence-based all miss the two agents the page explicitly names. Naltrexone (opioid antagonist — reduces reward) and acamprosate (GABA/glutamate modulation — reduces craving) are the established pharmacotherapies for maintaining sobriety in alcohol use disorder.
qb_sud_009.pearl: AUD maintenance pharmacotherapy: naltrexone or acamprosate — not benzodiazepines, not SSRIs alone.
qb_sud_009.evidence: t_sud.md — For ongoing alcohol use disorder, offer naltrexone or acamprosate.

qb_sud_010.stem: A patient with opioid use disorder says: 'I'm not an addict. I can stop whenever I want — it hasn't caused me any real problems.' You are the student conducting the initial interview using a motivational interviewing approach. Which response is best?

options.t: "That's not accurate — research shows that opioid use changes your brain's reward system in ways that make 'just stopping' very difficult. Let me explain what the evidence says."

trap.name: The righting reflex
trap.note: Arguing against the patient's self-assessment triggers sustain talk and damages the alliance — MI directs curiosity, not confrontation.

options.t: "I hear you saying it hasn't caused problems, but the data is clear — untreated opioid use disorder has a high mortality rate, and I want you to understand that risk."

trap.name: Quoting statistics at patients
trap.note: Presenting risk statistics as an argument for change produces resistance rather than engagement — MI meets ambivalence with curiosity rather than factual correction.

options.t: "I understand you feel that way. Before we go further, I need you to complete this substance use disorder questionnaire for our documentation."

trap.name: Process over person
trap.note: Redirecting to paperwork when the patient is expressing ambivalence misses an opportunity for motivational engagement and communicates that the form matters more than the conversation.

options.t: "It sounds like you feel like you have it handled. I'm curious — has there been any time when using has gotten in the way of something that mattered to you?"

qb_sud_010.why: The righting reflex and Quoting statistics at patients are the two forms of pushing for change that motivational interviewing specifically avoids — they produce resistance. Process over person abandons the conversation entirely. The correct response reflects the patient's frame, rolls with resistance, and opens a door with curiosity — the Volkow brain-disease model frames addiction as a brain condition requiring engagement rather than moral correction.
qb_sud_010.pearl: MI meets ambivalence with curiosity, not confrontation — reflect, don't argue; the righting reflex produces sustain talk.
qb_sud_010.evidence: t_sud.md — Use motivational interviewing to meet ambivalence with curiosity rather than confrontation. Frame the whole encounter through the Volkow brain-disease model of addiction.

qb_sud_011.stem: A 19-year-old man is admitted for heroin withdrawal. He is visibly distressed, diaphoretic, tachycardic, and requesting immediate medication. A colleague asks, 'Is this patient in danger?' Which response most accurately conveys the clinical urgency?

options.t: Yes, severely — opioid withdrawal can progress to respiratory depression and circulatory collapse.

trap.name: Not lethal = not treatable inverted
trap.note: Opioid withdrawal rarely causes respiratory depression or circulatory collapse — those are signs of ongoing intoxication, not withdrawal.

options.t: Minimal — opioid withdrawal is uncomfortable but medically benign; supportive care and reassurance are sufficient without formal pharmacotherapy.

trap.name: Not lethal = not treatable
trap.note: Dismissing opioid withdrawal as benign invites AMA discharge during the highest-overdose-risk window — untreated withdrawal is a driver of dangerous post-discharge behavior even if it is rarely directly fatal.

options.t: Opioid withdrawal is rarely fatal, but leaving it untreated risks AMA discharge into the highest overdose-risk window — the treatment imperative is engaging the patient in MOUD, not the withdrawal severity alone.
Yes — untreated opioid withdrawal routinely progresses to seizures and delirium, creating the same risk as alcohol withdrawal.

trap.name: It's just withdrawal
trap.note: Seizures and delirium are features of alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal, not opioid withdrawal — conflating their lethality misjudges the urgency of both.

qb_sud_011.why: Not lethal = not treatable in two forms frame this item. Opioid withdrawal itself is rarely lethal — but dismissing it as benign is a clinical error because untreated withdrawal drives AMA discharge at the moment when tolerance is lowest and overdose risk is highest. The urgency is engagement in MOUD, not hemodynamic management.
qb_sud_011.pearl: Opioid withdrawal: rarely fatal but drives AMA discharge into the highest-overdose-risk window — the treatment priority is MOUD engagement, not the withdrawal itself.
qb_sud_011.evidence: t_sud.md — Opioid and stimulant withdrawal are intensely uncomfortable but rarely lethal. Naloxone plus MOUD linkage at discharge is a concrete, evidence-based way to save a life.

tier2.q: Why does the post-discharge period carry elevated overdose risk after an opioid withdrawal episode?

options.t: Opioid withdrawal produces a lasting sensitization that amplifies the effect of future doses for weeks.
Withdrawal depletes endogenous endorphins, causing rebound pain that requires higher subsequent doses.
Tolerance decreases substantially during withdrawal — the dose used before admission now exceeds the lethal threshold for a less-tolerant brain.
Post-discharge overdose risk is from co-ingestant adulterants (e.g., fentanyl), not from tolerance changes.

tier2.why: Tolerance is not a fixed property — it decreases during a period of abstinence or withdrawal. The patient who used 100 mg of heroin daily before admission may now have the tolerance of a naive user. Returning to the same dose can cause fatal respiratory depression. This is why the discharge window is the highest-risk window, and why naloxone must be provided regardless of whether MOUD is initiated.

qb_sud_012.stem: A 56-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is brought in by EMS after being found unresponsive. Blood alcohol level is 0.22. He remains obtunded 45 minutes after arrival despite being stable. A colleague says, 'He's just drunk — let's monitor and wait.' Which response is most accurate?

options.t: Agree — a BAC of 0.22 fully accounts for the clinical picture in a patient with alcohol use disorder.

trap.name: It's just intoxication
trap.note: Alcohol tolerance in a chronic user makes BAC an unreliable guide to consciousness level — obtundation disproportionate to BAC in a chronic user warrants a broader workup.

options.t: Disagree — obtundation in a patient who uses alcohol requires workup for Wernicke encephalopathy, subdural hematoma, infection, hepatic encephalopathy, and co-ingestants before attributing to alcohol alone.
Agree — wait for the alcohol to metabolize, but plan to obtain a CT head if not improved in 4 hours.

trap.name: It's just intoxication
trap.note: Deferring the workup 4 hours is dangerous — a subdural or Wernicke cannot wait; the evaluation must be active, not deferred.

options.t: Disagree — the next step is naloxone administration to reverse any opioid co-ingestion before other workup is done.

trap.name: Reflex antidote
trap.note: Naloxone is appropriate if opioid co-ingestion is suspected clinically (miosis, respiratory depression), but empiric naloxone does not substitute for the full differential evaluation.

qb_sud_012.why: It's just intoxication in two forms: accepting alcohol as the only explanation and deferring to a 4-hour reassessment both delay a workup that could catch a treatable emergency. The page explicitly states that altered mental status in a patient who uses substances is never automatically 'just withdrawal' — the same principle applies to intoxication. The differential includes Wernicke, subdural, infection, hepatic encephalopathy, and polysubstance use.
qb_sud_012.pearl: AMS + alcohol use disorder = real differential; BAC does not close the workup — Wernicke, subdural, infection, and hepatic encephalopathy must be actively excluded.
qb_sud_012.evidence: t_sud.md — Altered mental status in a patient who uses substances is never automatically 'just withdrawal.' Keep these live: Wernicke encephalopathy, head injury/subdural hematoma, occult infection/sepsis, hepatic encephalopathy, and polysubstance use.

qb_sud_013.stem: A 64-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder and documented Child-Pugh B cirrhosis is admitted for alcohol withdrawal. CIWA-Ar is 14. The team considers using chlordiazepoxide for symptom-triggered dosing. A student identifies a safety concern. Which response is most accurate?

options.t: In significant hepatic impairment, long-acting benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam) accumulate due to impaired oxidative metabolism — lorazepam or oxazepam are preferred because they undergo direct glucuronidation, which is preserved in hepatic disease.
Benzodiazepines are contraindicated in alcohol withdrawal for patients with cirrhosis — use phenobarbital or an antipsychotic instead.

trap.name: Contraindication confusion
trap.note: Benzodiazepines are not contraindicated in cirrhosis — the concern is accumulation with long-acting agents; switching to lorazepam or oxazepam addresses the risk while maintaining appropriate treatment.

options.t: Chlordiazepoxide is preferred in liver disease — its long half-life provides smoother coverage than short-acting agents and prevents rebound.

trap.name: Long half-life equals smooth coverage
trap.note: The long half-life is the problem in hepatic impairment, not a benefit — impaired metabolism causes drug accumulation and over-sedation.

options.t: All benzodiazepines are equally affected by hepatic dysfunction — no single agent is preferred over another in cirrhosis.

trap.name: All drugs equal
trap.note: Benzodiazepines differ substantially in metabolic pathway — lorazepam and oxazepam undergo glucuronidation, which is preserved in cirrhosis, making them distinctly preferable.

qb_sud_013.why: Contraindication confusion and Long half-life equals smooth coverage are the two active errors. The clinical principle: lorazepam and oxazepam are preferred in hepatic impairment precisely because their glucuronidation pathway is preserved while oxidative metabolism (which processes chlordiazepoxide and diazepam) is impaired in cirrhosis. All drugs equal ignores a clinically important pharmacokinetic distinction.
qb_sud_013.pearl: Hepatic impairment + alcohol withdrawal: use lorazepam or oxazepam (glucuronidation preserved); avoid long-acting benzodiazepines that accumulate.
qb_sud_013.evidence: t_sud.md 'Benzodiazepine choice in hepatic impairment' — Lorazepam, oxazepam, and temazepam (the LOT drugs) bypass oxidative CYP450 metabolism; they are conjugated by glucuronidation, a pathway that is relatively preserved in cirrhosis, and produce no clinically significant active metabolites. Chlordiazepoxide and diazepam rely on hepatic oxidative metabolism and produce long-lived active metabolites that accumulate in significant hepatic impairment, risking progressive over-sedation and worsening hepatic encephalopathy (Schuckit, N Engl J Med 2014; Saitz, Alcohol Health Res World 1998).

qb_sud_014.stem: A 49-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder is admitted after a tonic-clonic seizure at home. He has a documented prior alcohol withdrawal seizure from two years ago. CIWA-Ar on arrival is 12. Which statement best characterizes his risk and clinical priority?

options.t: The seizure occurred before admission; since he is now calmer, observation without immediate pharmacologic intervention is appropriate.

trap.name: Underestimate the emergency
trap.note: A prior withdrawal seizure and a current CIWA-Ar of 12 indicate high risk for further seizures and progression to delirium tremens — this is not a wait-and-observe clinical picture.

options.t: The seizure risk has passed — withdrawal seizures occur in the first 24–48 hours; further seizures are not expected after a first event.

trap.name: Underestimate the emergency
trap.note: Post-seizure clinical presentation with a CIWA-Ar of 12 does not indicate that risk has passed — recurrent seizures and DT progression are the specific concern in this window.

options.t: Start a fixed-schedule antipsychotic — antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and provide targeted coverage for alcohol withdrawal psychosis.

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold — they are the wrong agent in a patient at active seizure risk from alcohol withdrawal; benzodiazepines are the treatment.

options.t: A prior withdrawal seizure predicts recurrence — give a benzodiazepine now with front-loaded or scheduled dosing and watch for DTs.

qb_sud_014.why: Underestimate the emergency in two forms, and Agitation = antipsychotic. Prior withdrawal seizure is explicitly the most robust predictor of future seizure risk. Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and are contraindicated for seizure prevention in alcohol withdrawal. Prompt benzodiazepine with front-loaded or fixed-schedule dosing, supplemented by CIWA-Ar-triggered doses, is the treatment, and DT vigilance is the priority. Score-gated dosing alone is not enough after a prior withdrawal seizure.
qb_sud_014.pearl: Prior withdrawal seizure = strong predictor of future seizures; give a benzodiazepine promptly with front-loaded or fixed-schedule dosing plus symptom-triggered supplementation (not score-gated dosing alone) + DT monitoring.
qb_sud_014.evidence: t_sud.md — Alcohol withdrawal: score serially with the CIWA-Ar and treat symptom-driven with benzodiazepines, escalating vigilance for seizures and delirium tremens in high-risk patients.

tier2.q: Why does abrupt alcohol cessation cause seizures, whereas opioid withdrawal does not?

options.t: Alcohol directly damages neurons, and the damaged cells become epileptogenic on cessation.
Opioid withdrawal does cause seizures, but at a lower incidence than alcohol withdrawal.

Alcohol downregulates GABA-A receptors with chronic use — abrupt cessation uncovers an unopposed glutamatergic hyperexcitable state, removing tonic GABAergic inhibition and generating the kindling-based seizure risk.
The seizure risk is from concurrent electrolyte disturbances (hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia), not from the alcohol withdrawal itself.

tier2.why: Chronic alcohol use potentiates GABA-A activity. In response, the brain compensatory downregulates GABA receptors and upregulates glutamate receptors. When alcohol is abruptly removed, the GABAergic brake is gone and the glutamatergic accelerator is overactive — the resulting hyperexcitability produces seizures and, at its worst, delirium tremens. Opioid withdrawal does not affect the seizure threshold through this mechanism — it causes autonomic distress but not neuronal hyperexcitability.

qb_pha_003.stem: A student argues that quetiapine should be chosen over haloperidol for a patient with psychosis because 'it's a second-generation agent and therefore more effective.' An attending asks what the CATIE trial established about this reasoning. Which response is most accurate?

options.t: The student is correct — second-generation antipsychotics have uniformly superior efficacy to first-generation agents in head-to-head trials.

trap.name: Newer = better
trap.note: CATIE found no consistent efficacy advantage for second-generation over first-generation agents — the differences between antipsychotics are primarily in side-effect profile.

options.t: CATIE showed that antipsychotics differ primarily in side-effect profile — metabolic effects, EPS, QTc, and prolactin — not in raw efficacy; agents should be chosen based on the patient's specific risk profile.
CATIE found that olanzapine is the most effective antipsychotic overall and should be the default first choice.

trap.name: Selective citation
trap.note: CATIE found olanzapine had better discontinuation rates in some analyses, but it was also the most metabolically harmful; the lesson is to choose by the full side-effect profile, not to default to olanzapine.

options.t: First-generation antipsychotics are preferred in first-episode psychosis because their longer evidence base makes them more predictable.

trap.name: Older = better
trap.note: The CATIE framing cuts both ways — neither generation is universally preferred; individual side-effect risk drives the choice.

qb_pha_003.why: Newer = better is the target trap. CATIE's fundamental lesson: the FGA/SGA distinction is not a reliable efficacy hierarchy. Choose by side-effect profile — the patient's metabolic risk, EPS vulnerability, QTc baseline, and prolactin sensitivity are the discriminating factors.
qb_pha_003.pearl: CATIE: choose antipsychotics by side-effect profile, not generation — no consistent efficacy advantage for SGAs over FGAs.
qb_pha_003.evidence: psychopharm_primer.md — The single most useful framing comes from CATIE: choose by side-effect profile, not by 'newer is better' — agents differ more in what they do to weight, glucose, lipids, prolactin, QTc, and movement than in raw efficacy.

qb_pha_004.stem: A 23-year-old man is starting risperidone for his first psychotic episode. The student is asked to set up his monitoring schedule. What does the standard require for ALL patients starting any antipsychotic?

options.t: Baseline ECG — all antipsychotics require cardiac clearance due to QTc prolongation risk.

trap.name: QTc always
trap.note: ECG is warranted when a QTc-prolonging agent is used or there is a cardiac history, but it is not mandatory for all antipsychotics; metabolic monitoring is the universal requirement.

options.t: Serum drug level at steady state — therapeutic monitoring ensures adequate receptor occupancy.

trap.name: Drug levels = necessary
trap.note: Antipsychotic serum levels are not routinely monitored for most agents in clinical practice; metabolic monitoring is the standard universal requirement.

options.t: Urine drug screen at baseline — substance use can confound both the psychotic presentation and antipsychotic response.

trap.name: Most relevant test first
trap.note: A urine drug screen may be clinically appropriate at admission but is not the monitoring requirement built into the antipsychotic prescription; metabolic monitoring is.

options.t: Baseline weight, fasting glucose, and lipid profile — then ongoing tracking; metabolic monitoring is part of the antipsychotic prescription for every agent.

qb_pha_004.why: QTc always, Drug levels = necessary, and Most relevant test first all substitute a different monitoring task for the universal one. Metabolic monitoring — baseline weight, glucose, and lipids, then tracking — is built into the antipsychotic prescription regardless of the agent chosen. The page explicitly states: 'metabolic monitoring is part of the prescription.'
qb_pha_004.pearl: Every antipsychotic: baseline weight, fasting glucose, lipids — then ongoing tracking. Metabolic monitoring is part of the prescription.
