qb_anx_010.stem: A 26-year-old combat veteran is admitted for a depressive episode. He is being interviewed by a female medical student when he abruptly terminates the interview and states he cannot continue. He has nightmares, is hypervigilant, and startle-reactive. The student asks the attending how to understand this behavior clinically. Which is most accurate?

options.t: The patient is likely psychotic — the refusal to engage with an examiner is a negative symptom or paranoia.

trap.name: Avoidance = psychosis
trap.note: Avoidance and refusal to engage in a specific context are PTSD hyperarousal and avoidance symptoms, not negative symptoms or paranoia; psychosis would require positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations) that are absent here.

options.t: The patient is non-adherent and should be counseled on the importance of clinical cooperation.

trap.name: Avoidance = non-compliance
trap.note: Framing trauma-driven avoidance as non-compliance places responsibility on the patient and misses the clinical diagnosis; the appropriate response is accommodating the trauma context, not counseling compliance.

options.t: This may represent a personality disorder — emotional dysregulation and interview termination suggest borderline features.

trap.name: Avoidance = personality disorder
trap.note: A veteran with nightmares, hypervigilance, startle response, and context-specific interview termination fits a PTSD pattern, not a personality disorder; personality pathology requires a pervasive pattern across contexts.

options.t: PTSD may surface as behavioral reactions to specific examiners or triggers; this combat veteran's avoidance of a female examiner is a recognized PTSD presentation — accommodate the trigger rather than pathologizing the refusal.

qb_anx_010.why: Avoidance = psychosis, Avoidance = non-compliance, and Avoidance = personality disorder all pathologize what is a PTSD-specific behavioral response. The page is explicit: 'PTSD may surface as hyperarousal, nightmares, or a behavioral reaction to restraint, seclusion, or a same-gender vs. opposite-gender examiner.' Accommodation (e.g., offering a male examiner) is the clinical response.
qb_anx_010.pearl: PTSD may present on the unit as interview refusal or agitation related to specific triggers (examiner gender, restraint, procedures) — accommodate the trigger rather than pathologizing the refusal.
qb_anx_010.evidence: t_anxiety.md — PTSD may surface as hyperarousal, nightmares, or a 'behavioral' reaction to restraint, seclusion, or a same-gender vs. opposite-gender examiner.

link.label: Open the Anxiety, OCD & Trauma page

qb_anx_011.stem: A 39-year-old woman with PTSD is ready for discharge after a brief inpatient stay. She was started on sertraline. The resident says, 'She's on an SSRI — she's set.' The attending asks the student to identify what is missing from this discharge plan.

options.t: She should also have a benzodiazepine prescription for acute anxiety management in the first few weeks after discharge.

trap.name: Discharge benzo for anxiety
trap.note: The page explicitly advises against leaving patients on standing benzodiazepines without an explicit time-limited rationale — adding a new benzodiazepine at discharge for PTSD is not the answer.

options.t: The discharge plan is complete — SSRIs are the evidence-based treatment for PTSD, and outpatient titration will complete the course.

trap.name: Medication alone is sufficient
trap.note: SSRIs are first-line pharmacotherapy for PTSD, but the page emphasizes that 'medication rarely finishes the job alone' — definitive treatment requires behavioral therapy (PE or CPT) delivered by a qualified outpatient clinician.

options.t: She needs a referral to outpatient therapy that can deliver prolonged exposure (PE) or cognitive processing therapy (CPT) — medication alone does not finish the job; the behavioral component is the definitive treatment for PTSD.
The sertraline dose should be maximized before discharge — achieving therapeutic dosing during inpatient stay makes outpatient follow-up less urgent.

trap.name: Maximize dose before discharge
trap.note: Maximizing the dose before discharge is not the standard; the missing component is the behavioral therapy referral — the discharge checklist requires confirming outpatient follow-up that can deliver evidence-based PTSD therapy, not just dose adjustment.

qb_anx_011.why: Discharge benzo for anxiety, Medication alone is sufficient, and Maximize dose before discharge all miss the key gap. The page states: 'Confirm the SSRI/SNRI is at a tolerated dose with a clear titration plan, and verify outpatient follow-up that can deliver ERP, PE, or CPT — the medication rarely finishes the job alone.' PE or CPT referral is the explicit discharge requirement.
qb_anx_011.pearl: Medication alone rarely finishes the PTSD treatment job — discharge requires a referral to outpatient PE or CPT; confirming the behavioral therapy access is a discharge criterion.
qb_anx_011.evidence: t_anxiety.md — Confirm the SSRI/SNRI is at a tolerated dose with a clear titration plan, and verify outpatient follow-up that can deliver ERP, PE, or CPT — the medication rarely finishes the job alone.

link.label: Open the Anxiety, OCD & Trauma page

qb_anx_012.stem: A student is preparing a PTSD psychoeducation handout and wants to explain the difference between prolonged exposure (PE) and cognitive processing therapy (CPT). Both are listed as evidence-based treatments in the patient's discharge plan. Which statement about the distinction is most accurate?

options.t: PE and CPT are the same treatment with different names used by different institutions.

trap.name: PE = CPT
trap.note: PE and CPT are distinct evidence-based protocols with different mechanisms and session structures; conflating them would leave patients unable to recognize which therapy they are receiving.

options.t: PE focuses on identifying and challenging maladaptive beliefs ('stuck points') about the trauma and its meaning; CPT focuses on repeated imaginal and in-vivo exposure to trauma-related memories and avoided stimuli.

trap.name: PE and CPT descriptions swapped
trap.note: The descriptions here are swapped — PE works through fear extinction via imaginal and in-vivo exposure to trauma cues; CPT targets cognitive 'stuck points' about safety, trust, and meaning. Knowing which mechanism belongs to which label is the key distinction.

options.t: PE focuses on gradual, repeated imaginal and in-vivo exposure to the trauma memory and avoided triggers to reduce conditioned fear; CPT targets cognitive stuck points — maladaptive beliefs about safety, trust, power, esteem, and intimacy altered by the trauma.
PE is behavioral (no cognitive component) and requires revisiting the trauma narrative; CPT is purely cognitive (no behavioral component) and avoids discussing the trauma entirely.

trap.name: Behavioral vs cognitive = entirely separate
trap.note: Both PE and CPT are cognitive-behavioral approaches with overlapping elements; CPT does include a trauma account component in some protocols, and PE includes cognitive elements — framing them as entirely separate is an oversimplification.

qb_anx_012.why: PE = CPT and Behavioral vs cognitive = entirely separate flatten the distinction. The page names both PE and CPT as first-line behavioral treatments for PTSD. Knowing that PE works through fear extinction via exposure and CPT works through cognitive restructuring of stuck points is the key clinical distinction for recommending or describing the referral.
qb_anx_012.pearl: PE = repeated exposure to trauma memory and avoided triggers; CPT = cognitive stuck points about safety/trust/esteem altered by trauma — both are first-line for PTSD, mechanisms differ.
qb_anx_012.evidence: t_anxiety.md — Definitive treatment is behavioral — ERP for OCD, PE/CPT for PTSD, interoceptive exposure for panic.

tier2.q: A patient with PTSD has significant disability from maladaptive beliefs — she believes she is permanently damaged, that the world is entirely unsafe, and that she was responsible for the assault. Which therapy would most directly target these specific cognitions?

options.t: Prolonged exposure (PE) — revisiting the trauma memory repeatedly reduces the activation tied to these beliefs through habituation and corrective experience.

Cognitive processing therapy (CPT) — directly targeting 'stuck points' (maladaptive appraisals about self, others, and the world) is the mechanism CPT was designed around, making it the more direct match for this cognitive profile.
DBT skills training — distress tolerance skills reduce the emotional activation that sustains these beliefs.
Exposure and response prevention (ERP) — gradual exposure to feared beliefs while preventing safety behaviors will extinguish the associated fear.

tier2.why: CPT is specifically designed around the 'stuck point' model: the idea that trauma disrupts assimilated beliefs about safety, trust, power, esteem, and intimacy, and that recovery requires directly challenging and revising these disrupted cognitions through structured written and verbal exercises. PE works primarily through fear extinction via repeated exposure to the trauma memory — it addresses the cognitions indirectly, through the corrective emotional experience of confronting the memory without harm. For a patient whose primary disability is cognitive (who I am now, is the world safe, was I responsible), CPT's direct targeting of these appraisals is the more mechanistically matched choice.

qb_eth_007.stem: During an outpatient psychiatry session, a 34-year-old man with schizophrenia (prominent persecutory delusions) states, 'I have a gun at home. When John Smith gets out of prison next month, I'm going to kill him.' John Smith is his estranged brother. Which action is most appropriate?

options.t: Act on the duty to protect — warn the victim, notify police, or hospitalize; confidentiality yields to this threat.
Maintain confidentiality — the threat is against a family member, and family threats are not covered by the Tarasoff duty.

trap.name: Family exception to Tarasoff
trap.note: There is no family exception to the duty to protect; a specific, credible threat to an identifiable person triggers the duty regardless of the relationship between patient and potential victim.

options.t: Document the threat and reassess at the next session — the duty to warn only applies to imminent threats.

trap.name: Imminence required for Tarasoff
trap.note: The Tarasoff duty does not require the threat to be imminent — a serious, credible threat to an identifiable victim (here, named with a specific plan) is sufficient to trigger the duty; waiting is not appropriate.

options.t: Consult with a supervisor and take no other action until legal counsel is contacted — clinicians must confirm the legal requirement before taking any action.

trap.name: Legal clearance required first
trap.note: While consultation is wise, clinicians do not need to wait for legal clearance before acting on an imminent safety obligation — the duty to protect is a clinical and legal standard, and delay can result in harm.

qb_eth_007.why: Family exception, Imminence required, and Legal clearance first all create barriers to a clinically required action. The page states: 'A specific threat to a specific person overrides confidentiality.' The duty to protect may be fulfilled by warning the victim, notifying police, hospitalizing the patient, or intensifying treatment — and specifics vary by state, but the tested principle is clear.
qb_eth_007.pearl: Tarasoff: a specific threat to an identifiable victim overrides confidentiality — warn, notify police, or hospitalize; inaction in a credible threat is not a safe option.
qb_eth_007.evidence: ethics_legal.md — A serious threat to an identifiable victim triggers a duty to protect (Tarasoff) — confidentiality yields.

qb_eth_008.stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician with multiple bruises in various stages of healing. His mother explains that he 'bruises easily.' The student suspects possible physical abuse but is uncertain. There are no obvious fractures, and the child denies being hurt. Which is the correct action?

options.t: Do not report yet — a definitive diagnosis of abuse must be established before filing a report, and reporting uncertainty could harm an innocent family.

trap.name: Proof required to report
trap.note: Mandatory reporting requires reasonable suspicion, not proof; waiting for certainty is not the standard and may leave the child unprotected.

options.t: File a mandatory report with child protective services immediately — mandatory reporters must report on reasonable suspicion, not proof, and good-faith reporters are legally protected.
Refer to a social worker and wait for a social assessment before deciding whether to report — the social worker's professional judgment supersedes the clinician's obligation.

trap.name: Social work replaces report
trap.note: Involving a social worker is appropriate and may be parallel to the report, but it does not replace the clinician's mandatory reporting obligation — mandated reporters are required to report independently of social work consultation.

options.t: Conduct a formal forensic assessment before reporting — premature reports reduce the accuracy of subsequent forensic interviews.

trap.name: Forensic assessment before report
trap.note: Forensic child abuse evaluations are an investigative step, not a prerequisite to reporting; the mandatory report initiates the protective process and must come before the formal forensic evaluation.

qb_eth_008.why: Proof required to report, Social work replaces report, and Forensic assessment before report all create delays in a child protection obligation. The page states: 'Reporting requires reasonable suspicion, not proof, and mandated reporters are generally protected when reporting in good faith.' Multiple healing bruises is reasonable suspicion; that is the threshold.
qb_eth_008.pearl: Mandatory reporting for child abuse requires reasonable suspicion, not proof — good-faith reporters are protected; report now and let CPS investigate.
qb_eth_008.evidence: ethics_legal.md — Report suspected child abuse or neglect and elder/dependent-adult abuse — reporting requires reasonable suspicion, not proof, and mandated reporters are generally protected when reporting in good faith.

qb_eth_003.stem: A 38-year-old man with schizophrenia is involuntarily hospitalized following an acute psychotic episode with danger to others. On day 2, he states that he refuses to take haloperidol. The team wants to medicate him over his objection because 'he's committed.' Which statement is most accurate?

options.t: Involuntary hospitalization authorizes involuntary medication — the commitment order supersedes the patient's medication refusal.

trap.name: Commitment = consent to medicate
trap.note: Commitment status does not equal consent to medication; this is explicitly stated in the ethics principles and is one of the most commonly tested distinctions in psychiatric ethics.

options.t: The team should use a shorter-acting intramuscular formulation — minimizing the degree of involuntary intervention makes the override ethically permissible.

trap.name: Route reduces ethical constraint
trap.note: Changing the route of administration does not change the ethical standard; the question is whether the refusal can be overridden, not how to make an unauthorized medication seem less coercive.

options.t: Involuntary hospitalization does NOT authorize involuntary medication; overriding the refusal requires either a true emergency (imminent danger) or a separate legal or adjudicated process independent of the commitment.
The patient's schizophrenia diagnosis implies impaired judgment — a psychiatric diagnosis automatically confers authority to override medication refusal.

trap.name: Diagnosis = impaired capacity
trap.note: A psychiatric diagnosis does not automatically negate capacity; capacity is decision-specific and clinical — a patient with schizophrenia may or may not have capacity for a specific medication decision, and capacity must be assessed, not assumed.

qb_eth_003.why: Commitment = consent to medicate, Route reduces ethical constraint, and Diagnosis = impaired capacity are all versions of the same error. The page is clear: 'Involuntary hospitalization does NOT by itself authorize involuntary medication.' Overriding refusal requires an imminent-danger emergency or a separate legal/adjudicated process. Commitment status and medication consent are independent legal states.
qb_eth_003.pearl: Commitment ≠ consent to medicate — involuntary hospitalization does not override medication refusal; a separate emergency or legal process is required.
qb_eth_003.evidence: ethics_legal.md — Involuntary hospitalization does NOT by itself authorize involuntary medication. Separate the four legal states: voluntary vs committed, and has-capacity vs court-determined-incompetent.

qb_eth_004.stem: A patient with delirium cannot provide coherent consent for an emergent procedure. The family asks if the patient 'has been declared incompetent.' The resident responds that the patient 'lacks capacity.' The family seems confused by the distinction. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.t: Capacity and competence are synonymous — they differ only in which professional makes the determination.

trap.name: Capacity = competence
trap.note: Capacity and competence are distinct on a critical dimension: who determines them. Conflating them misrepresents the legal process required for competence determination.

options.t: Competence is a clinical determination made by a physician or psychiatrist; capacity is a legal determination that requires a court order when the clinical team is uncertain about the patient's decision-making status.

trap.name: Clinical/legal assignment reversed
trap.note: This option has the legal/clinical assignment backwards — capacity is the clinical assessment made by any physician for a specific decision at a point in time; competence is what a court determines when formal legal adjudication is required.

options.t: Incompetence is determined by a psychiatrist through formal neuropsychological testing; capacity is determined by a court based on a jury's judgment.

trap.name: Roles reversed
trap.note: This option has the processes reversed — psychiatrists assess capacity clinically; courts determine competence; neuropsychological testing may inform the assessment but is not the standard definition.

options.t: Capacity is clinical and decision-specific — assessed by any physician for a particular decision at a point in time; competence is a legal determination made by a court, applicable more globally.

qb_eth_004.why: Capacity = competence, Description with keys swapped (B), and Roles reversed all miss the key discriminators. The page states: 'Capacity is decision-specific and clinical (a physician assesses it); competence is a legal determination (a court decides).' Option D captures both discriminators — the clinical/legal distinction AND the decision-specific nature of capacity.
qb_eth_004.pearl: Capacity = clinical, decision-specific (physician decides); competence = legal determination (court decides) — they are not interchangeable.
qb_eth_004.evidence: ethics_legal.md — Capacity is decision-specific and clinical (a physician assesses it); competence is a legal determination (a court decides).

qb_eth_005.stem: A 62-year-old man is informed of the risks, benefits, and alternatives of a recommended ECT course; his cognition is grossly intact on interview, though no formal capacity assessment has been documented. He is under no coercion and says, 'I understand what you've told me, and I want to have ECT.' Which component of informed consent has NOT yet been addressed?

options.t: He has expressed a choice — the consent is now complete because all required elements are present.

trap.name: Choice = consent
trap.note: Expressing a choice alone does not complete informed consent — three components are required: capacity, disclosure, and voluntariness. The question asks which has NOT been addressed; verifying all three requires checking capacity systematically.

options.t: The emergency exception permits ECT without formal consent in this case — ECT is a medical urgency.

trap.name: Emergency exception for ECT
trap.note: There is no emergency exception without an actual emergency — a cognitively intact patient recommending an elective ECT course requires standard informed consent; the emergency exception is for situations where consent cannot be obtained and delay causes harm.

options.t: Voluntariness has not been assessed — the stem confirms disclosure and that the patient made a choice, but does not confirm he is free from undue influence, coercion, or therapeutic misconception.

trap.name: Voluntariness fully assessed
trap.note: The stem says the patient 'is under no coercion' — voluntariness IS addressed; the missing component is different.

options.t: A formal clinical capacity assessment has not been explicitly performed — consent requires capacity, disclosure (risks/benefits/alternatives), and voluntariness; disclosure and voluntariness are confirmed in the stem, but capacity is asserted by the word 'intact cognition' without a documented four-ability assessment.

qb_eth_005.why: Choice = consent and Emergency exception for ECT overlook the structure of valid consent. Valid consent requires ALL three: capacity + disclosure + voluntariness. Disclosure is confirmed (risks/benefits/alternatives given), voluntariness is confirmed ('under no coercion'), but formal capacity documentation — the four abilities: communicate a choice, understand, appreciate, reason — is described as 'intact cognition' without a documented assessment. This is the gap.
qb_eth_005.pearl: Informed consent = capacity + disclosure + voluntariness — all three must be documented; 'intact cognition' is not the same as a documented capacity assessment.
qb_eth_005.evidence: ethics_legal.md — Valid consent requires capacity, disclosure (risks/benefits/alternatives), and voluntariness. The four abilities: communicate a choice, understand, appreciate, and reason.

qb_eth_006.stem: A 15-year-old presents to an outpatient clinic requesting evaluation and treatment for alcohol use disorder. He does not want his parents informed. His parents are alive, married, and have not relinquished guardianship. Which framework applies?

options.t: Parental consent is always required for minors — the 15-year-old cannot consent to or receive evaluation without parental involvement.

trap.name: Minor always requires parental consent
trap.note: Many jurisdictions allow minor-only consent for substance use treatment specifically — this is one of the statutory exceptions to the general parental consent rule for minors.

options.t: In many states, minors may consent to and receive substance use treatment without parental consent — this is one of the recognized statutory exceptions to the general parental consent rule; however, specific state law governs.
Since he is 15, he is an emancipated minor in most states — emancipation applies to all minors above age 14.

trap.name: Emancipation by age
trap.note: Emancipation is a legal status based on specific criteria (marriage, military service, court order), not simply being 14 or 15 years old; not all adolescents are emancipated.

options.t: Adolescent confidentiality cannot be protected in substance use treatment — HIPAA requires parental access to minor treatment records in all clinical contexts.

trap.name: HIPAA overrides minor confidentiality
trap.note: HIPAA defers to state law on minor confidentiality; when state law permits minor-only consent for substance use treatment, HIPAA permits corresponding confidentiality protections for that care.

qb_eth_006.why: Minor always requires parental consent, Emancipation by age, and HIPAA overrides minor confidentiality all misstate the legal framework. The page states: 'In many states, care for STIs, contraception, substance use, and some mental-health services' are exceptions to the general parental consent requirement. The correct answer acknowledges the exception while noting state variation.
qb_eth_006.pearl: In many states, minors can consent to substance use treatment without parental involvement — a recognized statutory exception, with state law governing the specifics. Consent to treat is not consent to disclose: the records are separately governed by 42 CFR Part 2.
qb_eth_006.evidence: ethics_legal.md — Parents/guardians generally consent for minors, with exceptions (emancipated/mature minors and, in many states, care for STIs, contraception, substance use, and some mental-health services).

qb_per_005.stem: A 27-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder is admitted following a suicide attempt by overdose. The treating team is considering starting lorazepam to help manage her emotional lability and distress between therapy sessions. Which evidence-based statement most accurately characterizes this plan?

options.t: Benzodiazepines should not be started for BPD symptoms or crisis distress — of the classes studied, they had the highest suicide risk.
A short 5-day lorazepam course is safe — the risk only applies to chronic outpatient benzodiazepine use, not brief inpatient administration.

trap.name: Inpatient benzos safe short-term
trap.note: The evidence does not exempt brief inpatient use; the Lieslehto 2023 data on benzodiazepines in BPD does not restrict the signal to outpatient or chronic use.

options.t: Benzodiazepines are acceptable in BPD when prescribed at the lowest effective dose — the risk-benefit ratio favors treatment for acute distress.

trap.name: Low dose = safe
trap.note: The page gives no dose-based exception — the recommendation is to avoid starting or escalating benzodiazepines for BPD symptoms or crisis distress; the risk-benefit calculation in this population does not favor initiation.

options.t: Lorazepam is first-line for BPD crisis management — emotional lability is its primary pharmacological target.

trap.name: Benzo for BPD emotional dysregulation
trap.note: No medication treats BPD itself; benzodiazepines are specifically contraindicated in this context, and emotional dysregulation is targeted through skills and DBT-informed approaches, not standing benzodiazepines.

qb_per_005.why: Inpatient benzos safe short-term, Low dose = safe, and Benzo for BPD emotional dysregulation all lead to starting a drug class to avoid for this indication. The rule, scoped as the key scopes it: never start or escalate benzodiazepines for BPD symptoms or crisis distress — highest risk of suicide attempt or suicide death of any class (Lieslehto 2023); reach for skills, not pills. Withdrawal and catatonia remain benzodiazepine indications. In that Swedish registry cohort benzodiazepine use was associated with suicide attempt or death at HR 1.61 (95% CI 1.45–1.78), the highest of the classes studied — an association, not proof of cause — and benzodiazepines also worsen disinhibition.
qb_per_005.pearl: Never start or escalate benzodiazepines for BPD symptoms or crisis distress — they are associated with the highest suicide risk of any psychotropic class studied in this population; use skills, not pills.
qb_per_005.evidence: t_personality.md — Minimize polypharmacy; no medication treats BPD itself, and accumulating agents adds risk without benefit. In particular, do not start or escalate benzodiazepines — they carry the highest risk of attempted or completed suicide of any psychotropic class studied in BPD (HR 1.61, 95% CI 1.45–1.78; Lieslehto 2023) and worsen disinhibition.

qb_per_006.stem: A patient with borderline personality disorder has been admitted for one week. Day-shift nurses describe her as 'demanding and exhausting,' while night-shift nurses call her 'our most engaged patient.' The team recognizes this as splitting. Which response most directly addresses the splitting dynamic?

options.t: Have the primary clinician confront the patient with both accounts of her behavior — addressing the pattern directly will reduce the manipulative splitting.

trap.name: Confront the patient
trap.note: Confronting the patient about splitting as a conscious behavior misframes it as deliberate manipulation; splitting is a feature of the illness, not a character flaw, and confrontation damages the therapeutic alliance.

options.t: Bring the divergent staff perceptions to the next team meeting; establish a unified care plan with consistent limits, shared documentation, and identical responses from all staff.
Rotate staff assignments so different nurses interact with the patient each shift, preventing any single staff member from becoming the 'good' or 'bad' object.

trap.name: Rotation reduces splitting
trap.note: Staff rotation removes the consistency that is the antidote to splitting — the evidence-based approach is a unified team response with consistent limits; rotation prevents the team from communicating a coherent message.

options.t: Document the staff disagreement in the chart as evidence of inconsistent care quality and file a milieu management concern.

trap.name: Document the disagreement
trap.note: The divergent staff perceptions are a clinical feature of the patient's BPD, not a care-quality failure — the response is clinical (unified team approach), not an administrative report.

qb_per_006.why: Confront the patient, Rotation reduces splitting, and Document the disagreement all fail the unified-team response. The source states: 'Apply consistent, transparent limit-setting and communicate as a unified team — shared notes and handoffs blunt splitting.' Bringing divergent perceptions to rounds is the clinical intervention.
qb_per_006.pearl: Splitting in BPD is treated by team unity — shared notes, consistent limits, and bringing divergent perceptions to rounds; confronting the patient or rotating staff backfires.
qb_per_006.evidence: t_personality.md — Apply consistent, transparent limit-setting and communicate as a unified team — shared notes and handoffs blunt splitting and prevent staff from being divided into 'good' and 'bad.' Bring observed splitting or team-division to rounds so the plan stays unified.

qb_per_003.stem: A 24-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder has had 6 psychiatric admissions in the past 2 years, each following an episode of suicidal ideation and non-suicidal self-injury after an interpersonal rupture. She describes ongoing passive suicidal ideation at baseline. Tonight she is calm, the relationship dispute that triggered this admission has somewhat resolved, and her self-harm behaviors have decreased. How should the team conceptualize the discharge planning?

options.t: She should be admitted as long as suicidal ideation is present — admission ends only when suicidal ideation resolves completely.

trap.name: Admission until SI resolves
trap.note: Chronic baseline suicidality in BPD does not resolve between episodes — waiting for complete resolution would mean indefinite hospitalization; the clinical task is to distinguish the acute crisis from the chronic baseline.

options.t: Discharge should be planned now that the acute crisis has resolved — her chronic suicidality is managed primarily through collaborative safety planning and outpatient therapy, not serial acute admissions.
Transfer to a long-term residential program is the appropriate step — repeated admissions indicate that outpatient treatment has failed.

trap.name: Repeated admissions = step up
trap.note: Repeated admissions in BPD often reflect inadequate outpatient structure, not the failure of outpatient treatment as a modality; serial inpatient admissions can reinforce hospital use as a coping strategy, worsening the pattern.

options.t: Increase the frequency of psychiatric medications — the recurrent admissions indicate inadequate pharmacotherapy.

trap.name: Polypharmacy for BPD
trap.note: No medication treats BPD itself; the page explicitly advises minimizing polypharmacy; repeated admissions call for better collaborative safety planning and structured outpatient therapy, not more medications.

qb_per_003.why: Admission until SI resolves, Repeated admissions = step up, and Polypharmacy for BPD all fail to apply the chronic-vs-acute distinction. The page is explicit: 'For chronic suicidality, collaborative safety planning is often preferable to repeated or prolonged admission, which can reinforce the hospital as the primary coping strategy.' Discharge planning after acute-on-chronic resolution is the correct frame.
qb_per_003.pearl: Chronic BPD suicidality ≠ acute crisis — distinguish the baseline from escalation; safety planning + outpatient DBT, not serial admissions, manage the chronic pattern.
qb_per_003.evidence: t_personality.md — For chronic suicidality, collaborative safety planning is often preferable to repeated or prolonged admission, which can reinforce the hospital as the primary coping strategy.

qb_per_004.stem: A 31-year-old woman with a documented BPD diagnosis is admitted with severe depressive symptoms, inability to get out of bed, anhedonia, and new passive suicidal ideation. A third-year student says, 'She has BPD — this is probably just her mood lability.' The attending asks the student to reflect on this reasoning. What is the specific error in this approach?

options.t: BPD should not be diagnosed in women under 35 — the patient's age makes the diagnosis questionable.

trap.name: Age-based BPD exclusion
trap.note: There is no age restriction on BPD diagnosis below 35; DSM-5 allows the diagnosis from age 18 onward, and the clinical question here is about diagnostic overshadowing, not diagnostic validity.

options.t: The student should have assessed self-harm first before considering mood symptoms.

trap.name: Sequence error
trap.note: Sequencing the assessment differently does not address the core reasoning error — the student is dismissing potentially treatable mood symptoms by attributing them to the BPD diagnosis.

options.t: BPD mood lability is transient and identity-driven; sustained anhedonia and neurovegetative symptoms over days are fully explained by BPD dysregulation and do not warrant evaluation for superimposed major depression.

trap.name: BPD explains all symptoms
trap.note: BPD mood shifts are characteristically brief and reactive; sustained neurovegetative symptoms — inability to get out of bed, anhedonia, passive suicidal ideation — exceed what BPD dysregulation alone explains and mandate a full evaluation for superimposed MDD.

options.t: The student is using diagnostic overshadowing — attributing the depressive symptoms to the BPD diagnosis and under-investigating a potentially treatable mood episode; a BPD diagnosis does not protect a patient from also having major depression.

qb_per_004.why: Age-based BPD exclusion and Sequence error miss the core error. Option C is the error itself in clinical clothing — its accurate opening (BPD mood lability is transient and reactive) is used to license the false conclusion that sustained anhedonia and neurovegetative symptoms need no evaluation for superimposed major depression; key D names that error and its mechanism. The page calls this 'the cardinal error: diagnostic overshadowing — letting a personality label cause you to under-treat a real, acute, treatable illness.'
qb_per_004.pearl: Diagnostic overshadowing in BPD: never let a personality diagnosis suppress investigation of a treatable comorbid mood, psychotic, or substance disorder.
qb_per_004.evidence: t_personality.md — The cardinal error is diagnostic overshadowing: letting a personality label cause you to under-treat a real, acute, treatable illness. A BPD diagnosis does not protect a patient from also having a serious mood, psychotic, or medical condition.

qb_cdev_001.stem: A 22-year-old man with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability who lives in a group home is admitted for acute behavioral escalation — he became agitated and hit a staff member after a change in his daily routine. A nurse says, 'He has ASD — this is probably just how he behaves.' Which response reflects the correct clinical approach?

options.t: Agree — behavioral escalation is expected in ASD and does not require further workup.

trap.name: Baseline dismissal
trap.note: Attributing new behavioral escalation to the baseline diagnosis without investigation is the cardinal error of diagnostic overshadowing; new or worsening behaviors always earn a workup for pain, medical causes, and psychiatric comorbidity.

options.t: New behavioral escalation in a patient with ASD or ID earns a medical workup — diagnostic overshadowing (assuming new behavior is just the developmental disorder) is the cardinal error; screen for pain, constipation, infection, dental problems, and medication effects before attributing to baseline.
Start risperidone immediately — it is FDA-approved for autism and will treat the behavioral dyscontrol.

trap.name: Medication before assessment
trap.note: Initiating an antipsychotic before identifying the cause of the behavioral change is poor clinical practice; if pain or a medical cause is driving the behavior, medicating without treating the cause harms the patient.

options.t: Contact the group home about the routine change — environmental causes are the only plausible explanation for behavioral escalation in ASD.

trap.name: Environmental cause only
trap.note: The routine change may be a precipitant, but medical workup must come first — pain, constipation, dental problems, and infection are nonverbal communication channels in ASD and frequently underlie behavioral escalation.

qb_cdev_001.why: Baseline dismissal, Medication before assessment, and Environmental cause only all skip the foundational step. The page's first pearl: 'Diagnostic overshadowing is the cardinal error — new symptoms in ASD/ID earn a workup, not a shrug.' Behavior is communication; medical drivers must be excluded before attributing to baseline or starting a psychotropic.
qb_cdev_001.pearl: Diagnostic overshadowing in ASD/ID: new behavioral escalation always earns a workup for pain, constipation, infection, dental issues, and medications before attributing to baseline.
qb_cdev_001.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Diagnostic overshadowing is the cardinal error — new symptoms in ASD/ID earn a workup, not a shrug. Behavior is communication; look for pain and medical drivers before sedation.

qb_cdev_002.stem: An 18-year-old with autism spectrum disorder is admitted for aggressive behavior. His parents ask if medication can 'help with his autism.' The team considers starting risperidone. Which statement about the pharmacological target of risperidone in ASD is most accurate?

options.t: Risperidone is FDA-approved to improve the core social-communication deficits of autism, including eye contact, reciprocal conversation, and restricted interests.

trap.name: Antipsychotic treats core ASD features
trap.note: No medication treats the core social-communication features of ASD; the FDA approval for risperidone is specifically limited to irritability and aggression associated with autism in children and adolescents.

options.t: Risperidone is effective for all ASD-related behavioral symptoms when used at sufficient doses — including social withdrawal, repetitive behaviors, and communication deficits — so the dose should be raised until those improve.

trap.name: Sufficient dose treats all features
trap.note: The FDA approval is explicitly limited to irritability/aggression associated with autism in children and adolescents; dose escalation does not expand the approved indication or the therapeutic range of the drug.

options.t: Risperidone and aripiprazole are FDA-approved for autism-associated irritability in children and adolescents (off-label at 18) — neither treats the core social-communication features.
Risperidone is a first-line agent for all behaviors in any patient with autism regardless of severity — it should be started prophylactically to prevent aggression.

trap.name: Prophylactic antipsychotic in ASD
trap.note: Prophylactic antipsychotic initiation is not evidence-based in ASD; the indication is irritability/aggression when present, with explicit target symptom documentation, not preventive standing orders.

qb_cdev_002.why: Antipsychotic treats core ASD features, Sufficient dose treats all features, and Prophylactic antipsychotic all misstate the indication. Risperidone and aripiprazole are FDA-approved for irritability (including aggression and self-injury) associated with autism in children and adolescents (risperidone 5–16 years, aripiprazole 6–17 years; use at 18 is off-label) — they do not treat the core social-communication features. The page is specific: 'target symptoms explicitly, monitor metabolically, and avoid reflexive standing antipsychotics.'
qb_cdev_002.pearl: Risperidone/aripiprazole treat autism-associated irritability/aggression (FDA-approved in children and adolescents; off-label in adults) — they do NOT treat core social-communication features; always document the target symptom.
qb_cdev_002.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Antipsychotics (risperidone, aripiprazole) treat autism-associated irritability, not the core social-communication features.

qb_cdev_003.stem: A 16-year-old boy with a childhood diagnosis of ADHD is admitted following his first episode of several days of markedly decreased sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech, and impulsive behavior. His parents report that his ADHD has 'always been there' but this episode is 'completely different.' His Vanderbilt score from 3 years ago documented inattention and hyperactivity across home and school settings. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.t: This is undertreated ADHD — intensifying stimulant therapy will address the behavioral escalation.

trap.name: ADHD intensification for episodic change
trap.note: Intensifying stimulants during a probable manic episode is contraindicated — stimulants are not started during acute mania or psychosis; the cross-situational childhood ADHD baseline is distinct from this episodic presentation.

options.t: The childhood ADHD diagnosis rules out bipolar disorder — the two cannot co-occur.

trap.name: ADHD excludes bipolar
trap.note: ADHD and bipolar disorder can co-occur; the ADHD diagnosis does not protect against a first manic episode. The key discriminator is that ADHD is chronic and cross-situational from childhood, while mania is episodic with mood elevation, decreased sleep, and grandiosity.

options.t: The decreased sleep, grandiosity, and pressured speech are likely stimulant side effects from his ADHD medications — reduce the dose and reassess before considering a mood diagnosis.

trap.name: Stimulant side effect attribution
trap.note: Stimulants can cause insomnia or irritability, but the combination of markedly decreased sleep, grandiosity, and pressured speech over several days is a manic syndrome, not a medication side-effect profile; stimulants do not produce grandiosity or manic-quality thought acceleration.

options.t: ADHD is chronic and cross-situational from childhood; episodic presentations with mood elevation, decreased need for sleep, and grandiosity are mood or substance flags, not ADHD exacerbations — this clinical picture warrants a first manic episode evaluation, not a stimulant adjustment.

qb_cdev_003.why: ADHD intensification for episodic change and ADHD excludes bipolar both apply the wrong clinical framework. Option C is also incorrect: the stem never establishes stimulant treatment, and several days of decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, and pressured speech constitute a manic syndrome rather than a stimulant side effect — the correct move is a first manic episode evaluation now (holding any stimulant), not a dose reduction with a deferred mood assessment. The page explicitly states: 'ADHD is chronic, pervasive, and cross-situational from childhood; mania is episodic with mood elevation, decreased need for sleep, and grandiosity — episodic ADHD-like symptoms are a mood or substance flag.'
qb_cdev_003.pearl: ADHD is chronic and cross-situational from childhood; a new episodic presentation with decreased sleep, grandiosity, and pressured speech is a first manic episode flag — not an ADHD exacerbation.
qb_cdev_003.evidence: t_neurodev.md — ADHD is chronic, pervasive, and cross-situational from childhood; mania is episodic with mood elevation, decreased need for sleep, and grandiosity. Episodic 'ADHD-like' symptoms are a mood or substance flag.

qb_cdev_004.stem: A 26-year-old man with autism spectrum disorder is admitted by his group home for a change in behavior. Over the past 10 days he has become mute, stopped eating, and is found in fixed postures for hours at a time. He previously spoke in simple sentences and was active in daily activities. Which diagnosis must be actively evaluated?

options.t: Worsening autism — the increase in stereotyped behaviors and withdrawal represents a regression to a lower developmental level.

trap.name: Regression = autism worsening
trap.note: Mutism, posturing, and immobility in an autistic adult represent catatonia — a treatable medical/psychiatric syndrome — until proven otherwise; labeling it autism regression misses a potentially dangerous and treatable condition.

options.t: Treatment-resistant depression — the mutism and akinesia reflect severe depression refractory to prior treatment.

trap.name: Mutism = severe depression
trap.note: While depression can cause akinesia and withdrawal, the specific combination of mutism + fixed posturing + sudden onset in an autistic patient points to catatonia first; catatonia evaluation takes priority over depression attribution.

options.t: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — posturing and immobility indicate a drug reaction if the patient is on an antipsychotic.

trap.name: NMS by default with antipsychotic
trap.note: If the patient is on an antipsychotic, NMS must be considered, but NMS requires fever, autonomic instability, and elevated CK — the broad differential here includes catatonia as the primary diagnostic task, which may occur with or without antipsychotic use in ASD.

options.t: Catatonia — new mutism, fixed posturing, and immobility in an autistic patient represent catatonia until proven otherwise; catatonia is under-recognized in ASD and requires specific evaluation and treatment.

qb_cdev_004.why: Regression = autism worsening, Mutism = severe depression, and NMS by default all bypass the specific catatonia recognition task. The page explicitly calls out: 'Catatonia is under-recognized in autistic patients — look for it.' New mutism, immobility, and posturing in a previously communicative autistic adult is the classic presentation — it requires a catatonia evaluation (Bush-Francis scale), not dismissal as regression.
qb_cdev_004.pearl: Catatonia is under-recognized in ASD — new mutism, fixed posturing, and immobility in an autistic patient = catatonia evaluation, not regression or depression attribution.
qb_cdev_004.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Catatonia in autism — under-recognized and important; new mutism, immobility, posturing, or stupor in an autistic patient should prompt a catatonia evaluation.

qb_rel_003.stem: A student is seeing a 38-year-old man who is admitted after an alcohol-related incident — his second alcohol-related admission this year. When the student mentions concerns about his drinking, the patient says, 'Look, I drink to handle stress — I don't have a problem. Everyone drinks.' The student's instinct is to explain why the drinking is dangerous and list the health consequences. Which response best reflects motivational interviewing?

options.t: 'That label isn't the point — and it sounds like work stress has been really heavy lately. You've ended up here twice this year. What's your take on that?' [Rolling with resistance, reflecting back the fact without argument, then opening with a genuine question]
'Your liver enzymes are elevated and your blood pressure is high — the data clearly show that alcohol is harming you.' [Presenting the medical evidence directly to motivate change]

trap.name: The righting reflex
trap.note: Supplying arguments for change is the righting reflex — it produces defensiveness and sustain talk. MI works by evoking the patient's own reasons, not installing yours.

options.t: 'I think you should stop drinking entirely — it's the only way to protect your health.' [A clear recommendation from the clinician]

trap.name: Advice without readiness
trap.note: Unsolicited direct advice before a patient is in the preparation stage typically produces resistance, not change; the MI principle is to match the communication style to the patient's readiness.

options.t: 'Would you be willing to try an abstinence contract for the next 30 days — just to see if you feel better?' [Proposing a behavior change target]

trap.name: Planning before evoking
trap.note: Planning (Step 4) precedes a contract proposal; the patient has not shown readiness yet, so jumping to a plan bypasses Engaging, Focusing, and Evoking — the MI processes that build readiness first.

qb_rel_003.why: The righting reflex, Advice without readiness, and Planning before evoking all push the patient into a defensive position. MI's core insight: 'People talk themselves into change. Your job is not to supply the arguments but to evoke the patient's own reasons.' Rolling with resistance and reflecting the ambiguity without arguing is the MI move.
qb_rel_003.pearl: Resist the righting reflex — don't argue for change; roll with resistance, reflect change talk, and let the patient articulate their own reasons.
qb_rel_003.evidence: motivational_interviewing.md — The one idea: People talk themselves into change. Your job is not to supply the arguments (the 'righting reflex' — resist it) but to evoke the patient's own reasons. Pushing usually produces sustain talk; curiosity produces change talk.

link.label: Open the Family Therapy Modalities page

qb_rel_004.stem: A family asks the treatment team what they can do during their loved one's hospitalization for schizophrenia to help with recovery. The team is considering whether to invest the time in a formal family meeting. Which argument best supports making structured family psychoeducation the default approach?

options.t: Family involvement is primarily a courtesy — it improves patient satisfaction but has no measurable impact on relapse rates.

trap.name: Family work = courtesy
trap.note: Family psychoeducation has among the strongest inpatient evidence in all of psychiatry — it is not a courtesy; it directly reduces relapse rates with an NNT of 7.

options.t: Families frequently refuse structured family meetings, so the effort should be reserved for families who specifically request it.

trap.name: Patient/family refusal as barrier
trap.note: The research shows the main barrier to family work is clinician avoidance, not family refusal — underdelivering family work is primarily a clinician behavior problem.

options.t: Family psychoeducation is the highest-evidence family intervention — it led 11 models for 12-month relapse prevention (Rodolico et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2022; 90 RCTs) with an NNT of 7 (Pharoah, Cochrane 2010; 53 RCTs); dose matters: ≤2 sessions is ineffective, with NICE recommending ≥10 sessions over ≥3 months.
Family involvement should wait until the patient is stable — in the acute phase, it increases stimulation and worsens psychosis.

trap.name: Stability first
trap.note: While the inpatient approach to family work is brief, psychoeducational, and low-stimulation (with acutely psychotic patients: brief, concrete, limited interpretation), family engagement should begin in the hospital, not wait for full stabilization — family involvement nearly triples 7-day follow-up odds.

qb_rel_004.why: Family work = courtesy, Patient/family refusal as barrier, and Stability first all undermine the evidence-based standard. Family psychoeducation has NNT 7 for 12-month relapse prevention — one of the strongest NNTs in inpatient psychiatry. The dose requirement (≥10 sessions over ≥3 months) means starting the work during the admission and securing the outpatient continuation.
qb_rel_004.pearl: Family psychoeducation for schizophrenia: NNT 7 for 12-month relapse prevention; ≥10 sessions over ≥3 months; dose matters — start during admission.
qb_rel_004.evidence: family_modalities.md — NNT 7 — treat seven families to prevent one relapse (Pharoah, Cochrane 2010; 53 RCTs). Dose matters: ≤2 sessions is ineffective; NICE recommends ≥10 sessions over ≥3 months.

qb_rel_005.stem: A student is using the MI readiness ruler with a patient who has poorly controlled diabetes and drinks heavily. He rates the importance of cutting back alcohol as '4 out of 10.' Which follow-up question best uses the readiness ruler to elicit change talk?

options.t: 'You said 4 — why not a 2? What keeps it that high?' [Evoking the patient's own reasons for change by asking why the number isn't even lower]
'Why isn't your number higher? You should care more about your health.' [Naming the mismatch between the rating and the clinical severity]

trap.name: Confrontational reflect
trap.note: Pointing out the gap confrontationally activates resistance — the MI principle is to work with the ambivalence, not against it; questioning the 'low' number as a character deficit shuts down change talk.

options.t: 'That's a 4 — you're clearly not ready to change right now. Let's talk about something else.' [Accepting the score and moving on]

trap.name: Score = readiness fixed
trap.note: A 4 on the readiness ruler is not a signal to abandon the exploration; it is the starting point for evoking change talk by asking 'why not lower?' and 'what would move you up?'

options.t: 'A 4 means ambivalence — let's complete a full decisional balance worksheet together right now.' [Shifting to a structured CBT exercise]

trap.name: Decisional balance as MI
trap.note: Decisional balance worksheets are a structured CBT exercise, not a core MI move; the readiness ruler is followed by open questions that elicit the patient's own reasons — not a structured checklist.

qb_rel_005.why: Confrontational reflect, Score = readiness fixed, and Decisional balance as MI all bypass the evocative purpose of the readiness ruler. The MI readiness ruler follow-up sequence: '...why not a 2?' forces change talk by asking the patient to articulate why they're not lower. 'What would move you from a 4 to a 6?' explores the next steps. Both are evocative, not confrontational.
qb_rel_005.pearl: MI readiness ruler: after the patient rates importance (e.g., 4/10), ask 'why not a 2?' — this forces the patient to articulate their own change talk rather than pushing your reasons.
qb_rel_005.evidence: motivational_interviewing.md — A 30-second tool: the readiness ruler. 'You said 4 — why not a 2?' (forces change talk). 'What would move you from a 4 to a 6?'

link.label: Open the Family Therapy Modalities page

qb_rel_006.stem: The family of a patient with schizophrenia is described in the chart as 'high expressed emotion' — high criticism and high emotional over-involvement. The resident says, 'We can't do much about the family climate — it's just how they are.' Which response is most evidence-based?

options.t: Agree — expressed emotion is a fixed family trait that does not respond to clinical intervention.

trap.name: EE is fixed
trap.note: Expressed emotion is modifiable — behavioral family therapy and family psychoeducation specifically reduce EE; treating it as fixed is both incorrect and missed opportunity.

options.t: High EE only predicts relapse in schizophrenia, not in other psychiatric illnesses — it is not relevant beyond psychosis.

trap.name: EE = schizophrenia only
trap.note: Expressed emotion predicts relapse across multiple psychiatric conditions including mood disorders; the family therapy modalities page cites EE-relapse data for schizophrenia because that is the strongest evidence base, but EE is a transdiagnostic concept.

options.t: High EE is a family problem but not a clinical problem — it is outside the scope of inpatient psychiatric intervention.

trap.name: EE = out of scope
trap.note: Family climate is explicitly clinical data; the page calls it modifiable and quantifies its impact on relapse risk — addressing EE is within the scope of inpatient psychiatry through family meetings.

options.t: Expressed emotion (EE) substantially raises relapse odds — roughly doubling to quintupling across studies (Butzlaff & Hooley 1998) — while family warmth is protective, but EE is modifiable through behavioral family therapy and family psychoeducation, making the family climate a tractable clinical target.

qb_rel_006.why: EE is fixed, EE = schizophrenia only, and EE = out of scope all represent clinical fatalism about a modifiable variable. The page states EE 'roughly doubles to quintuples relapse odds depending on the study (Butzlaff & Hooley 1998 meta-analysis), while family warmth is protective — and family climate is modifiable, which is why meetings help lower it.'
qb_rel_006.pearl: Expressed emotion (EE) substantially raises relapse odds (roughly doubling to quintupling across studies; Butzlaff & Hooley 1998) and is MODIFIABLE — behavioral family therapy and psychoeducation specifically target and reduce it; EE is a tractable clinical problem.
qb_rel_006.evidence: family_modalities.md — Expressed emotion: high-EE roughly doubles to quintuples relapse odds depending on the study (Butzlaff & Hooley 1998 meta-analysis), while family warmth is protective. Family climate is modifiable — meetings help lower it.

qb_rel_007.stem: A 27-year-old woman is being discharged after a suicidal crisis. The resident asks her to 'sign a contract that she won't hurt herself.' The student wonders whether this is the evidence-based approach. Which response reflects the current standard?

options.t: Yes — a no-suicide contract is the gold standard for discharge safety planning; it establishes a binding commitment to safety.

trap.name: Contract = gold standard
trap.note: No-suicide contracts have no supporting evidence and can create false reassurance — the current standard is collaborative safety planning, which has real outcome data.

options.t: Yes — contracts are more legally protective for the clinician than safety plans, which is why they are standard at discharge.

trap.name: Contract = legal protection
trap.note: Contracts have no established legal protection advantage and do not reduce suicide attempts; they have been replaced by evidence-based safety planning in clinical standards.

options.t: No — a collaborative safety plan (Stanley-Brown model) is the evidence-based tool; no-suicide contracts have no supporting evidence and can create false reassurance that displaces genuine clinical assessment.
Neither approach has evidence — rely on clinical judgment and family support for suicidal patients at discharge.

trap.name: No evidence either way
trap.note: Safety planning WITH follow-up has evidence: approximately 50% fewer suicidal behaviors (Stanley 2018); it is not evidence-neutral.

qb_rel_007.why: Contract = gold standard, Contract = legal protection, and No evidence either way all misrepresent the evidence. The brief psychotherapy page explicitly states: 'Abandon no-suicide contracts — they don't work.' Safety planning (Stanley-Brown) with follow-up reduces suicidal behaviors by approximately 50%.
qb_rel_007.pearl: Safety planning (Stanley-Brown) with follow-up ≈ 50% fewer suicidal behaviors — abandon no-suicide contracts, which have no evidence and create false reassurance.
qb_rel_007.evidence: brief_psychotherapy.md — Safety planning (Stanley-Brown) + crisis response planning: Safety Planning Intervention with follow-up ≈ 50% fewer suicidal behaviors (Stanley 2018); abandon no-suicide 'contracts' — they don't work.

qb_rel_008.stem: A 52-year-old man with severe depression is withdrawn, stays in bed all day, and says 'nothing matters anymore.' The student asks how to perform a brief psychotherapy intervention given a 15-minute window. Which approach is most appropriate for this presentation?

options.t: Behavioral activation — schedule one small, specific valued activity for today; this is the highest-yield, lowest-cognitive-demand inpatient move for behavioral shutdown.
Psychodynamic interpretation — explore the unconscious drivers of the behavioral withdrawal during this session.

trap.name: Insight therapy for shutdown
trap.note: Psychodynamic interpretation requires cognitive engagement that a severely depressed, withdrawn patient cannot sustain; the mismatch between mechanism (insight) and the presenting driver (behavioral shutdown) makes BA the more evidence-based choice.

options.t: Prolonged exposure — begin reliving any traumatic experiences that may underlie the depression.

trap.name: PE for depression
trap.note: Prolonged exposure is for PTSD — its mechanism (trauma memory reconsolidation) does not match behavioral shutdown; applying PE to a shutdown depressed patient mismatches mechanism and technique.

options.t: Wait for medication to take effect before beginning any psychotherapy — behavioral shutdown is too severe for psychotherapy engagement.

trap.name: Medication before psychotherapy
trap.note: Brief behavioral activation is specifically designed for patients with low engagement — scheduling a single valued activity is achievable even with severe depression; waiting for full medication response before any behavioral intervention delays recovery unnecessarily.

qb_rel_008.why: Insight therapy for shutdown, PE for depression, and Medication before psychotherapy all mismatch mechanism to technique. The brief psychotherapy table: 'Withdrawn, inactive, anhedonic — behavioral shutdown → reach for behavioral activation (BA): schedule one small, valued activity. Superior to TAU for depression (SMD −0.78) and anxiety, on par with CBT; lowest cognitive demand → best inpatient fit.'
qb_rel_008.pearl: Behavioral activation is the highest-yield, lowest-effort inpatient move for the shutdown depressed patient — schedule one small valued activity; it requires no cognitive engagement.
qb_rel_008.evidence: brief_psychotherapy.md — Behavioral activation (BA) — schedule one small, valued activity. Superior to TAU for depression (SMD −0.78) and anxiety (−0.33), on par with CBT; lowest cognitive demand → best inpatient fit.

qb_rel_009.stem: A patient with recurrent MDD completed three individual therapy sessions during an 8-day hospitalization. At discharge, the student writes in the note: 'CBT skills taught inpatient; patient discharged with psychotherapy complete.' The attending asks the student to reconsider the framing. Which is more accurate?

options.t: The note is accurate — three CBT sessions is the evidence-based minimum for inpatient psychotherapy, and the skills have been transferred.

trap.name: Three sessions = complete
trap.note: No evidence-based framework defines 3 inpatient sessions as 'complete' — the purpose of inpatient psychotherapy is to start the work and secure the outpatient handoff, not to complete treatment.

options.t: Inpatient psychotherapy starts the work and secures the handoff — the discharge note should name the specific therapeutic thread started, identify the named outpatient clinician who will continue it, and make the handoff explicit.
Psychotherapy is an outpatient intervention — inpatient therapy has no meaningful impact and should not be documented as a treatment component.

trap.name: Inpatient therapy = ineffective
trap.note: Inpatient psychotherapy has a documented pooled benefit (SMD ~0.24, NNT ~7) — framing it as ineffective dismisses evidence; the point is that it must continue outpatient to complete the benefit.

options.t: Three CBT sessions is sufficient only if the patient was 'CBT-naive' — if she had prior CBT, the inpatient work is redundant.

trap.name: Prior CBT = redundant inpatient therapy
trap.note: Prior CBT experience does not make inpatient psychotherapy redundant; patients return to therapy at every level of care as needed, and the inpatient component serves crisis stabilization and continuity, regardless of prior exposure.

qb_rel_009.why: Example: 'BA for behavioral shutdown' is the specific thread; naming the clinician prevents the work from being dropped at discharge. Three sessions = complete, Inpatient therapy = ineffective, and Prior CBT = redundant all miss the purpose. The page: 'The skill is to read the mechanism driving this patient's crisis right now and match one brief technique to it — then hand the work off to outpatient care.' 'Write the handoff so the outpatient clinician can continue the thread — the point of inpatient therapy is to start it and secure the follow-up.'
qb_rel_009.pearl: Inpatient psychotherapy starts the thread and secures the handoff — document the technique, name the outpatient clinician, and make the handoff explicit; it does not complete treatment.
qb_rel_009.evidence: brief_psychotherapy.md — Write the handoff so the outpatient clinician can continue the thread — the point of inpatient therapy is to start it and secure the follow-up.

link.label: Open the Family Therapy Modalities page

qb_rel_010.stem: The treatment team reviews its data and finds that structured family meetings occurred in only 8% of admissions over the past year, despite family members being available and willing in most cases. The team discusses why. Which explanation is most consistent with the literature?

options.t: Families of inpatient psychiatric patients predominantly refuse to participate in structured family meetings when offered.

trap.name: Family refusal
trap.note: The research specifically identifies clinician avoidance — not family refusal — as the dominant barrier to delivering family work; this is a clinician behavior finding, not a family behavior finding.

options.t: Structured family work requires >90 minutes per family — the time investment is prohibitive in an acute inpatient setting.

trap.name: Time as primary barrier
trap.note: While time is a real constraint, the research identifies clinician avoidance as the main barrier, not time alone — and some high-yield modalities (solution-focused, single-session work) can be effective in one meeting.

options.t: The main barrier to family psychoeducation being delivered is clinician avoidance — structured family work is available to the minority of families who receive it largely because of clinician behavior, not family behavior.
Insurance authorization is the dominant barrier — family meetings require separate billing codes that are denied in most health systems.

trap.name: Billing as dominant barrier
trap.note: Billing complexity may be a factor, but the research (Dixon 1999; Eassom 2014) specifically identifies clinician avoidance as the dominant explanation for the historically low delivery of structured family work.

qb_rel_010.why: Family refusal, Time as primary barrier, and Billing as dominant barrier all attribute the gap to external factors. The literature finding is counterintuitive and important: 'Reaches a minority of families — structured family work is delivered in only ~0–53% of cases (historically <10%), and the main barrier is clinician avoidance, not patient refusal (Dixon 1999; Eassom 2014).' This is a clinician self-awareness finding.
qb_rel_010.pearl: The main barrier to family psychoeducation in inpatient psychiatry is clinician avoidance, not patient or family refusal — the gap is a clinician behavior problem.
qb_rel_010.evidence: family_modalities.md — Reaches a minority of families — structured family work is delivered in only ~0–53% of cases (historically <10%), and the main barrier is clinician avoidance, not patient refusal (Dixon 1999; Eassom 2014).

qb_rel_011.stem: A 24-year-old woman with BPD cuts herself on the unit. The charge nurse says, 'Document it and flag it. Don't talk to her about it — it just encourages the behavior.' The student wonders about the evidence-based approach. Which response is most accurate?

options.t: The nurse is right — direct conversation about self-harm incidents reinforces the behavior by providing attention; the clinical standard is documentation without engagement.

trap.name: Engagement reinforces behavior
trap.note: Withholding engagement after self-harm misses the chain analysis opportunity that is central to DBT — it treats the symptom as behavior to extinguish rather than as communication to understand.

options.t: The appropriate response is immediate medication review — self-harm indicates the current regimen is inadequate.

trap.name: Self-harm = medication failure
trap.note: Self-harm in BPD is a behavioral coping strategy — the clinician-level response is to understand its function through chain analysis, not to reflexively adjust medications.

options.t: Place the patient on 1:1 observation and restrict milieu privileges pending a formal incident review — the safety breach requires an institutional response before therapeutic engagement resumes.

trap.name: Incident response first
trap.note: While safety monitoring and documentation are appropriate after self-harm on the unit, withholding therapeutic engagement delays the chain analysis that is central to the DBT model; the clinical response is to engage and understand the behavior, not to manage the incident bureaucratically before engaging.

options.t: A chain analysis — walking the sequence of antecedents, emotions, and behaviors with the patient non-punitively — turns the incident into a clinical formulation and a coping plan; this is the DBT standard and replaces documentation-only or punitive responses.

qb_rel_011.why: Engagement reinforces behavior, Self-harm = medication failure, and Punitive documentation all fail to apply the DBT-informed clinical standard. The page states: 'Chain analysis replaces a punitive response to self-harm — understand the behavior, don't just document it.' The chain analysis is a brief, structured, non-punitive conversation about what preceded the self-harm that turns the incident into a formulation.
qb_rel_011.pearl: After self-harm: chain analysis (non-punitive, with the patient) replaces documentation-only or punitive responses — it transforms the incident into a formulation and a coping plan.
qb_rel_011.evidence: brief_psychotherapy.md — Chain analysis — walk the sequence with the patient, non-punitively. Turns an incident into a formulation and a plan; core DBT move. Chain analysis replaces a punitive response to self-harm — understand the behavior, don't just document it.

qb_rel_012.stem: A 32-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has refused treatment for 2 years. His wife is desperate to help and asks the team what she can do. The team is considering a traditional confrontational intervention approach. Which family therapy modality is specifically evidence-based for this scenario?

options.t: CRAFT (Community Reinforcement and Family Training) — the family member changes her own behavior in specific ways that reduce the reinforcement of drinking and increase the appeal of treatment-seeking, without confrontation or blame.
Structural family therapy (Minuchin) — the focus is on realigning the roles and boundaries in the marriage to reduce the enabling dynamic.

trap.name: Structural for substance refusal
trap.note: Structural therapy addresses role and boundary dysfunction but does not provide the specific behavioral strategies for family members managing a treatment-refusing person with SUD; CRAFT is specifically designed for this scenario.

options.t: A family confrontation (traditional intervention) — bringing family and friends together to confront the patient with consequences is the most evidence-based approach.

trap.name: Confrontational intervention
trap.note: Traditional confrontational interventions have mixed evidence and can damage the therapeutic alliance; CRAFT specifically trains families to use non-blame behavioral strategies and has a larger evidence base for engagement.

options.t: Emotionally focused therapy (EFT) — addressing the attachment disruption in the marriage will resolve the motivational impasse for the patient.

trap.name: EFT for treatment refusal
trap.note: EFT is couples-attachment focused and is the modality for a distressed couple's negative cycle — it is not specifically designed for a family member trying to invite a treatment-refusing person into care.

qb_rel_012.why: Structural for substance refusal, Confrontational intervention, and EFT for treatment refusal all apply less-specific frameworks. CRAFT is the specific modality: 'the family changes its own behavior to invite treatment — no blame.' It trains the wife to use behavioral strategies (reinforcing non-drinking behavior, withdrawing reinforcement of drinking, using teachable moments) that increase the patient's engagement with treatment.
qb_rel_012.pearl: CRAFT: the family changes its OWN behavior to invite treatment — no blame, no confrontation; evidence-based for families of treatment-refusing people with SUD.
qb_rel_012.evidence: family_modalities.md — CRAFT (Community Reinforcement & Family Training): the family changes its own behavior to invite treatment — no blame.

qb_rel_013.stem: A quality-improvement team wants to identify the single inpatient psychological intervention with the strongest readmission-prevention evidence. Which intervention has the hardest numbers?

options.t: Safety planning (Stanley-Brown) — approximately 50% fewer suicidal behaviors.

trap.name: Safety planning hardest numbers
trap.note: Safety planning has strong evidence (50% reduction in suicidal behaviors), but the question asks about readmission prevention specifically — psychoeducation has the hardest readmission-specific numbers.

options.t: Psychoeducation — the hardest inpatient numbers for readmission prevention: readmission NNT 5 (Xia, Cochrane 2011) and relapse NNT 9; and it costs nothing except time.
Behavioral activation — the most evidence-based inpatient psychological intervention for any condition.

trap.name: BA = strongest overall
trap.note: BA has the strongest evidence for acute depression (SMD −0.78) and is the best-fit inpatient technique, but readmission NNT 5 for psychoeducation specifically addresses the readmission-prevention question.

options.t: Problem-solving therapy (PST) — NNT 12 for repeat self-harm re-presentation.

trap.name: PST hardest numbers
trap.note: PST has an NNT of 12 for self-harm re-presentation — meaningful evidence, but psychoeducation's readmission NNT of 5 is the strongest number on the brief psychotherapy page.

qb_rel_013.why: Safety planning hardest numbers, BA = strongest overall, and PST hardest numbers each reference real evidence for different outcomes. For readmission prevention specifically, psychoeducation's NNT 5 is the standout: 'Psychoeducation has the hardest inpatient numbers (readmission NNT 5) — and it's free.' This is the quality-improvement answer.
qb_rel_013.pearl: Psychoeducation has the hardest inpatient readmission numbers: NNT 5 (Xia, Cochrane 2011) — the highest-evidence, lowest-cost psychological intervention for preventing readmission.
qb_rel_013.evidence: brief_psychotherapy.md — Psychoeducation has the hardest inpatient numbers (readmission NNT 5) — and it's free.

qb_otherdx_001.stem: A 17-year-old with severe anorexia nervosa has been starved for 4 months and is starting nutritional rehabilitation. On day 3 of refeeding, her phosphate drops to 2.1 mg/dL. She is also mildly confused and has new-onset leg weakness. What is the most important diagnosis to recognize?

options.t: Refeeding syndrome — the shift to anabolic metabolism drives phosphate into cells; hypophosphatemia is its hallmark.
Electrolyte depletion from malnutrition alone — she was already malnourished on admission, so the low phosphate reflects pre-existing deficiency rather than a refeeding process.

trap.name: Pre-existing deficiency only
trap.note: While pre-existing malnutrition contributes to baseline deficiencies, the precipitous drop in phosphate after initiating refeeding is the refeeding syndrome pattern — the metabolic shift of refeeding, not chronic depletion, is the mechanism.

options.t: Conversion disorder — the confusion and leg weakness represent a functional neurological symptom disorder superimposed on the eating disorder.

trap.name: Functional explanation for metabolic emergency
trap.note: Confusion and leg weakness in the context of a falling phosphate during refeeding is refeeding syndrome until proven otherwise — it is a medical emergency, not a functional disorder.

options.t: Thiamine deficiency — the neurological symptoms indicate Wernicke encephalopathy from B1 deficiency.

trap.name: Thiamine over phosphate
trap.note: Thiamine deficiency is a real risk in eating disorders and requires prophylactic replacement when refeeding starts, but a falling phosphate on day 3 of refeeding with weakness and confusion is the classic refeeding syndrome presentation — phosphate is the hallmark electrolyte.

qb_otherdx_001.why: Pre-existing deficiency only, Functional explanation for metabolic emergency, and Thiamine over phosphate all miss the refeeding-specific mechanism. The page calls refeeding syndrome 'the complication that kills' — hypophosphatemia is the hallmark. Note that D (thiamine) is also clinically relevant and the page specifically says to give thiamine (and other vitamins) when refeeding starts — but the presenting electrolyte abnormality and timing point to refeeding syndrome as the primary diagnosis. Hypophosphatemia can cause cardiac failure, arrhythmia, respiratory failure, and delirium.
qb_otherdx_001.pearl: Refeeding syndrome: watch phosphate — the hallmark is hypophosphatemia after starting nutrition; risk tracks malnutrition, so monitor phosphate daily; supplement phosphate; give thiamine.
qb_otherdx_001.evidence: t_eating.md — Refeeding syndrome — the complication that kills: hypophosphatemia is the hallmark; the danger is cardiac failure, arrhythmia, respiratory failure, and delirium. Supplement phosphate and give thiamine (and other vitamins) when refeeding starts.

tier2.q: Why does hypophosphatemia develop after initiating refeeding in a severely malnourished patient, rather than during the starvation period itself?

options.t: Carbohydrate refeeding increases renal phosphate excretion — the kidneys preferentially excrete phosphate when insulin levels rise.

Refeeding shifts metabolism from catabolic to anabolic — glucose and insulin drive phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells for new cellular synthesis; since total body stores are depleted from malnutrition, the extracellular pool drops precipitously.
Starvation preserves phosphate by reducing cellular metabolic demand — refeeding simply re-activates the pre-existing phosphate deficiency that was masked.
Thiamine deficiency prevents phosphate absorption from the gut — refeeding exposes this deficiency because oral phosphate intake increases.

tier2.why: During starvation, catabolism releases phosphate from cells into the extracellular space, partially maintaining serum levels despite total body depletion. When refeeding begins, glucose triggers insulin release, which drives phosphate (along with potassium and magnesium) into cells for anabolic processes (glycolysis, ATP synthesis, protein synthesis).
