qb_eth_015.pearl: Minors usually need parental consent, with jurisdiction-dependent confidential-service, emancipated-minor, and emergency exceptions.

link.label: Open the Ethics & the Law page

qb_eth_016.stem: A hospitalized patient invites the student doctor to meet socially and offers a substantial personal gift. What is the appropriate response?

options.t: Decline both, with a respectful explanation
Accept both to preserve rapport

trap.name: Rapport-over-boundaries trap
trap.note: Rapport does not justify boundary violations; the therapeutic frame protects the patient.

options.t: Accept the gift but decline the social meeting

trap.name: Partial-boundary trap
trap.note: A substantial personal gift is itself a boundary crossing to avoid.

options.t: Revisit the invitation after discharge if both agree

trap.name: Timing trap
trap.note: Professional boundary concerns do not disappear at discharge.

qb_eth_016.why: Professional boundaries protect patients: decline social invitations and substantial personal gifts respectfully. Sexual or romantic involvement with a patient is never acceptable, and significant gifts or dual relationships are boundary crossings to avoid.
qb_eth_016.pearl: Decline significant gifts and dual relationships respectfully; sexual or romantic involvement with a patient is never acceptable.

qb_otherdx_012.stem: A 20-year-old has months of overwhelming daytime sleepiness with sudden, brief episodes of bilateral leg weakness triggered by laughter, plus vivid hallucinations while falling asleep and episodes of waking paralysis. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Obstructive sleep apnea

trap.name: Mechanism trap
trap.note: OSA causes fragmented sleep and sleepiness but not cataplexy, the emotion-triggered muscle-tone loss described.

options.t: Narcolepsy with cataplexy
A primary psychotic disorder

trap.name: Hallucination trap
trap.note: Hypnagogic hallucinations at sleep onset are a narcolepsy feature, not a primary psychosis.

options.t: Generalized anxiety disorder

trap.name: Wrong-domain trap
trap.note: The tetrad points to narcolepsy, not anxiety.

qb_otherdx_012.why: The narcolepsy tetrad — excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy (emotion-triggered muscle-tone loss), sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations — with low CSF orexin/hypocretin defines narcolepsy type 1; MSLT shows short REM latency.
qb_otherdx_012.pearl: Narcolepsy: sleepiness + cataplexy + sleep paralysis + hypnagogic hallucinations; low orexin.

link.label: Open the Somatic Symptom & Related page

qb_otherdx_013.stem: A woman develops sudden left-arm paralysis after an argument; exam shows a positive Hoover sign and findings inconsistent with any neuroanatomic lesion, and workup is normal. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Malingering to obtain an external incentive

trap.name: Intent trap
trap.note: Functional neurologic symptoms are not consciously produced for external gain.

options.t: Factitious disorder imposed on self

trap.name: Sick-role trap
trap.note: Factitious disorder involves deliberate falsification for the sick role; conversion is not intentional.

options.t: Functional neurological symptom disorder
Acute ischemic stroke

trap.name: Exam trap
trap.note: A positive Hoover sign and neuroanatomically incompatible findings with normal workup argue against a structural lesion.

qb_otherdx_013.why: Neurologic symptoms with internal inconsistency incompatible with recognized disease, such as a positive Hoover sign, define functional neurological symptom disorder when not intentionally produced. It is a rule-in diagnosis based on positive signs, not merely normal tests.
qb_otherdx_013.pearl: Functional neurological symptom disorder is ruled in by positive inconsistent signs, not by accusation or exclusion alone.

qb_otherdx_014.stem: A woman with a severe childhood trauma history has recurrent gaps in memory for everyday events and describes two distinct identity states with different names and behaviors that others have witnessed. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Borderline personality disorder

trap.name: Identity-disturbance trap
trap.note: BPD identity disturbance is an unstable self-image, not distinct alternating identity states with amnesia.

options.t: Malingering for external gain

trap.name: Intent trap
trap.note: The presentation, corroborated by others and tied to severe trauma, is not simply feigned for gain.

options.t: Schizophrenia with primary psychosis

trap.name: Psychosis conflation
trap.note: 'Split personality' is not schizophrenia; DID involves identity states and amnesia, not primary psychosis.

options.t: Dissociative identity disorder

qb_otherdx_014.why: Two or more distinct personality states plus recurrent amnesia beyond ordinary forgetting, strongly associated with severe early trauma, defines dissociative identity disorder — commonly confused with (but distinct from) schizophrenia.
qb_otherdx_014.pearl: DID = ≥2 distinct identity states + amnesia, linked to severe early trauma; not schizophrenia.

candidates.quote: Lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia → NMS; clonus + hyperreflexia → SS. The three distractors all describe NMS features: lead-pipe rigidity (A), dramatically elevated CK (B), and subacute onset tied to the dopamine blocker rather than the serotonergic change (C). Ankle clonus with lower-extremity hyperreflexia (D) is the hallmark physical finding of serotonin syndrome — it reflects serotonin-mediated hyperactivation of spinal reflex arcs and is absent in NMS, where rigidity comes from central dopaminergic dysfunction. The added clinical clues — onset after the sertraline increase, mild rather than dramatic CK — also favor SS over NMS. In practice, both syndromes require stopping the offending agent; the physical exam reflex pattern is the fastest bedside discriminator.

qb_rel_001.stem: A family meeting is held the day before planned discharge for a 52-year-old man admitted after a suicide attempt by overdose. When the agenda reaches safety and warning signs, his wife says: 'We'll keep a close eye on him. And you don't need to worry about the guns — he would never use them, and they're put away.' The attending invites your input. Which response is best?

options.t: 'It makes sense that everyone is exhausted and scared. Before discharge, who can confirm that the firearms — and any stockpiled medications — are actually secured, and how will we know it's done?'
'Firearms are involved in about half of US suicides and are lethal in 85 to 90 percent of attempts — "put away" isn't good enough.'

trap.name: Quoting statistics at families
trap.note: The numbers explain the why to you — recited at a frightened family they become an argument, and arguing invites defense of the status quo.

options.t: 'That's reassuring — we'll document that the family will keep him safe and that the guns are secured.'

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: Family support is data, not a substitute for risk reasoning — a safety plan with unconfirmed means safety is a known failure mode, not a completed task.

options.t: 'Discharge can't move forward unless you agree to remove every firearm from the home today.'

trap.name: Making the family responsible
trap.note: The goal is to understand what support is realistic, not to hand the family the treatment — and disposition ultimatums are not the student's call.

qb_rel_001.why: The best response validates first, stays inside the student role, and converts 'put away' into a concrete, verifiable step — who secures the items and how the team will know. Quoting lethality statistics at the family is the righting reflex in evidence clothing; accepting reassurance leaves means safety unconfirmed at the exact moment risk peaks; and an ultimatum makes the family responsible for treatment while overstepping the student's role.
qb_rel_001.pearl: Means safety is a lethality intervention, not a formality — 'who can confirm items are secured before discharge?' is a clinical act.
qb_rel_001.evidence: exp_family.md 'Why It Matters' — documented lethal-means assessment was associated with fewer suicide attempts and deaths at 180 days (0.83% vs 3.3%; Boggs et al. 2020, quasi-experimental); suicide risk peaks in the first week post-discharge (Chung et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2017).

qb_mood_002.stem: A 38-year-old man with bipolar I disorder, stable on lithium maintenance for two years, presents with a 2-day course of worsening tremor, confusion, and vomiting. Five days ago he began ibuprofen for back pain. Which of the following best explains his presentation?

options.t: A breakthrough manic episode — agitation and confusion signal mood destabilization

trap.name: Treat the number, not the patient
trap.note: Mania does not cause vomiting and an acute 2-day toxic picture — this is a medication interaction problem, not a mood relapse.

options.t: Viral encephalitis — the confusion warrants urgent neuroimaging and lumbar puncture

trap.name: Missing the interaction
trap.note: Attributing a toxic picture to an infectious cause before checking the medication list in a patient on a narrow-therapeutic-window drug is a systematic miss.

options.t: Serotonin syndrome — lithium combined with ibuprofen triggers excess serotonin activity

trap.name: Wrong toxidrome
trap.note: Serotonin syndrome requires serotonergic agents and presents with clonus and hyperreflexia — neither fits; the clinical picture and the drug interaction both point to lithium toxicity.

options.t: Lithium toxicity precipitated by ibuprofen reducing renal lithium clearance

qb_mood_002.why: Treat the number not the patient, Missing the interaction, and Wrong toxidrome are the traps. Lithium has a narrow therapeutic window; NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated renal clearance and push lithium levels into the toxic range — a textbook drug interaction. The 2-day picture of tremor, confusion, and vomiting in a lithium-maintained patient who just started an NSAID is lithium toxicity until proven otherwise.
qb_mood_002.pearl: NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors/ARBs, thiazides, and dehydration push lithium levels toward toxicity — check the list when lithium patients deteriorate.
qb_mood_002.evidence: t_mood.md 'Lithium' — lithium runs a narrow therapeutic window (acute ~0.8–1.2 mEq/L; maintenance ~0.6–0.8, lower in older adults); NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors/ARBs, thiazides, and dehydration push levels toward toxicity.

tier2.q: Why does ibuprofen raise lithium levels?

options.t: Ibuprofen displaces lithium from plasma protein binding, increasing free drug levels
Ibuprofen inhibits hepatic metabolism of lithium, slowing its clearance
Ibuprofen blocks gut absorption of lithium, causing erratic bioavailability and rebound toxicity
Lithium is cleared almost entirely by the kidney; NSAIDs impair prostaglandin-dependent renal handling, reducing lithium clearance and raising serum levels

tier2.why: Lithium is not protein-bound and not hepatically metabolized — it is excreted almost entirely by the kidney. NSAIDs impair prostaglandin-mediated renal perfusion and tubular handling, reducing lithium clearance. This is why the page flags them alongside dehydration and other drugs that reduce glomerular filtration or tubular function as conditions that push levels toward toxicity.

qb_psy_001.stem: A 27-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history is admitted for new-onset paranoid ideation, disorganized behavior, and auditory hallucinations. Her chart notes she was started on high-dose prednisone three weeks ago for an autoimmune flare. Before establishing a primary psychiatric diagnosis, the most important step is which of the following?

options.t: Take a thorough medication and medical history and consider a substance- or medication-induced cause before labeling this a primary psychotic disorder
Start a second-generation antipsychotic immediately — symptom control should not await diagnostic clarity

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: Treating before excluding a secondary cause may mask a reversible etiology and commit the patient to a diagnosis that is not hers.

options.t: Diagnose schizophreniform disorder based on symptom type and the absence of a prior psychiatric history

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: Schizophreniform disorder requires exclusion of medical and substance causes — the diagnosis cannot be established while a high-dose corticosteroid is on board.

options.t: Reassure the family that first-episode psychosis in young adults is almost always primary and will respond to antipsychotics

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: First-episode psychosis has a broad differential — medication-induced, autoimmune, and substance-related causes must be excluded before prognosis can be offered.

qb_psy_001.why: Psychosis = schizophrenia is the trap in two forms: treating immediately or diagnosing before excluding secondary causes. Psychosis is a syndrome with a broad differential — corticosteroids are a recognized cause of secondary psychosis, and the clinical picture (new-onset, no prior history, active steroid course) demands a medical workup first. Face-value reassurance skips that step and commits to a prognosis without a diagnosis.
qb_psy_001.pearl: Psychosis is a syndrome — exclude delirium, substances, medications, and autoimmune causes before settling on a primary disorder.
qb_psy_001.evidence: t_psychosis.md 'Differential and can't-miss mimics' — Always exclude secondary/medical psychosis before settling on a primary disorder. Screen for substance-induced causes (stimulants, cannabis, hallucinogens, withdrawal) and any medical or medication cause; corticosteroids are a recognized secondary cause (general clinical principle, not individually named on this source page). Do not miss autoimmune/limbic encephalitis.

qb_psy_002.stem: A 37-year-old man with schizophrenia has been stable on haloperidol 5 mg/day and sertraline 100 mg/day for a comorbid depressive episode. His sertraline was increased to 150 mg two days ago. He now presents with fever (38.9°C), agitation, diaphoresis, and muscle rigidity. CK is mildly elevated at 680 U/L. The differential includes serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Which finding, if present on examination, would most strongly support serotonin syndrome over neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

options.t: Uniform lead-pipe resistance throughout the passive range of motion of the upper and lower extremities, with normal deep tendon reflexes.

trap.name: Lead-pipe rigidity = NMS, not SS
trap.note: Lead-pipe rigidity — uniform resistance throughout the passive range of motion — is the hallmark of NMS, produced by dopaminergic pathway dysfunction. Serotonin syndrome produces clonus and hyperreflexia, not lead-pipe rigidity; choosing this option confuses the two syndromes' defining physical features.

options.t: Creatine kinase (CK) above 5,000 U/L with rising creatinine suggesting early rhabdomyolysis.

trap.name: Markedly elevated CK = NMS signature
trap.note: Dramatically elevated CK (often tens of thousands) is a hallmark of NMS, driven by sustained muscular rigidity and potential rhabdomyolysis. CK in serotonin syndrome may be mildly elevated but rarely reaches NMS levels; a markedly elevated CK increases suspicion for NMS, not SS.

options.t: Gradual onset of rigidity and fever developing over 48–72 hours after the haloperidol was started three months ago, with no change in the serotonergic regimen.

trap.name: Subacute onset + dopamine blocker = NMS pattern
trap.note: A gradual onset timed to a dopamine-blocking agent rather than to a serotonergic change is the NMS pattern. Serotonin syndrome typically occurs within hours of a serotonergic dose increase or drug addition — the history in this option (no serotonergic change, onset tied to the antipsychotic) would favor NMS.

options.t: Ankle clonus with brisk, brisker-than-baseline deep tendon reflexes throughout the lower extremities.

qb_psy_002.why: Lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia → NMS; clonus + hyperreflexia → SS. The three distractors all describe NMS features: lead-pipe rigidity (A), dramatically elevated CK (B), and subacute onset tied to the dopamine blocker rather than the serotonergic change (C). Ankle clonus with lower-extremity hyperreflexia (D) is the hallmark physical finding of serotonin syndrome — it reflects serotonin-mediated hyperactivation of spinal reflex arcs and is absent in NMS, where rigidity comes from central dopaminergic dysfunction. The added clinical clues — onset after the sertraline increase, mild rather than dramatic CK — also favor SS over NMS. In practice, both syndromes require stopping the offending agent; the physical exam reflex pattern is the fastest bedside discriminator.
qb_psy_002.pearl: NMS vs. SS at the bedside: lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia → NMS (dopamine blocker, subacute onset); clonus + hyperreflexia → SS (serotonergic agent, rapid onset hours).
qb_psy_002.evidence: psychotic_disorders_inpatient_teaching.md 'Neuroleptic malignant syndrome vs. serotonin syndrome' — The key discriminator: lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia = NMS; clonus + hyperreflexia (especially ankle clonus) = SS. Onset timeline and offending agent class support the differentiation (Boyer and Shannon, N Engl J Med 2005; Strawn et al., Am J Psychiatry 2007).

qb_anx_001.stem: A 29-year-old woman admitted for a manic episode is started on risperidone. Two days later she is restless, pacing the hallway, unable to sit through meals, and says she 'can't stop moving.' She denies worsening mood symptoms. Which of the following best explains her presentation?

options.t: Worsening mixed mania with motor agitation — increase the risperidone

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Adding more dopamine blockade to akathisia worsens the very symptom it is meant to treat — the restlessness is medication-induced, not mood-driven.

options.t: New-onset generalized anxiety disorder unmasked by hospitalization stress

trap.name: Missing the iatrogenic cause
trap.note: A new anxiety disorder diagnosis requires ruling out medication-induced causes — akathisia began 48 hours after a dopamine blocker was started.

options.t: Restless legs syndrome — the urge to move is confined to the lower extremities at rest

trap.name: RLS vs akathisia
trap.note: RLS is a distal, rest-provoked urge that improves with movement — akathisia is a global inner restlessness that does not resolve with movement and is not limb-specific.

options.t: Akathisia — medication-induced inner restlessness from dopamine blockade that worsens with more antipsychotic

qb_anx_001.why: Agitation = antipsychotic is the dangerous error: escalating the dopamine blocker intensifies akathisia. Missing the iatrogenic cause leads to a wrong new diagnosis. RLS vs akathisia distinguishes them by distribution and provocation — RLS is limb-specific and rest-provoked; akathisia is global, medication-timed, and worsens with increased dosing.
qb_anx_001.pearl: Akathisia is the classic inpatient miss — inner restlessness from antipsychotics that worsens with more dopamine blockade, not less.
qb_anx_001.evidence: t_anxiety.md 'Differential on the unit' — akathisia is the classic miss: restless, driven motor anxiety from antipsychotics that worsens if you reflexively treat it as 'agitation' with more dopamine blockade.

qb_anx_002.stem: A 28-year-old woman admitted for a severe depressive episode is also found to have untreated PTSD — she endorses daily nightmares, hypervigilance, and avoidance behaviors that have persisted for two years since an assault. She has no history of substance use disorder. After addressing the acute safety concern, which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy for her PTSD?

options.t: Start scheduled lorazepam — benzodiazepines reduce hyperarousal and improve sleep, targeting PTSD's core neurobiological substrate

trap.name: The reflexive benzodiazepine
trap.note: Benzodiazepines drive dependence, falls, and delirium and are not a treatment for PTSD — standing benzodiazepines for anxiety disorders are explicitly to be avoided on the inpatient unit.

options.t: Start an SSRI or SNRI, counsel her about delayed onset, and plan trauma-focused therapy (prolonged exposure or CPT) as a discharge goal
Start propranolol — beta blockade prevents autonomic consolidation of traumatic memories and is first-line for established PTSD

trap.name: Wrong mechanism for PTSD
trap.note: Propranolol is studied as an acute peritraumatic adjunct — it is not first-line pharmacotherapy for established PTSD; SSRIs and SNRIs are.

options.t: Start an antipsychotic for the intrusive re-experiencing — flashback-like episodes indicate psychotic features requiring dopamine blockade

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: Intrusive re-experiencing in PTSD is not psychosis — antipsychotics are not first-line for PTSD and conflating the two is the inpatient trap that delays correct treatment.

qb_anx_002.why: The reflexive benzodiazepine is the most common trap — standing benzos for PTSD create dependence without treating the disorder and are explicitly avoided on the inpatient unit. SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line across all anxiety disorders and PTSD; definitive treatment pairs medication with trauma-focused therapy (prolonged exposure or CPT) planned at discharge. Propranolol is studied in acute peritraumatic settings, not as first-line pharmacotherapy for established PTSD. Antipsychotics conflate re-experiencing with psychosis.
qb_anx_002.pearl: SSRIs/SNRIs are first-line for PTSD — benzodiazepines are a liability on the unit; pair medication with trauma-focused therapy (PE or CPT) at discharge.
qb_anx_002.evidence: t_anxiety.md 'Acute inpatient management' — SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line across anxiety disorders, OCD, and PTSD; avoid standing benzodiazepines on the unit; pair pharmacology with disorder-specific behavioral work — prolonged exposure (PE) and cognitive processing therapy (CPT) for PTSD.

qb_pha_002.stem: A 34-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has just been started on clozapine. He reports feeling better than he has in years. Which ongoing monitoring is most critical for this medication?

options.t: Monthly liver function tests — clozapine is heavily metabolized by the liver and hepatotoxicity is the primary dose-limiting toxicity

trap.name: Wrong monitoring target
trap.note: Hepatotoxicity is not the primary safety concern for clozapine — agranulocytosis is the life-threatening adverse effect that drives ongoing ANC monitoring.

options.t: Weekly absolute neutrophil count (ANC) monitoring — clozapine carries a risk of severe neutropenia (agranulocytosis)
Serum clozapine levels at every visit — toxicity is reliably predicted by drug concentration

trap.name: Treat the number, not the patient
trap.note: Serum levels inform clinical decisions but do not replace the ANC monitoring that the prescribing information calls for.

options.t: Monthly QTc interval on ECG — clozapine's primary dose-limiting toxicity is cardiac arrhythmia

trap.name: Wrong monitoring target
trap.note: QTc prolongation is the primary concern for other antipsychotics (thioridazine, ziprasidone); clozapine's specific safety monitoring is the ANC for agranulocytosis.

qb_pha_002.why: Wrong monitoring target in two forms — LFTs and QTc — and Treat the number not the patient (serum levels without ANC) are the traps. Clozapine's key safety monitoring is the absolute neutrophil count per the prescribing information (the REMS was eliminated in 2025, so this now rests on the prescriber) due to the risk of potentially fatal agranulocytosis. Serum levels and LFTs may be checked but do not constitute the primary safety obligation.
qb_pha_002.pearl: Clozapine requires ANC monitoring for agranulocytosis per its prescribing information (the REMS was eliminated in 2025); also watch for myocarditis, severe constipation/ileus, and seizures.
qb_pha_002.evidence: psychopharm_primer.md — Clozapine's power comes packaged with ongoing ANC monitoring (per prescribing information; the FDA eliminated the clozapine REMS in 2025) — and watch for myocarditis, severe constipation/ileus, and seizures.

link.label: Open the Suicide Risk pocket card

qb_saf_001.stem: A 19-year-old man is admitted after a near-lethal suicide attempt. He has expressed persistent hopelessness and a stated wish to die for three days. On hospital day 4, nurses report he seems 'much better' — calm, well-rested, and telling the team he is ready to go home. His affect is bright and he is chatty with staff. No clinical change or social development explains the shift. Best next step?

options.t: Begin discharge planning — improvement is the goal of admission and this patient has achieved it

trap.name: Sudden improvement = recovery
trap.note: Unexplained brightening after severe suicidality is an established escalation trigger — it is not the same as clinical improvement with a clear cause.

options.t: Reduce his observation level and move him to a lower-acuity room to reinforce the progress

trap.name: Quiet patient = stable patient
trap.note: The calm, engaged patient after a lethal attempt is precisely the scenario the escalation list exists for — reducing vigilance based on surface behavior is the error.

options.t: Escalate to the attending immediately — unexplained sudden improvement after severe suicidality is a warning sign requiring reassessment
Update the safety plan and schedule discharge within 24 hours while the patient is engaged

trap.name: Safety plan = discharge permission slip
trap.note: A safety plan is one component of the risk formulation — it does not substitute for the clinical escalation this presentation demands.

qb_saf_001.why: Sudden improvement = recovery is the most dangerous trap: the pocket card explicitly lists unexplained sudden improvement as an immediate escalation trigger. Quiet patient = stable patient reduces vigilance at exactly the wrong moment. Safety plan = discharge permission slip conflates a tool with a risk decision.
qb_saf_001.pearl: Sudden unexplained improvement after severe suicidality is an escalation trigger, not evidence of recovery.
qb_saf_001.evidence: pg_suicide.md 'What to escalate immediately' — Sudden improvement after severe suicidality without clear explanation.

qb_saf_002.stem: A patient is pacing the hallway, speaking loudly, and waving his hands. He has not threatened anyone and is not in immediate danger of harming himself or others. You are the student. Which response is best?

options.t: Let a nearby staff member know you are engaging, then approach calmly — without blocking his exit or yours — introduce yourself, acknowledge that he looks upset, and offer him a choice — 'Would it help to step somewhere quieter where staff can still see us, or is there something I can get you?'
Return to the nursing station and request a PRN intramuscular medication order before approaching

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Medication is not the default first step when verbal de-escalation has not been attempted — the framework starts with presence and listening, not a syringe.

options.t: Call for additional staff and prepare for restraint in case the patient escalates

trap.name: Restraint first
trap.note: Restraint is the last resort of the least-restrictive principle — preemptive preparation for restraint before de-escalation has been tried violates that principle.

options.t: Instruct him firmly to return to his room or staff will have to intervene

trap.name: Commands over choices
trap.note: Issuing a command rather than offering a choice removes the patient's sense of control — the opposite of what the de-escalation framework centers.

qb_saf_002.why: Agitation = antipsychotic, Restraint first, and Commands over choices are the three forms of the same error: defaulting to force or medication before de-escalation. The Project BETA framework begins with calm presence, acknowledgment of distress, and genuine choices — not commands or preemptive escalation.
qb_saf_002.pearl: Verbal de-escalation — calm presence, acknowledgment, and genuine choices — is the default first response to agitation, not a courtesy step before medication; tell a staff member before you engage, and stay near your exit without blocking the patient's.
qb_saf_002.evidence: agitation.md 'Verbal de-escalation, first' — This is the default response, not a courtesy step. The Project BETA de-escalation framework (Richmond et al. 2012) centers respect, simple boundaries, listening, and offering choices rather than issuing commands.

qb_per_001.stem: A 26-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder tells her student doctor that she trusts only her and that the other staff 'just don't care.' Night nurses describe her as cooperative and warm; day nurses report she screams at them. How is this pattern best understood?

options.t: The patient has genuine rapport with the student and a legitimate complaint about day staff behavior

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: Taking the patient's report at face value misses the clinical process — the same person being warm to nights and hostile to days is the diagnostic picture, not a staff quality problem.

options.t: Splitting — a feature of BPD in which people are experienced as entirely good or bad, requiring team consistency as the antidote
Deliberate manipulation — the patient is consciously exploiting the split to get preferential treatment

trap.name: Manipulation framing
trap.note: Labeling splitting as manipulation invites punitive responses and misses the clinical process — it is a symptom of affect dysregulation, not a conscious strategy.

options.t: A delusional belief about staff intentions that warrants diagnostic reassessment for a psychotic disorder

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: Splitting is not a fixed false belief — the patient's experience of staff shifts with context and person, which is characteristic of BPD, not psychosis.

qb_per_001.why: Face-value reassurance takes the report at face value and misses the clinical process. Manipulation framing leads to punitive responses that worsen therapeutic alliance. Psychosis = schizophrenia misapplies a diagnostic frame to a personality-disorder phenomenon. Splitting — all-good or all-bad experiencing of staff — is a feature of BPD; the intervention is team communication and consistency, not confrontation.
qb_per_001.pearl: Splitting is a feature of BPD, not a character flaw — team consistency and shared notes are the antidote, not confrontation.
qb_per_001.evidence: t_personality.md — Splitting — experiencing staff as all-good or all-bad — is common and is a feature of the illness, not a character flaw or manipulation.

qb_per_002.stem: A 22-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder is admitted in crisis with severe anxiety and sleep disturbance. She has been engaged in DBT for six months with good skill use documented. She is asking for 'something for her nerves.' The pharmacologic approach most consistent with evidence-based practice for BPD is which of the following?

options.t: Prescribe lorazepam PRN — addressing the anxiety will help her engage with skills

trap.name: The reflexive benzodiazepine
trap.note: Benzodiazepines in BPD are associated with the highest risk of suicide attempt or suicide death of any psychotropic class studied and worsen disinhibition — they are contraindicated in this context.

options.t: Add a nightly benzodiazepine for sleep — insomnia is fueling the crisis cycle

trap.name: The reflexive benzodiazepine
trap.note: Scheduled benzodiazepines compound the dependence and suicide risk seen with this class in BPD — sleep disturbance in crisis is treated with the crisis, not with hypnotics.

options.t: Add an SSRI — anxiety in a BPD patient with good DBT engagement suggests an undertreated mood component requiring pharmacological augmentation.

trap.name: Polypharmacy first
trap.note: Adding a second antidepressant without evidence of benefit in BPD, when DBT skill use is documented, substitutes medication for the more effective behavioral approach.

options.t: Minimize pharmacotherapy — if needed, a single low-risk agent for ≤1 week, such as a sedating antihistamine, rather than a benzodiazepine.

qb_per_002.why: The reflexive benzodiazepine in two forms (PRN and scheduled) and Polypharmacy first are the traps. No medication treats BPD itself; the evidence base supports skills over pills, and benzodiazepines in BPD are associated with the highest risk of suicide attempt or suicide death of any psychotropic class studied (HR 1.61, Lieslehto 2023, registry data). The NICE-aligned approach is a single, low-risk agent at the minimum dose for ≤1 week — NICE names a sedative antihistamine (low side-effect burden, low misuse potential, relatively safe in overdose) rather than a benzodiazepine.
qb_per_002.pearl: Benzodiazepines in BPD are associated with the highest risk of suicide attempt or suicide death of any class studied (registry data) — reach for skills, not pills.
qb_per_002.evidence: t_personality.md — do not start or escalate benzodiazepines — they carry the highest risk of attempted or completed suicide of any psychotropic class studied in BPD (HR 1.61, Lieslehto 2023) and worsen disinhibition. If a crisis genuinely needs pharmacology, follow the NICE rule: a single agent at the minimum effective dose for ≤1 week (NICE names a sedative antihistamine — low side-effect burden, low misuse potential, relatively safe in overdose — rather than a benzodiazepine).

qb_chd_001.stem: A 19-year-old college student is brought to the inpatient unit by his parents after three weeks of dramatically decreased need for sleep (sleeping two to three hours and feeling rested), expansive and grandiose mood, pressured speech, and impulsive spending. His parents note he has always been 'a little hyper' in school but never like this. He takes no medications and denies substance use. Most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Bipolar disorder, manic episode — the episodic 3-week course with decreased need for sleep and grandiosity distinguishes this from ADHD
ADHD, first recognized in adulthood — the impulsivity and hyperactivity confirm childhood-onset ADHD now decompensated

trap.name: ADHD vs mania
trap.note: ADHD is chronic, pervasive, and cross-situational from childhood — an episodic, 3-week onset with grandiosity and dramatically decreased need for sleep is not ADHD, even with a baseline 'hyper' history.

options.t: Brief psychotic disorder — the grandiosity indicates loss of reality testing

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: Grandiosity in the setting of a manic episode is a mood symptom — it does not automatically indicate a primary psychotic disorder.

options.t: Adjustment disorder — the academic stress of college explains the sleep changes and mood elevation

trap.name: Adjustment by default
trap.note: Attributing a full manic symptom cluster to situational stress avoids the diagnosis and delays treatment — adjustment disorder cannot account for decreased need for sleep and grandiosity sustained over three weeks.

qb_chd_001.why: ADHD vs mania is the key discrimination: ADHD is chronic and cross-situational from childhood, not episodic with decreased need for sleep and grandiosity. Psychosis = schizophrenia misreads a mood symptom as a primary psychotic feature. Adjustment by default collapses a manic episode into a stress reaction.
qb_chd_001.pearl: ADHD is chronic and cross-situational from childhood; mania is episodic — episodic ADHD-like symptoms are a mood or substance flag.
qb_chd_001.evidence: t_neurodev.md — ADHD vs bipolar mania: ADHD is chronic, pervasive, and cross-situational from childhood; mania is episodic with mood elevation, decreased need for sleep, and grandiosity. Episodic 'ADHD-like' symptoms are a mood or substance flag.

qb_oth_001.stem: A 16-year-old with anorexia nervosa is medically admitted at about 75% of median BMI with a resting heart rate of 42 bpm. Potassium, phosphate, and magnesium are normal, and she has no other acute illness. Which initial nutrition plan is most appropriate?

options.t: Start at no more than 1,000 kcal/day and advance slowly over the first one to two weeks, because a low starting target is the safest way to prevent refeeding syndrome.

trap.name: Underfeeding as safety
trap.note: Her malnutrition is moderate and she has no highest-risk features, so a low start prolongs underfeeding without making refeeding safer — refeeding risk tracks the degree of malnutrition, not the starting calories. A cautious start is kept for the highest-risk patients.

options.t: Give a prophylactic anxiolytic and observe for 24 hours before introducing any nutrition, because anxiety raises metabolic demand.

trap.name: Sedation before nutrition
trap.note: Refeeding risk is metabolic (phosphate, potassium, and magnesium shifts), not anxiety-driven; sedation is not part of refeeding, and delaying nutrition only prolongs starvation.

options.t: Hold all nutrition until her electrolytes have been stable for 48 hours, then begin feeding.

trap.name: Normalize first
trap.note: Her electrolytes are already normal, and feeding is not delayed to normalise electrolytes in any case — monitoring and repletion run alongside refeeding.

options.t: Start at a higher-calorie target, advance daily, and check phosphate, potassium, and magnesium closely; give thiamine.

qb_oth_001.why: Underfeeding as safety, Sedation before nutrition, and Normalize first all delay nutrition without making refeeding safer. For a medically admitted adolescent with moderate malnutrition and no highest-risk features, current guidance supports starting at a higher-calorie target and advancing daily with close phosphate, potassium, and magnesium monitoring, because refeeding risk tracks the degree of malnutrition rather than the starting calories. A cautious start is reserved for the highest-risk patients — for example adults with BMI < 13 plus acute illness or abnormal electrolytes.
qb_oth_001.pearl: Refeeding: risk tracks malnutrition, not the starting calories — start higher unless highest-risk, check phosphate/K/Mg daily, give thiamine, and don't underfeed.
qb_oth_001.evidence: t_eating.md — Refeeding syndrome = watch the phosphate — risk tracks the degree of malnutrition, not the starting calories; most patients can start higher with daily phosphate/K/Mg checks, and the most malnourished or medically unstable start cautiously; give thiamine.

qb_eth_001.stem: A 45-year-old man with schizophrenia is voluntarily admitted and refuses his prescribed antipsychotic. When asked, he explains what the medication is for, articulates specific concerns about its side effects, understands the risks of not taking it, and asks whether alternatives exist. Best next step?

options.t: Conduct a formal capacity assessment; if he has capacity, his refusal must be respected, documented, and an alternative offered
Override the refusal — voluntarily admitted patients accept the prescribed treatment plan as a condition of admission

trap.name: Refusal = no capacity
trap.note: Voluntary admission does not imply consent to every prescribed treatment — a patient with demonstrated decision-making abilities retains the right to refuse.

options.t: Seek an emergency court order — a schizophrenia diagnosis with medication refusal requires judicial review

trap.name: Refusal = no capacity
trap.note: A psychiatric diagnosis does not equal incapacity — capacity is four specific, assessable abilities; if he has them, a court order for medication requires a non-emergency legal process, not reflexive judicial referral.

options.t: Discharge him against medical advice — he is voluntary and refusing treatment

trap.name: Discharge for refusal
trap.note: Discharging a patient for refusing a medication without first assessing capacity bypasses the clinical and ethical obligation — the appropriate response is assessment, not expulsion.

qb_eth_001.why: Refusal = no capacity in two forms — assumed from admission type and assumed from diagnosis — is the central error. Capacity is decision-specific and clinical: the four abilities are assessed, not inferred from the admission voluntary/involuntary status or from a psychiatric diagnosis. Discharge for refusal conflates refusal with grounds for discharge. This patient's demonstrated abilities (communicating, understanding, appreciating, reasoning) point toward capacity — in which case his refusal must be honored.
qb_eth_001.pearl: Capacity is decision-specific and clinical — a psychiatric diagnosis and even a refusal do not equal incapacity; assess the four abilities.
qb_eth_001.evidence: ethics_legal.md — Capacity is decision-specific and clinical (a physician assesses it). The four abilities: communicate a choice, understand, appreciate, and reason. Competent patients (including many involuntarily hospitalized ones) generally retain the right to refuse medication. Overriding that refusal requires either a true emergency or a separate legal/adjudicated process.

qb_rel_002.stem: A family meeting is held on hospital day 3 for a 29-year-old man admitted for a first manic episode. His mother interrupts repeatedly: 'He does this every time he stops his medication — he's selfish and he makes us all suffer.' She is tearful and wringing her hands. The attending invites the student to observe what is happening. What is the student's best understanding of this dynamic?

options.t: The mother's criticism is accurate and should be incorporated into the discharge plan as a documented adherence barrier

trap.name: Criticism as fact
trap.note: Accepting high expressed emotion as objective reporting misses the fear and grief driving it — and forecloses the most clinically valuable phase of the meeting.

options.t: The meeting should be suspended — the mother's distress is dysregulating the patient and the therapeutic goals cannot be met

trap.name: Terminate for emotion
trap.note: Cutting off the emotional climate phase forfeits the part of the family meeting where outcomes change most — this phase should be protected, not terminated.

options.t: The mother should be gently corrected about the medication-stopping narrative to address the factual inaccuracy

trap.name: Correct the narrative
trap.note: Redirecting to facts before the emotional climate is acknowledged closes off the therapeutic opportunity — expressed emotion must be heard before it can shift.

options.t: The mother is showing expressed emotion — criticism that likely masks fear and grief — and the student's task is to validate the feeling behind it before moving to problem-solving

qb_rel_002.why: Criticism as fact accepts EE as objective reporting; Terminate for emotion cuts off the highest-yield phase of the meeting; Correct the narrative redirects to facts before the emotional climate has been heard. Expressed emotion — criticism, hostility, emotional over-involvement — is the measurable family dynamic that predicts relapse. De-shaming and validating the underlying fear or grief, without correcting in the moment, is what the playbook calls the phase that most changes outcomes.
qb_rel_002.pearl: Expressed emotion — criticism, hostility, emotional over-involvement — often masks fear; validate it without correcting it in the moment, because this phase is where outcomes change.
qb_rel_002.evidence: family_playbook.md 'Hear the family and read the emotional climate' — Listen for expressed emotion — criticism, hostility, and emotional over-involvement — without correcting it in the moment. De-shame: frame symptoms and behavior as illness and regulation, not character or fault. This is the phase that most changes outcomes; protect the time for it.

qb_cog_008.stem: Psychiatry is consulted on an 82-year-old man in the surgical ICU on postoperative day 3. He is quiet, slow to respond, and sleeping between nursing checks — his nurse reports he was interactive at yesterday's evening assessment. His CAM is positive. The covering team wonders why this presentation is more concerning than a 'hyperactive' delirious patient. Which statement best explains the clinical risk?

options.t: Hyperactive delirium carries worse outcomes — the agitation, pulling at lines, and fall risk create more immediate danger than a quiet, withdrawn presentation.

trap.name: Hyperactive = higher risk
trap.note: Hyperactive delirium is more visible and more likely to trigger intervention — hypoactive delirium carries worse overall outcomes because it is commonly missed, mislabeled as depression, and associated with higher mortality.

options.t: The two subtypes have equivalent outcomes — motor presentation does not predict prognosis; treatment targets the underlying cause regardless of subtype.

trap.name: Subtypes equivalent
trap.note: Motor subtype does affect outcomes — hypoactive delirium carries worse prognosis in part because under-recognition delays treatment of the underlying cause.

options.t: Hypoactive delirium responds better to antipsychotics — the reduced agitation creates a therapeutic window for pharmacologic intervention that hyperactive delirium does not allow.

trap.name: Hypoactive = better pharmacologic target
trap.note: Antipsychotics are not for delirium prevention or routine management in either subtype — they are reserved for dangerous agitation; hypoactive delirium is not a 'pharmacologic window,' it is a missed diagnosis with worse mortality.

options.t: Hypoactive delirium carries worse outcomes precisely because it goes unrecognized — the quiet, non-interactive patient does not trigger intervention; it is commonly mislabeled as depression and associated with higher mortality.

qb_cog_008.why: Hyperactive = higher risk, Subtypes equivalent, and Hypoactive = better pharmacologic target all invert the clinical reality. The source states: 'The hypoactive form is the one that gets missed, and it carries worse outcomes precisely because no one is alarmed by a quiet patient.' Recognition requires deliberate screening — the CAM is the tool.
qb_cog_008.pearl: Hypoactive delirium = the dangerous one: commonly missed, worse outcomes, easily mislabeled as depression.
qb_cog_008.evidence: delirium.md — The hypoactive form is the one that gets missed, and it carries worse outcomes precisely because no one is alarmed by a quiet patient. Hypoactive delirium is the dangerous one: commonly missed, worse outcomes, and easily mislabeled as depression.

qb_cog_009.stem: A 68-year-old woman is admitted after 4 months of progressive cognitive decline and withdrawal. Neuropsychological testing suggests a moderate amnestic syndrome. She has no known prior psychiatric or neurological history. Which is the most appropriate first-line laboratory workup before assigning a neurodegenerative diagnosis?

options.t: CBC, CMP, TSH, B12/folate, and consider RPR/HIV — reversible causes must be excluded before a neurodegenerative diagnosis is established.
Anti-NMDA receptor antibody panel — autoimmune encephalitis mimics dementia and should be ruled out first in all new presentations.

trap.name: Jump to autoimmune
trap.note: Anti-NMDA antibodies are appropriate in subacute encephalitis with psychiatric features, seizures, or movement disorder — a progressive 4-month amnestic syndrome warrants the standard reversible-cause panel first.

options.t: Brain MRI with gadolinium — structural imaging is the single most important diagnostic step for a new dementia presentation.

trap.name: Imaging before labs
trap.note: Structural imaging does belong in the initial workup of a new cognitive diagnosis — it is the only way NPH or a chronic subdural is found — but the stem asks for the first-line *laboratory* screen, and gadolinium is not what makes imaging useful here. MRI is preferred and expedited for atypical, rapid, focal, or early-onset presentations.

options.t: APOE genotyping — an APOE ε4 allele would confirm Alzheimer disease and guide management.

trap.name: Genetic confirmation
trap.note: APOE status informs population-level risk but does not diagnose AD and is not part of the standard workup — reversible causes must be excluded first.

qb_cog_009.why: Jump to autoimmune and Genetic confirmation both skip the foundational step. The reversible-cause panel — B12/folate, TSH, CMP, and when indicated RPR/HIV — must precede neurodegenerative labeling because these conditions are treatable and clinically indistinguishable at presentation. APOE genotyping is not a diagnostic standard. Structural imaging is part of the same initial workup rather than a later step, but it is not the laboratory screen this stem asks for, and it does not require gadolinium.
qb_cog_009.pearl: Every new cognitive diagnosis gets both halves of the reversible screen: the panel (B12/folate, TSH, CMP, ± RPR/HIV) and structural imaging — labs cannot exclude NPH or a chronic subdural.
qb_cog_009.evidence: t_neurocog.md 'Initial workup' — Labs to catch reversible causes: CBC, CMP, TSH, B12/folate, and — when indicated — HIV and RPR/treponemal testing. Neuroimaging (CT or MRI) as part of the initial workup of any new cognitive diagnosis — it is the only way the NPH and chronic subdural hematoma on the reversible list above get found — with MRI preferred, and expedited for atypical, rapid, focal, or early-onset presentations.

qb_cog_010.stem: A 78-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment is admitted for worsening confusion and agitation over the past week. She recently started diphenhydramine nightly for insomnia and oxybutynin for urge incontinence. The student reviews her medication list. Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.t: Add risperidone for the agitation — it is the most evidence-based pharmacotherapy for behavioral symptoms in cognitive impairment.

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Adding a dopamine blocker before addressing the obvious medication-related drivers is pharmacologically backwards and potentially harmful.

options.t: Order a 24-hour EEG — medication-induced encephalopathy can produce seizure patterns that explain cognitive worsening.

trap.name: Jump to testing
trap.note: Costly procedural workup before deprescribing the medications most likely causing the problem is a diagnostic error of omission.

options.t: Flag diphenhydramine and oxybutynin as high-risk anticholinergic agents for the team, escalate for deprescribing, and recommend non-pharmacologic sleep and bladder strategies.
Reassure the family that mild cognitive impairment commonly worsens under medical stress and will recover once she is discharged.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: Dismissing a potentially reversible pharmacologic cause without addressing identifiable high-risk medications is a clinical error of omission.

qb_cog_010.why: Agitation = antipsychotic and Face-value reassurance both bypass the diagnosis. Anticholinergic burden is a recognized, reversible driver of cognitive worsening in older adults — diphenhydramine and oxybutynin are among the Beers Criteria's most flagged agents. Jump to testing substitutes cost for the straightforward clinical action. The geriatric psychiatry principle: the drug list is often the diagnosis; deprescribing is active treatment.
qb_cog_010.pearl: In older adults with cognitive change, the medication list is often the diagnosis — assess anticholinergic burden and deprescribe before adding anything.
qb_cog_010.evidence: t_geri.md 'Acute inpatient management' — Apply the Beers Criteria and assess cumulative anticholinergic burden, then actively deprescribe deliriogenic and high-risk agents. 'High-yield pearls' — The drug list is often the diagnosis — deprescribing is active treatment.

tier2.q: Why do anticholinergic medications disproportionately impair cognition in older adults?

options.t: Older adults have reduced hepatic metabolism, causing higher serum drug levels than predicted for a given dose.
Older adults have reduced cholinergic reserve due to aging and often concurrent dementia — blocking acetylcholine impairs attention and memory in a system already depleted.
Anticholinergic agents cause orthostatic hypotension, reducing cerebral perfusion and producing cognitive symptoms.
The mechanism is peripheral: urinary retention and constipation trigger systemic inflammation that secondarily impairs cognition.

tier2.why: It is a pharmacodynamic-reserve problem, not primarily pharmacokinetic. Acetylcholine is essential for attention and memory; older adults — especially those with early Alzheimer or MCI — have fewer cholinergic neurons. Blocking the remaining ones with an anticholinergic produces an outsized, often rapid cognitive effect that clinically mimics dementia progression. This is why cholinesterase inhibitors (which increase acetylcholine) treat AD, and anticholinergics are its pharmacologic enemy.

qb_cog_012.stem: A 74-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history is brought to the emergency department by her family. She has developed, over the past month, a fixed belief that her neighbors are poisoning her food and has stopped eating. She is alert, coherent, and oriented. There is no mood disturbance. Which is the most important next step?

options.t: Diagnose late-onset schizophrenia — paranoid delusions in late life unexplained by a mood disorder represent a primary psychotic illness.

trap.name: Psychosis = schizophrenia
trap.note: First-episode psychosis in a 74-year-old has an extensive organic differential — labeling it late-onset schizophrenia without a medical workup is premature diagnostic closure.

options.t: Start an antipsychotic immediately — the refusal to eat constitutes an acute safety emergency requiring empirical treatment.

trap.name: Treat before diagnosis
trap.note: The safety concern is real but empirical antipsychotic treatment without an organic workup can mask a reversible medical or neurological cause.

options.t: Reassure the family that paranoid ideation is a normal variant of cognitive aging.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: Paranoid ideation is not a normal aging variant — in an older adult with no prior psychiatric history, it is a medical red flag requiring evaluation.

options.t: Conduct a medical workup to exclude organic causes of new-onset psychosis — including delirium, medication effect, CNS lesion, metabolic derangement, and autoimmune encephalitis — before establishing a primary psychiatric diagnosis.

qb_cog_012.why: Psychosis = schizophrenia, Treat before diagnosis, and Face-value reassurance all skip the foundational step. New-onset psychosis in an older adult without a prior psychiatric history is a medical emergency until proven otherwise. The differential includes delirium, CNS lesion, metabolic cause, autoimmune encephalitis, and medication-induced psychosis — all requiring workup before a primary psychotic diagnosis is made.
qb_cog_012.pearl: New psychosis in an older adult is a medical emergency until proven otherwise — work up before labeling or treating.
qb_cog_012.evidence: t_geri.md 'High-yield pearls' — New psychosis in an older adult is delirium or a medical cause until proven otherwise.

qb_cog_014.stem: A 29-year-old woman with schizophrenia has been mute and posturing for 2 days. Today she is found febrile to 39.6°C, diaphoretic, hypotensive, with lead-pipe rigidity and a markedly elevated CK. Her antipsychotic was increased yesterday. Best next step?

options.t: Administer additional lorazepam challenge doses and observe on the psychiatric unit — the rigidity suggests catatonic stupor responding to benzodiazepines.

trap.name: Underestimate the emergency
trap.note: Autonomic instability + hyperthermia + rigidity + elevated CK after antipsychotic escalation is a medical emergency requiring transfer, not continued psychiatric unit observation.

options.t: Increase the antipsychotic — this is a catatonic variant of treatment-resistant psychosis requiring more aggressive dopamine blockade.

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: In a febrile patient with elevated CK and rigidity after an antipsychotic was escalated, this is NMS/malignant catatonia — increasing the dopamine blocker accelerates the emergency.

options.t: Stop all antipsychotics, move to a medical unit for monitoring, continue lorazepam, and arrange ECT if there is no rapid improvement.
Treat empirically for sepsis — fever, hypotension, and elevated CK indicate bacterial infection requiring antibiotics.

trap.name: Sepsis first
trap.note: Sepsis is on the differential but the timing (antipsychotic escalated yesterday), catatonic signs on exam, and the specific combination of lead-pipe rigidity + fever + elevated CK after a dopamine blocker constitute NMS/malignant catatonia until proven otherwise.

qb_cog_014.why: Underestimate the emergency and Agitation = antipsychotic are the two clinical catastrophes. This is NMS/malignant catatonia: fever, autonomic instability, lead-pipe rigidity, elevated CK after antipsychotic escalation. The correct sequence is stop all antipsychotics, transfer to a medical unit for hemodynamic monitoring, continue lorazepam — benzodiazepines remain first-line pharmacotherapy for malignant catatonia while ECT is arranged — and pursue ECT emergently if the patient does not rapidly improve; the error in option A is observation on the psychiatric unit, not the lorazepam, and certainly not more antipsychotic. Obtain urgent psychiatry and neurology consultation.
qb_cog_014.pearl: Malignant catatonia overlaps with NMS: fever + rigidity + elevated CK + autonomic instability after antipsychotic exposure — stop antipsychotics, transfer to medical, continue lorazepam, and consider ECT urgently.
qb_cog_014.evidence: catatonia.md — The emergency you must never miss is malignant catatonia: autonomic instability, hyperthermia, and rigidity that clinically overlaps with neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). ECT is the treatment for severe, malignant, or benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia and should not be delayed when the patient is deteriorating.

tier2.q: Why does ECT have a role in malignant catatonia when benzodiazepines have not been effective?

options.t: ECT provides dopamine agonism that directly counteracts antipsychotic receptor blockade.
ECT is used because it avoids all pharmacologic agents, preventing further receptor blockade.

ECT directly treats the catatonic syndrome regardless of etiology — it is the definitive treatment for malignant or benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia and it can work before the antipsychotic has fully cleared (the antipsychotic is still stopped).
ECT is a last resort used only after a second antipsychotic trial has failed in treatment-resistant psychosis.

tier2.why: ECT acts directly on the motor and autonomic systems driving catatonia — its mechanism bypasses the pharmacologic state that triggered the syndrome. The BAP 2023 catatonia guideline endorses ECT for severe, refractory, or malignant catatonia as a treatment that should not be delayed when the patient is deteriorating. The example here illustrates this: benzodiazepines alone may be insufficient for malignant presentations, so ECT should not be delayed if lorazepam does not produce rapid improvement — the antipsychotic is still stopped, and ECT can be lifesaving before it has fully cleared.

qb_cog_015.stem: An 82-year-old man with moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease is currently on donepezil 10 mg daily. His neurologist asks the student to identify what pharmacotherapy optimization is supported by evidence for this stage of disease.

options.t: Increase donepezil to the maximum tolerated dose — dose escalation of cholinesterase inhibitors alone is the evidence-based approach for moderate-to-severe disease.

trap.name: Dose escalation alone
trap.note: Dose escalation of a cholinesterase inhibitor alone is not the evidence-based approach for moderate-to-severe AD — memantine should be added.

options.t: Add memantine — combination of a cholinesterase inhibitor and memantine (NMDA antagonist) is the evidence-based pharmacotherapy for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease.
Switch to a rivastigmine patch — transdermal delivery is more effective than oral donepezil in advanced disease.

trap.name: Newer = better
trap.note: Formulation does not determine efficacy — donepezil is appropriate; the treatment gap is the absence of memantine, not the delivery route.

options.t: Start a monoclonal anti-amyloid antibody — these agents are now standard of care for all stages of Alzheimer.

trap.name: Newer = better
trap.note: Anti-amyloid antibodies modestly slow early Alzheimer progression and require amyloid confirmation and specialized monitoring; they are not standard of care for all stages and are not started on an inpatient psychiatry unit.

qb_cog_015.why: Dose escalation alone and Newer = better in two forms. For mild-to-moderate AD, cholinesterase inhibitors alone are the standard. For moderate-to-severe AD, adding memantine is the evidence-based optimization. Anti-amyloid antibodies are specialist-initiated, amyloid-confirmed, and restricted to early disease.
qb_cog_015.pearl: Cholinesterase inhibitors for mild-to-moderate AD; add memantine for moderate-to-severe disease.
qb_cog_015.evidence: t_neurocog.md 'Acute inpatient management' — Cognitive symptoms: cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) for mild–moderate Alzheimer/Lewy body disease; add memantine (NMDA antagonist) for moderate–severe disease.

qb_cog_016.stem: A 73-year-old woman with recurrent major depression (last treated 5 years ago) is referred for cognitive evaluation after 3 months of 'memory problems.' On formal cognitive testing she scores in the impaired range on delayed recall but consistently answers 'I don't know' rather than confabulating; she is slow to initiate answers and appears effortfully disengaged. She remains alert and attentive, and scores 22 on the PHQ-9. Most appropriate next step?

options.t: Diagnose major neurocognitive disorder — the cognitive test scores confirm a dementia syndrome independent of mood.

trap.name: Scores = diagnosis
trap.note: Cognitive test performance in the context of active major depression does not establish dementia — scores may normalize with successful mood treatment in pseudodementia.

options.t: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor — the episodic memory impairment indicates Alzheimer-spectrum disease requiring pharmacotherapy.

trap.name: Treat the number, not the patient
trap.note: Cholinesterase inhibitors are not indicated until reversible causes, including depression, are excluded — treating the score without treating the depression is the error.

options.t: Order an amyloid PET scan — direct amyloid visualization definitively distinguishes depression-associated cognitive impairment from Alzheimer disease.

trap.name: Jump to advanced imaging
trap.note: Amyloid PET is a research and specialist tool, not a first-line workup step — the well-established clinical approach is to treat the depression and reassess cognition.

options.t: Prioritize treatment of the depressive episode and reassess cognitive function after remission — the pattern of 'I don't know' responses, effortful disengagement, and a PHQ-9 of 22 is consistent with pseudodementia that may resolve with antidepressant treatment.

qb_cog_016.why: Scores = diagnosis, Treat the number not the patient, and Jump to advanced imaging all bypass the pseudodementia maneuver. 'I don't know' responses with effortful disengagement and preserved alertness — rather than confabulation and unawareness — is the clinical signature of depression-associated cognitive impairment (Caine 1981). The correct next step is antidepressant treatment and follow-up cognitive assessment.
qb_cog_016.pearl: Pseudodementia: 'I don't know' with effortful disengagement and preserved alertness — treat the depression first and reassess cognition; scores may fully normalize.
qb_cog_016.evidence: t_geri.md — Depression can masquerade as cognitive impairment — the pseudodementia presentation (Caine 1981), where patients say 'I don't know' rather than confabulate, show effortful disengagement, and improve cognitively when mood is treated.

link.label: Open the Suicide Risk pocket card

qb_saf_003.stem: A 22-year-old man is admitted following a suicide attempt by acetaminophen overdose. When the student asks about means restriction, he asks only: 'Do you have access to anything dangerous at home?' The patient answers 'no.' The attending asks what a complete means safety assessment requires. Which response is best?

options.t: Ask the patient if he feels safe returning home — a verbal assurance of safety constitutes adequate means restriction documentation.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: A general feeling-of-safety answer is not a means safety assessment — specific items must be asked about explicitly and the plan for restriction must be named.

options.t: Ask specifically about firearms, stockpiled medications, sharps and ligatures, and who will remove or secure each item — then ask how it will be confirmed before discharge.
Have the patient and family sign a no-harm contract — a signed document constitutes the means safety plan.

trap.name: Safety plan = discharge permission slip
trap.note: No-harm contracts are not evidence-based as a risk-reduction measure and do not substitute for specific, actionable means restriction counseling.

options.t: Document 'means safety discussed' in the note — documenting the discussion fulfills the clinical obligation.

trap.name: Document and continue
trap.note: 'Means safety discussed' without specifying the items addressed and the restriction plan is weak documentation that does not fulfill the clinical obligation.

qb_saf_003.why: Face-value reassurance and Document and continue are both documentation traps. Means safety requires asking by item — firearms, stockpiled medications, sharps, ligatures, and the patient-specific methods the presentation revealed — and confirming who will secure them and how the team will know it happened. A general safety question or a no-harm contract does not accomplish this.
qb_saf_003.pearl: Means safety = ask by item (firearms, medications, sharps), name who will secure them, and confirm how the team will know.
qb_saf_003.evidence: pg_suicide.md 'Means Safety' — Ask specifically. Do not say only 'we discussed safety.' Include: Firearms. Stockpiled medication. Sharps or ligatures when relevant. Who will remove/secure means. How it will be confirmed.

qb_saf_005.stem: A 38-year-old woman is admitted after a near-lethal suicide attempt. She has three young children and is an ICU nurse. A student notes 'strong family ties and professional identity' as protective factors and proposes these substantially mitigate her acute risk. The attending asks the student to refine this reasoning. Which statement is most accurate?

options.t: The number of protective factors is inversely proportional to acute risk — more factors reliably indicate lower risk.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: The number of protective factors does not reliably predict acute risk — their credibility and availability during the risk window are what matter, not the count.

options.t: Protective factors reduce risk only if they are credible and available during the risk window — family who cannot be reached does not help in a crisis.
Professional status significantly reduces suicide risk — healthcare workers have lower suicide death rates than the general population.

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: Healthcare workers do not have lower suicide death rates — female nurses die by suicide at about twice the rate of women in the general population (Davis, JAMA Psychiatry 2021), and professional identity may create barriers to seeking help rather than functioning as a protective factor.

options.t: Protective factors and acute risk factors can be numerically compared — strong protective factors offset recent preparatory behavior in the calculation.

trap.name: Safety plan = discharge permission slip
trap.note: Protective factors and acute risk factors are not numerically additive — protective factors must be evaluated for real-time credibility, and preparatory behavior is a hard escalation indicator.

qb_saf_005.why: Face-value reassurance appears throughout. Protective factors are not protective if they are geographically distant, unavailable, or theoretically present but non-operative during the crisis. Healthcare worker status does not protect against suicide. The page states explicitly: 'Protective factors are not magic. They matter only if they are credible and available during the risk window.'
qb_saf_005.pearl: Protective factors matter only if they are credible and available during the risk window — not as a list, but as real-time assets.
qb_saf_005.evidence: pg_suicide.md — Protective factors are not magic. They matter only if they are credible and available during the risk window.

qb_saf_006.stem: A student is asked to draft the safety note for a patient admitted with active suicidal ideation, a stated plan, and unsecured firearm access. Which of the following best illustrates strong safety documentation?

options.t: "Patient endorses suicidal ideation. Reviewed the risks, benefits, and alternatives of hospitalization with the patient at length; patient verbalizes understanding of the plan and agrees to continued treatment on the inpatient unit."

trap.name: Document and continue
trap.note: Consent documentation does not substitute for a safety formulation — reviewing risks and benefits of hospitalization does not record chronic factors, acute drivers, protective factor limits, or modifiable targets.

options.t: "Denies SI/HI. No acute safety concerns."

trap.name: Denies SI = low risk
trap.note: This is the prototypical weak documentation: it records a denial without any formulation, omits the known risk factors, and provides no reasoning for the safety decision.

options.t: "Acute suicide risk elevated: active plan, persistent insomnia, escalating alcohol use, unsecured firearms. Chronic risk: prior attempt, family history. Targets: means restriction, substance stabilization. Continue inpatient care."
"Patient stated: 'I want to die and I have a gun at home.' Verbatim suicidal statement documented per policy."

trap.name: Quotes = documentation
trap.note: Verbatim quotes capture content but do not constitute a risk formulation — the clinician's reasoning about severity, modifying factors, and the safety plan is absent; a defensible note requires formulation, not just transcription.

qb_saf_006.why: Document and continue, Denies SI = low risk, and Quotes = documentation all replace formulation with something easier to write. Strong safety documentation names chronic factors, acute drivers, protective factors with limits (omitted in the keyed example for brevity — add them), modifiable targets, and the current plan. 'Denies SI/HI. No acute safety concerns.' is the example the page uses for the weakest possible documentation.
qb_saf_006.pearl: Strong safety documentation = chronic factors + acute drivers + protective factors with limits + modifiable targets + current plan — not 'denies SI/HI.'
qb_saf_006.evidence: pg_suicide.md 'Documentation Sentence' — Strong: [detailed formulation with acute risk factors, chronic risk, means safety status, and plan]. Weak: 'Denies SI/HI. No acute safety concerns.'

qb_saf_008.stem: A medical student is alone with a patient who says: 'I feel so much better — can you put in a good word with the team about going home today?' The student has not been briefed on this patient's risk. Which response is most appropriate?

options.t: Affirm to the patient that she appears improved and will relay this to the team, then complete a brief suicide screen to provide the team with an update.

trap.name: Student clears patient
trap.note: Affirming improvement to the patient and conducting an independent assessment crosses the student role boundary — the student cannot produce or communicate a dispositive safety determination.

options.t: Explain that discharge is the team's decision, then complete and document a formal suicide risk assessment in the medical record based on this conversation.

trap.name: Student clears patient
trap.note: Independently completing and documenting a formal risk assessment in the chart is well outside the student role — the student's job is to gather and relay the patient's report to the team, not to produce a signed clinical assessment.

options.t: Reassure the patient that the team is working toward discharge and provide the hospital's crisis line number.

trap.name: Reassure and defer
trap.note: Providing a crisis line to an admitted patient implies discharge is coming; the student is implying endorsement of a decision the team hasn't made, without any supervisory loop.

options.t: Tell the patient that discharge is the team's decision and that you will let the attending know she wants to discuss it — then inform the team promptly.

qb_saf_008.why: Student clears patient in two forms — direct affirmation and independent documentation — both cross the role boundary. The student's role is to ask, observe, and report to the team — not to clear a patient for discharge or to produce an independent safety assessment. Reassure and defer leaves the student in a limbo of implied endorsement without any supervisory loop.
qb_saf_008.pearl: Students can ask, observe, and report to the team — they cannot independently clear a patient for discharge or conduct a solo risk assessment.
qb_saf_008.evidence: pg_suicide.md 'Student Role' — You cannot: Clear a patient for discharge independently.

qb_saf_010.stem: A team is debriefing after a physical restraint episode involving a Black patient on the inpatient unit. A student asks what the published evidence shows about racial disparities in restraint use in inpatient psychiatry. Which statement correctly reflects the data?

options.t: Black patients are restrained at similar rates to White patients after adjusting for clinical acuity — the apparent disparity is explained by severity of presentation and does not belong in the post-restraint debrief.

trap.name: No disparity exists
trap.note: The disparity persists after adjustment for measured clinical factors — adjustment cannot rule out every residual confounder, but a disparity that survives it is treated as a quality-of-care issue.

options.t: Black patients are more likely to receive verbal de-escalation before physical restraint — the data show greater resource deployment, not disparity.

trap.name: No disparity exists
trap.note: The evidence shows the opposite — Black patients face higher adjusted odds of physical restraint, not more de-escalation.

options.t: Black patients faced roughly 1.85× the adjusted odds of a restraint event in a large inpatient psychiatric sample — a disparity that persists after adjustment and should be treated as a quality-of-care issue.
Joint Commission non-discrimination standards adopted in 2015 have eliminated racial disparities in restraint use.

trap.name: No disparity exists
trap.note: The disparity is ongoing and documented — regulatory standards have not eliminated it.

qb_saf_010.why: No disparity exists in three forms. The page explicitly states: 'Black patients face roughly 1.85× the adjusted odds of a restraint event on inpatient psychiatric units (Singal et al., Psychiatric Services 2024), and higher adjusted odds of physical and chemical restraint during emergency psychiatric evaluation in the ED as well (aOR ~1.35; Smith et al., Psychiatric Services 2022) — that disparity is a quality-of-care issue, not a footnote.' Singal et al. is one health system's retrospective chart review (adolescents and adults), so adjustment cannot exclude residual confounding by acuity: the defensible claim is a disparity that persists after adjustment, and the page frames it as belonging in a post-restraint debrief.
qb_saf_010.pearl: In a large inpatient psychiatric sample, Black patients faced ~1.85× the adjusted odds of a restraint event — a disparity that persists after adjustment and belongs in every post-restraint debrief.
qb_saf_010.evidence: agitation.md 'Restraint and seclusion' — Black patients face roughly 1.85× the adjusted odds of a restraint event on inpatient psychiatric units (Singal et al., Psychiatric Services 2024), and higher adjusted odds of physical and chemical restraint during emergency psychiatric evaluation in the ED as well (aOR ~1.35; Smith et al., Psychiatric Services 2022) — that disparity is a quality-of-care issue, not a footnote.

qb_saf_011.stem: A patient with mania is pacing loudly in the hallway, slamming cabinet doors, and making hostile comments toward staff. He has not made a direct threat or moved toward anyone. You are the student and the first person to encounter him. Which response is best?

options.t: Signal a nearby staff member that you are approaching, then step calmly into the hallway — not blocking his exit — introduce yourself and acknowledge his frustration: 'I can see you're really upset right now. What's going on?' Then offer a choice of where to speak.
Return to the nursing station and request an involuntary IM medication order before approaching, so the team is ready to intervene.

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Medication is not the default first step when verbal de-escalation has not been attempted and no imminent threat exists — the framework starts with presence and listening.

options.t: Stand in the doorway and firmly instruct him to return to his room or further action will be taken.

trap.name: Commands over choices
trap.note: Issuing a command removes the patient's sense of control — the de-escalation framework centers offering choices, not issuing directives.

options.t: Alert the restraint team and position staff at the hallway exits in case the patient escalates.

trap.name: Restraint first
trap.note: Preemptively positioning the restraint team before de-escalation has been attempted violates least-restrictive principle when no imminent threat has occurred.

qb_saf_011.why: Agitation = antipsychotic, Commands over choices, and Restraint first are three forms of reaching for escalation before de-escalation. The Project BETA framework starts with calm presence, acknowledgment, genuine choices, and listening. The student also needs to stay near the exit and never block the patient's — personal safety and de-escalation are not competing goals. A student encountering an agitated patient should signal a staff member before engaging — personal safety and de-escalation are complementary, not competing goals.
qb_saf_011.pearl: Calm presence + acknowledging distress + offering choices = the first move in de-escalation; stay near your exit and never block the patient's.
qb_saf_011.evidence: agitation.md 'Verbal de-escalation, first' — The Project BETA de-escalation framework (Richmond et al. 2012) centers respect, simple boundaries, listening, and offering choices rather than issuing commands.

qb_saf_012.stem: A 67-year-old man with no psychiatric history, admitted for pneumonia, begins shouting at night and pulling at his oxygen tubing. He is combative with staff. The on-call resident asks the student how to approach this. What is the most appropriate first frame?

options.t: Start an antipsychotic immediately and then search for the cause — treating the agitation reduces the risk of self-harm while the workup proceeds.

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
