qb_rel_004.stem: A family asks the treatment team what they can do during their loved one's hospitalization for schizophrenia to help with recovery. The team is considering whether to invest the time in a formal family meeting. Which argument best supports making structured family psychoeducation the default approach?

options.t: Family involvement is primarily a courtesy — it improves patient satisfaction but has no measurable impact on relapse rates.

trap.name: Family work = courtesy
trap.note: Family psychoeducation has among the strongest inpatient evidence in all of psychiatry — it is not a courtesy; it directly reduces relapse rates with an NNT of 7.

options.t: Families frequently refuse structured family meetings, so the effort should be reserved for families who specifically request it.

trap.name: Patient/family refusal as barrier
trap.note: The research shows the main barrier to family work is clinician avoidance, not family refusal — underdelivering family work is primarily a clinician behavior problem.

options.t: Family psychoeducation is the highest-evidence family intervention — it led 11 models for 12-month relapse prevention (Rodolico et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2022; 90 RCTs) with an NNT of 7 (Pharoah, Cochrane 2010; 53 RCTs); dose matters: ≤2 sessions is ineffective, with NICE recommending ≥10 sessions over ≥3 months.
Family involvement should wait until the patient is stable — in the acute phase, it increases stimulation and worsens psychosis.

trap.name: Stability first
trap.note: While the inpatient approach to family work is brief, psychoeducational, and low-stimulation (with acutely psychotic patients: brief, concrete, limited interpretation), family engagement should begin in the hospital, not wait for full stabilization — family involvement nearly triples 7-day follow-up odds.

qb_rel_004.why: Family work = courtesy, Patient/family refusal as barrier, and Stability first all undermine the evidence-based standard. Family psychoeducation has NNT 7 for 12-month relapse prevention — one of the strongest NNTs in inpatient psychiatry. The dose requirement (≥10 sessions over ≥3 months) means starting the work during the admission and securing the outpatient continuation.
qb_rel_004.pearl: Family psychoeducation for schizophrenia: NNT 7 for 12-month relapse prevention; ≥10 sessions over ≥3 months; dose matters — start during admission.
qb_rel_004.evidence: family_modalities.md — NNT 7 — treat seven families to prevent one relapse (Pharoah, Cochrane 2010; 53 RCTs). Dose matters: ≤2 sessions is ineffective; NICE recommends ≥10 sessions over ≥3 months.

link.label: Open the Family Therapy Modalities page

qb_rel_006.stem: The family of a patient with schizophrenia is described in the chart as 'high expressed emotion' — high criticism and high emotional over-involvement. The resident says, 'We can't do much about the family climate — it's just how they are.' Which response is most evidence-based?

options.t: Agree — expressed emotion is a fixed family trait that does not respond to clinical intervention.

trap.name: EE is fixed
trap.note: Expressed emotion is modifiable — behavioral family therapy and family psychoeducation specifically reduce EE; treating it as fixed is both incorrect and missed opportunity.

options.t: High EE only predicts relapse in schizophrenia, not in other psychiatric illnesses — it is not relevant beyond psychosis.

trap.name: EE = schizophrenia only
trap.note: Expressed emotion predicts relapse across multiple psychiatric conditions including mood disorders; the family therapy modalities page cites EE-relapse data for schizophrenia because that is the strongest evidence base, but EE is a transdiagnostic concept.

options.t: High EE is a family problem but not a clinical problem — it is outside the scope of inpatient psychiatric intervention.

trap.name: EE = out of scope
trap.note: Family climate is explicitly clinical data; the page calls it modifiable and quantifies its impact on relapse risk — addressing EE is within the scope of inpatient psychiatry through family meetings.

options.t: Expressed emotion (EE) substantially raises relapse odds — roughly doubling to quintupling across studies (Butzlaff & Hooley 1998) — while family warmth is protective, but EE is modifiable through behavioral family therapy and family psychoeducation, making the family climate a tractable clinical target.

qb_rel_006.why: EE is fixed, EE = schizophrenia only, and EE = out of scope all represent clinical fatalism about a modifiable variable. The page states EE 'roughly doubles to quintuples relapse odds depending on the study (Butzlaff & Hooley 1998 meta-analysis), while family warmth is protective — and family climate is modifiable, which is why meetings help lower it.'
qb_rel_006.pearl: Expressed emotion (EE) substantially raises relapse odds (roughly doubling to quintupling across studies; Butzlaff & Hooley 1998) and is MODIFIABLE — behavioral family therapy and psychoeducation specifically target and reduce it; EE is a tractable clinical problem.
qb_rel_006.evidence: family_modalities.md — Expressed emotion: high-EE roughly doubles to quintuples relapse odds depending on the study (Butzlaff & Hooley 1998 meta-analysis), while family warmth is protective. Family climate is modifiable — meetings help lower it.

qb_rel_007.stem: A 27-year-old woman is being discharged after a suicidal crisis. The resident asks her to 'sign a contract that she won't hurt herself.' The student wonders whether this is the evidence-based approach. Which response reflects the current standard?

options.t: Yes — a no-suicide contract is the gold standard for discharge safety planning; it establishes a binding commitment to safety.

trap.name: Contract = gold standard
trap.note: No-suicide contracts have no supporting evidence and can create false reassurance — the current standard is collaborative safety planning, which has real outcome data.

options.t: Yes — contracts are more legally protective for the clinician than safety plans, which is why they are standard at discharge.

trap.name: Contract = legal protection
trap.note: Contracts have no established legal protection advantage and do not reduce suicide attempts; they have been replaced by evidence-based safety planning in clinical standards.

options.t: No — a collaborative safety plan (Stanley-Brown model) is the evidence-based tool; no-suicide contracts have no supporting evidence and can create false reassurance that displaces genuine clinical assessment.
Neither approach has evidence — rely on clinical judgment and family support for suicidal patients at discharge.

trap.name: No evidence either way
trap.note: Safety planning WITH follow-up has evidence: approximately 50% fewer suicidal behaviors (Stanley 2018); it is not evidence-neutral.

qb_rel_007.why: Contract = gold standard, Contract = legal protection, and No evidence either way all misrepresent the evidence. The brief psychotherapy page explicitly states: 'Abandon no-suicide contracts — they don't work.' Safety planning (Stanley-Brown) with follow-up reduces suicidal behaviors by approximately 50%.
qb_rel_007.pearl: Safety planning (Stanley-Brown) with follow-up ≈ 50% fewer suicidal behaviors — abandon no-suicide contracts, which have no evidence and create false reassurance.
qb_rel_007.evidence: brief_psychotherapy.md — Safety planning (Stanley-Brown) + crisis response planning: Safety Planning Intervention with follow-up ≈ 50% fewer suicidal behaviors (Stanley 2018); abandon no-suicide 'contracts' — they don't work.

qb_rel_008.stem: A 52-year-old man with severe depression is withdrawn, stays in bed all day, and says 'nothing matters anymore.' The student asks how to perform a brief psychotherapy intervention given a 15-minute window. Which approach is most appropriate for this presentation?

options.t: Behavioral activation — schedule one small, specific valued activity for today; this is the highest-yield, lowest-cognitive-demand inpatient move for behavioral shutdown.
Psychodynamic interpretation — explore the unconscious drivers of the behavioral withdrawal during this session.

trap.name: Insight therapy for shutdown
trap.note: Psychodynamic interpretation requires cognitive engagement that a severely depressed, withdrawn patient cannot sustain; the mismatch between mechanism (insight) and the presenting driver (behavioral shutdown) makes BA the more evidence-based choice.

options.t: Prolonged exposure — begin reliving any traumatic experiences that may underlie the depression.

trap.name: PE for depression
trap.note: Prolonged exposure is for PTSD — its mechanism (trauma memory reconsolidation) does not match behavioral shutdown; applying PE to a shutdown depressed patient mismatches mechanism and technique.

options.t: Wait for medication to take effect before beginning any psychotherapy — behavioral shutdown is too severe for psychotherapy engagement.

trap.name: Medication before psychotherapy
trap.note: Brief behavioral activation is specifically designed for patients with low engagement — scheduling a single valued activity is achievable even with severe depression; waiting for full medication response before any behavioral intervention delays recovery unnecessarily.

qb_rel_008.why: Insight therapy for shutdown, PE for depression, and Medication before psychotherapy all mismatch mechanism to technique. The brief psychotherapy table: 'Withdrawn, inactive, anhedonic — behavioral shutdown → reach for behavioral activation (BA): schedule one small, valued activity. Superior to TAU for depression (SMD −0.78) and anxiety, on par with CBT; lowest cognitive demand → best inpatient fit.'
qb_rel_008.pearl: Behavioral activation is the highest-yield, lowest-effort inpatient move for the shutdown depressed patient — schedule one small valued activity; it requires no cognitive engagement.
qb_rel_008.evidence: brief_psychotherapy.md — Behavioral activation (BA) — schedule one small, valued activity. Superior to TAU for depression (SMD −0.78) and anxiety (−0.33), on par with CBT; lowest cognitive demand → best inpatient fit.

qb_rel_009.stem: A patient with recurrent MDD completed three individual therapy sessions during an 8-day hospitalization. At discharge, the student writes in the note: 'CBT skills taught inpatient; patient discharged with psychotherapy complete.' The attending asks the student to reconsider the framing. Which is more accurate?

options.t: The note is accurate — three CBT sessions is the evidence-based minimum for inpatient psychotherapy, and the skills have been transferred.

trap.name: Three sessions = complete
trap.note: No evidence-based framework defines 3 inpatient sessions as 'complete' — the purpose of inpatient psychotherapy is to start the work and secure the outpatient handoff, not to complete treatment.

options.t: Inpatient psychotherapy starts the work and secures the handoff — the discharge note should name the specific therapeutic thread started, identify the named outpatient clinician who will continue it, and make the handoff explicit.
Psychotherapy is an outpatient intervention — inpatient therapy has no meaningful impact and should not be documented as a treatment component.

trap.name: Inpatient therapy = ineffective
trap.note: Inpatient psychotherapy has a documented pooled benefit (SMD ~0.24, NNT ~7) — framing it as ineffective dismisses evidence; the point is that it must continue outpatient to complete the benefit.

options.t: Three CBT sessions is sufficient only if the patient was 'CBT-naive' — if she had prior CBT, the inpatient work is redundant.

trap.name: Prior CBT = redundant inpatient therapy
trap.note: Prior CBT experience does not make inpatient psychotherapy redundant; patients return to therapy at every level of care as needed, and the inpatient component serves crisis stabilization and continuity, regardless of prior exposure.

qb_rel_009.why: Example: 'BA for behavioral shutdown' is the specific thread; naming the clinician prevents the work from being dropped at discharge. Three sessions = complete, Inpatient therapy = ineffective, and Prior CBT = redundant all miss the purpose. The page: 'The skill is to read the mechanism driving this patient's crisis right now and match one brief technique to it — then hand the work off to outpatient care.' 'Write the handoff so the outpatient clinician can continue the thread — the point of inpatient therapy is to start it and secure the follow-up.'
qb_rel_009.pearl: Inpatient psychotherapy starts the thread and secures the handoff — document the technique, name the outpatient clinician, and make the handoff explicit; it does not complete treatment.
qb_rel_009.evidence: brief_psychotherapy.md — Write the handoff so the outpatient clinician can continue the thread — the point of inpatient therapy is to start it and secure the follow-up.

link.label: Open the Family Therapy Modalities page

qb_rel_010.stem: The treatment team reviews its data and finds that structured family meetings occurred in only 8% of admissions over the past year, despite family members being available and willing in most cases. The team discusses why. Which explanation is most consistent with the literature?

options.t: Families of inpatient psychiatric patients predominantly refuse to participate in structured family meetings when offered.

trap.name: Family refusal
trap.note: The research specifically identifies clinician avoidance — not family refusal — as the dominant barrier to delivering family work; this is a clinician behavior finding, not a family behavior finding.

options.t: Structured family work requires >90 minutes per family — the time investment is prohibitive in an acute inpatient setting.

trap.name: Time as primary barrier
trap.note: While time is a real constraint, the research identifies clinician avoidance as the main barrier, not time alone — and some high-yield modalities (solution-focused, single-session work) can be effective in one meeting.

options.t: The main barrier to family psychoeducation being delivered is clinician avoidance — structured family work is available to the minority of families who receive it largely because of clinician behavior, not family behavior.
Insurance authorization is the dominant barrier — family meetings require separate billing codes that are denied in most health systems.

trap.name: Billing as dominant barrier
trap.note: Billing complexity may be a factor, but the research (Dixon 1999; Eassom 2014) specifically identifies clinician avoidance as the dominant explanation for the historically low delivery of structured family work.

qb_rel_010.why: Family refusal, Time as primary barrier, and Billing as dominant barrier all attribute the gap to external factors. The literature finding is counterintuitive and important: 'Reaches a minority of families — structured family work is delivered in only ~0–53% of cases (historically <10%), and the main barrier is clinician avoidance, not patient refusal (Dixon 1999; Eassom 2014).' This is a clinician self-awareness finding.
qb_rel_010.pearl: The main barrier to family psychoeducation in inpatient psychiatry is clinician avoidance, not patient or family refusal — the gap is a clinician behavior problem.
qb_rel_010.evidence: family_modalities.md — Reaches a minority of families — structured family work is delivered in only ~0–53% of cases (historically <10%), and the main barrier is clinician avoidance, not patient refusal (Dixon 1999; Eassom 2014).

qb_rel_011.stem: A 24-year-old woman with BPD cuts herself on the unit. The charge nurse says, 'Document it and flag it. Don't talk to her about it — it just encourages the behavior.' The student wonders about the evidence-based approach. Which response is most accurate?

options.t: The nurse is right — direct conversation about self-harm incidents reinforces the behavior by providing attention; the clinical standard is documentation without engagement.

trap.name: Engagement reinforces behavior
trap.note: Withholding engagement after self-harm misses the chain analysis opportunity that is central to DBT — it treats the symptom as behavior to extinguish rather than as communication to understand.

options.t: The appropriate response is immediate medication review — self-harm indicates the current regimen is inadequate.

trap.name: Self-harm = medication failure
trap.note: Self-harm in BPD is a behavioral coping strategy — the clinician-level response is to understand its function through chain analysis, not to reflexively adjust medications.

options.t: Place the patient on 1:1 observation and restrict milieu privileges pending a formal incident review — the safety breach requires an institutional response before therapeutic engagement resumes.

trap.name: Incident response first
trap.note: While safety monitoring and documentation are appropriate after self-harm on the unit, withholding therapeutic engagement delays the chain analysis that is central to the DBT model; the clinical response is to engage and understand the behavior, not to manage the incident bureaucratically before engaging.

options.t: A chain analysis — walking the sequence of antecedents, emotions, and behaviors with the patient non-punitively — turns the incident into a clinical formulation and a coping plan; this is the DBT standard and replaces documentation-only or punitive responses.

qb_rel_011.why: Engagement reinforces behavior, Self-harm = medication failure, and Punitive documentation all fail to apply the DBT-informed clinical standard. The page states: 'Chain analysis replaces a punitive response to self-harm — understand the behavior, don't just document it.' The chain analysis is a brief, structured, non-punitive conversation about what preceded the self-harm that turns the incident into a formulation.
qb_rel_011.pearl: After self-harm: chain analysis (non-punitive, with the patient) replaces documentation-only or punitive responses — it transforms the incident into a formulation and a coping plan.
qb_rel_011.evidence: brief_psychotherapy.md — Chain analysis — walk the sequence with the patient, non-punitively. Turns an incident into a formulation and a plan; core DBT move. Chain analysis replaces a punitive response to self-harm — understand the behavior, don't just document it.

link.label: Open the Family Therapy Modalities page

qb_rel_012.stem: A 32-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has refused treatment for 2 years. His wife is desperate to help and asks the team what she can do. The team is considering a traditional confrontational intervention approach. Which family therapy modality is specifically evidence-based for this scenario?

options.t: CRAFT (Community Reinforcement and Family Training) — the family member changes her own behavior in specific ways that reduce the reinforcement of drinking and increase the appeal of treatment-seeking, without confrontation or blame.
Structural family therapy (Minuchin) — the focus is on realigning the roles and boundaries in the marriage to reduce the enabling dynamic.

trap.name: Structural for substance refusal
trap.note: Structural therapy addresses role and boundary dysfunction but does not provide the specific behavioral strategies for family members managing a treatment-refusing person with SUD; CRAFT is specifically designed for this scenario.

options.t: A family confrontation (traditional intervention) — bringing family and friends together to confront the patient with consequences is the most evidence-based approach.

trap.name: Confrontational intervention
trap.note: Traditional confrontational interventions have mixed evidence and can damage the therapeutic alliance; CRAFT specifically trains families to use non-blame behavioral strategies and has a larger evidence base for engagement.

options.t: Emotionally focused therapy (EFT) — addressing the attachment disruption in the marriage will resolve the motivational impasse for the patient.

trap.name: EFT for treatment refusal
trap.note: EFT is couples-attachment focused and is the modality for a distressed couple's negative cycle — it is not specifically designed for a family member trying to invite a treatment-refusing person into care.

qb_rel_012.why: Structural for substance refusal, Confrontational intervention, and EFT for treatment refusal all apply less-specific frameworks. CRAFT is the specific modality: 'the family changes its own behavior to invite treatment — no blame.' It trains the wife to use behavioral strategies (reinforcing non-drinking behavior, withdrawing reinforcement of drinking, using teachable moments) that increase the patient's engagement with treatment.
qb_rel_012.pearl: CRAFT: the family changes its OWN behavior to invite treatment — no blame, no confrontation; evidence-based for families of treatment-refusing people with SUD.
qb_rel_012.evidence: family_modalities.md — CRAFT (Community Reinforcement & Family Training): the family changes its own behavior to invite treatment — no blame.

qb_rel_013.stem: A quality-improvement team wants to identify the single inpatient psychological intervention with the strongest readmission-prevention evidence. Which intervention has the hardest numbers?

options.t: Safety planning (Stanley-Brown) — approximately 50% fewer suicidal behaviors.

trap.name: Safety planning hardest numbers
trap.note: Safety planning has strong evidence (50% reduction in suicidal behaviors), but the question asks about readmission prevention specifically — psychoeducation has the hardest readmission-specific numbers.

options.t: Psychoeducation — the hardest inpatient numbers for readmission prevention: readmission NNT 5 (Xia, Cochrane 2011) and relapse NNT 9; and it costs nothing except time.
Behavioral activation — the most evidence-based inpatient psychological intervention for any condition.

trap.name: BA = strongest overall
trap.note: BA has the strongest evidence for acute depression (SMD −0.78) and is the best-fit inpatient technique, but readmission NNT 5 for psychoeducation specifically addresses the readmission-prevention question.

options.t: Problem-solving therapy (PST) — NNT 12 for repeat self-harm re-presentation.

trap.name: PST hardest numbers
trap.note: PST has an NNT of 12 for self-harm re-presentation — meaningful evidence, but psychoeducation's readmission NNT of 5 is the strongest number on the brief psychotherapy page.

qb_rel_013.why: Safety planning hardest numbers, BA = strongest overall, and PST hardest numbers each reference real evidence for different outcomes. For readmission prevention specifically, psychoeducation's NNT 5 is the standout: 'Psychoeducation has the hardest inpatient numbers (readmission NNT 5) — and it's free.' This is the quality-improvement answer.
qb_rel_013.pearl: Psychoeducation has the hardest inpatient readmission numbers: NNT 5 (Xia, Cochrane 2011) — the highest-evidence, lowest-cost psychological intervention for preventing readmission.
qb_rel_013.evidence: brief_psychotherapy.md — Psychoeducation has the hardest inpatient numbers (readmission NNT 5) — and it's free.

qb_otherdx_001.stem: A 17-year-old with severe anorexia nervosa has been starved for 4 months and is starting nutritional rehabilitation. On day 3 of refeeding, her phosphate drops to 2.1 mg/dL. She is also mildly confused and has new-onset leg weakness. What is the most important diagnosis to recognize?

options.t: Refeeding syndrome — the shift to anabolic metabolism drives phosphate into cells; hypophosphatemia is its hallmark.
Electrolyte depletion from malnutrition alone — she was already malnourished on admission, so the low phosphate reflects pre-existing deficiency rather than a refeeding process.

trap.name: Pre-existing deficiency only
trap.note: While pre-existing malnutrition contributes to baseline deficiencies, the precipitous drop in phosphate after initiating refeeding is the refeeding syndrome pattern — the metabolic shift of refeeding, not chronic depletion, is the mechanism.

options.t: Conversion disorder — the confusion and leg weakness represent a functional neurological symptom disorder superimposed on the eating disorder.

trap.name: Functional explanation for metabolic emergency
trap.note: Confusion and leg weakness in the context of a falling phosphate during refeeding is refeeding syndrome until proven otherwise — it is a medical emergency, not a functional disorder.

options.t: Thiamine deficiency — the neurological symptoms indicate Wernicke encephalopathy from B1 deficiency.

trap.name: Thiamine over phosphate
trap.note: Thiamine deficiency is a real risk in eating disorders and requires prophylactic replacement when refeeding starts, but a falling phosphate on day 3 of refeeding with weakness and confusion is the classic refeeding syndrome presentation — phosphate is the hallmark electrolyte.

qb_otherdx_001.why: Pre-existing deficiency only, Functional explanation for metabolic emergency, and Thiamine over phosphate all miss the refeeding-specific mechanism. The page calls refeeding syndrome 'the complication that kills' — hypophosphatemia is the hallmark. Note that D (thiamine) is also clinically relevant and the page specifically says to give thiamine (and other vitamins) when refeeding starts — but the presenting electrolyte abnormality and timing point to refeeding syndrome as the primary diagnosis. Hypophosphatemia can cause cardiac failure, arrhythmia, respiratory failure, and delirium.
qb_otherdx_001.pearl: Refeeding syndrome: watch phosphate — the hallmark is hypophosphatemia after starting nutrition; risk tracks malnutrition, so monitor phosphate daily; supplement phosphate; give thiamine.
qb_otherdx_001.evidence: t_eating.md — Refeeding syndrome — the complication that kills: hypophosphatemia is the hallmark; the danger is cardiac failure, arrhythmia, respiratory failure, and delirium. Supplement phosphate and give thiamine (and other vitamins) when refeeding starts.

tier2.q: Why does hypophosphatemia develop after initiating refeeding in a severely malnourished patient, rather than during the starvation period itself?

options.t: Carbohydrate refeeding increases renal phosphate excretion — the kidneys preferentially excrete phosphate when insulin levels rise.

Refeeding shifts metabolism from catabolic to anabolic — glucose and insulin drive phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells for new cellular synthesis; since total body stores are depleted from malnutrition, the extracellular pool drops precipitously.
Starvation preserves phosphate by reducing cellular metabolic demand — refeeding simply re-activates the pre-existing phosphate deficiency that was masked.
Thiamine deficiency prevents phosphate absorption from the gut — refeeding exposes this deficiency because oral phosphate intake increases.

tier2.why: During starvation, catabolism releases phosphate from cells into the extracellular space, partially maintaining serum levels despite total body depletion. When refeeding begins, glucose triggers insulin release, which drives phosphate (along with potassium and magnesium) into cells for anabolic processes (glycolysis, ATP synthesis, protein synthesis). This intracellular shift drops extracellular phosphate rapidly — in an already-depleted patient, the serum level can fall to dangerous levels within 24–72 hours of starting nutrition. This is why refeeding syndrome occurs early in the refeeding course and why the most malnourished patients are at highest risk.

qb_otherdx_002.stem: A 24-year-old woman is referred for 'weight-related anxiety.' She is at normal weight and denies dieting. However, she endorses recurrent binge episodes followed by self-induced vomiting several times weekly, and she reports that her self-worth is almost entirely based on her weight and shape. On exam, you note calluses on her right hand knuckles. Which diagnosis should be suspected?

options.t: Anorexia nervosa, binge-purging subtype — the purging behavior and weight preoccupation are classic for anorexia.

trap.name: Normal weight rules out AN misread as AN
trap.note: Anorexia nervosa requires significantly low weight — this patient is at normal weight; her presentation is much more consistent with bulimia nervosa.

options.t: Binge-eating disorder — binge episodes with distress are the defining feature; no compensatory behavior is required.

trap.name: Binge = BED
trap.note: Binge-eating disorder specifically involves binges WITHOUT regular compensatory behavior; this patient has self-induced vomiting as a compensatory behavior, which distinguishes bulimia nervosa from BED.

options.t: Bulimia nervosa — normal weight does not rule out bulimia; the binge-purge cycle, weight/shape self-evaluation, and Russell's sign (knuckle calluses) are the diagnostic markers.
Purging disorder — recurrent purging in the absence of objectively large binge episodes, with weight/shape concern, is classified as purging disorder.

trap.name: Purging without binges = purging disorder
trap.note: Purging disorder requires the absence of recurrent objective binge episodes — this patient has both binge episodes AND purging, which meets bulimia nervosa criteria; purging disorder is diagnosed only when purging occurs without the binge component.

qb_otherdx_002.why: Normal weight rules out AN, Binge = BED, and Purging without binges = purging disorder all miss the defining features — her recurrent, objectively large binge episodes with compensatory purging make this bulimia nervosa rather than purging disorder, which requires purging in the absence of binges. The page: 'Bulimia nervosa — weight is often normal or high — a normal weight does not rule it out. Look for Russell's sign (knuckle calluses), parotid enlargement, and dental enamel erosion.' All three examination findings distinguish BN from BED: the presence of compensatory behaviors (purging) is the key.
qb_otherdx_002.pearl: Normal weight DOES NOT rule out bulimia nervosa — look for binge-purge cycle + Russell's sign (knuckle calluses) + parotid swelling + dental erosion.
qb_otherdx_002.evidence: t_eating.md — Bulimia nervosa — weight is often normal or high — a normal weight does not rule it out. Look for Russell's sign (knuckle calluses), parotid enlargement, and dental enamel erosion.

qb_otherdx_003.stem: A 28-year-old woman who delivered 6 days ago is brought by her husband with confusion, talking to people who aren't there, and expressing beliefs that her baby 'was sent to test her faith.' She had been laughing and crying alternately. She was seen yesterday and appeared fine for two hours. What is the most critical diagnosis to consider?

options.t: Baby blues — mild postpartum mood changes are expected in the first 2 weeks and are self-limited.

trap.name: Baby blues by default
trap.note: Baby blues involves mild mood lability without functional impairment and certainly without psychotic features or confusion; the presentation here — new perceptual disturbance, delusions, and confusion — is not baby blues.

options.t: Postpartum depression — the mood lability and behavioral change represent a perinatal major depressive episode.

trap.name: Postpartum depression default
trap.note: Postpartum depression does not include psychotic features, delusions, or confusion in its non-psychotic form; the abrupt-onset psychosis with waxing-and-waning course within days of delivery is postpartum psychosis — a different and urgent entity.

options.t: Postpartum psychosis — this is a psychiatric emergency; abrupt onset within days of delivery, waxing-and-waning course, psychotic features centered on the infant, and the lucid interval does not provide reassurance.
Medical emergency — new psychosis postpartum indicates eclampsia or infection until proven otherwise.

trap.name: Medical cause only
trap.note: Medical causes must be excluded (thyroid, infection, eclampsia) but the waxing-and-waning course with psychotic features centered on the infant in the first week postpartum is the postpartum psychosis picture — the clinical priority is both psychiatric emergency evaluation AND medical workup simultaneously.

qb_otherdx_003.why: Baby blues by default, Postpartum depression default, and Medical cause only all fail to identify postpartum psychosis as the emergency. The page: 'Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency: rapid onset, waxing/waning presentation, and real risk to both mother and infant — admit and treat urgently.' The lucid interval yesterday is explicitly stated to not provide reassurance: 'A lucid interval does not rule out psychosis — the waxing/waning course is part of the illness.'
qb_otherdx_003.pearl: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency — abrupt onset, waxing/waning course, infant-focused delusions within days of delivery; a lucid interval does NOT rule it out.
qb_otherdx_003.evidence: t_perinatal.md — POSTPARTUM PSYCHOSIS IS A PSYCHIATRIC EMERGENCY: rapid onset, waxing/waning presentation, and real risk to both mother and infant — admit and treat urgently. A lucid interval does not rule out psychosis — the waxing/waning course is part of the illness, not reassurance.

tier2.q: What psychiatric history most strongly predicts postpartum psychosis, and why does this influence the medication decision at discharge?

options.t: A history of major depressive disorder — postpartum psychosis is an extension of unipolar depression and responds best to antidepressants.
A history of bipolar disorder — postpartum psychosis is strongly linked to bipolar spectrum illness; stopping maintenance mood stabilizer nearly triples the risk of postpartum relapse.
A history of schizophrenia — postpartum psychosis is simply a schizophrenic relapse triggered by the hormonal changes of delivery.
No prior psychiatric history predicts postpartum psychosis — it is idiopathic and equally likely in any postpartum patient.

tier2.why: Postpartum psychosis is strongly linked to bipolar disorder — patients with bipolar disorder have a risk approximately 100-fold higher than the general population. This matters for discharge because 'stopping maintenance medication nearly triples postpartum relapse (pooled ~35% overall; ~66% off medication vs ~23% on prophylaxis).' The medication-stop decision in a postpartum patient with bipolar disorder is itself a high-risk intervention — 'stop everything' is not a safe default.

qb_otherdx_004.stem: A 45-year-old woman is referred for psychiatric consultation for 'medically unexplained' chest pain and fatigue. Her symptoms are real and distressing, her workup is negative, and she spends hours daily researching health threats and 4–5 hours daily focused on her symptoms. Which DSM-5-TR principle is most relevant to the diagnosis?

options.t: Somatic symptom disorder requires that the symptoms have no identifiable organic cause — the diagnosis is made only after medical explanation is definitively excluded.

trap.name: SSD = medically unexplained
trap.note: This is the pre-DSM-5 framing — DSM-5-TR shifted the definition of SSD away from 'medically unexplained' to focus on the excessive psychological response; the symptom may or may not be medically explained.

options.t: Somatic symptom disorder requires at least 3 distinct somatic complaints across different organ systems.

trap.name: Multiple organ systems required
trap.note: The DSM-5-TR criterion is ≥1 distressing somatic symptom plus excessive thoughts/feelings/behaviors — not a minimum number of symptoms or organ systems; one symptom with excessive response qualifies.

options.t: These complaints are best diagnosed as illness anxiety disorder because the patient's main symptom is health preoccupation rather than multiple somatic symptoms.

trap.name: Preoccupation = IAD not SSD
trap.note: Illness anxiety disorder (IAD) features preoccupation with having a disease with minimal somatic symptoms — this patient has distressing somatic symptoms (chest pain, fatigue) plus the excessive cognitive response; this fits SSD, not IAD.

options.t: DSM-5-TR defines somatic symptom disorder by the excessive thoughts, feelings, and behaviors around symptoms — not by whether those symptoms are medically explained; a patient with a confirmed medical diagnosis can still meet SSD criteria if her response to symptoms is disproportionate.

qb_otherdx_004.why: SSD = medically unexplained, Multiple organ systems required, and Preoccupation = IAD all misstate the DSM-5-TR diagnosis. The page's first pearl: 'SSD is defined by the excessive response to symptoms, not by whether they're medically explained (a key DSM-5-TR shift from medically unexplained).' This is a tested concept: the diagnosis no longer hinges on medical explanation.
qb_otherdx_004.pearl: SSD (DSM-5-TR): defined by excessive thoughts/feelings/behaviors about symptoms — NOT by whether the symptoms are medically unexplained; a confirmed medical illness can coexist with SSD.
qb_otherdx_004.evidence: t_somatic.md — SSD is defined by the excessive response to symptoms, not by whether they're medically explained (a key DSM-5-TR shift from 'medically unexplained').

qb_otherdx_005.stem: A 36-year-old woman is admitted with a 3-day history of right-sided paralysis and inability to walk. Neurological workup is negative. When the examiner tests voluntary right hip extension, extension is absent; however, strong right hip extension is felt involuntarily when the patient flexes the left hip against resistance (positive Hoover sign). Which statement about the diagnosis is most accurate?

options.t: Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion) is diagnosed here by a positive examination finding — the Hoover sign; this is a rule-in diagnosis, not solely a diagnosis of exclusion.
The diagnosis requires a psychiatric interview confirming psychosocial stress as the precipitant before a neurological cause can be excluded.

trap.name: Psychiatric cause required
trap.note: DSM-5 removed the requirement for an identified psychological precipitant from the conversion disorder criteria; the diagnosis is made by positive examination signs (rule-in), not by excluding all neurology and confirming a psychological cause.

options.t: The diagnosis requires a complete neurological workup including MRI, EMG, and nerve conduction studies before conversion can be considered.

trap.name: Full workup before conversion
trap.note: Positive examination signs like the Hoover sign are themselves diagnostic and are not simply 'tests not yet done'; waiting for a complete negative workup before considering conversion delays a treatable diagnosis.

options.t: The positive examination finding is unreliable — the Hoover sign has poor sensitivity and should not anchor a diagnosis.

trap.name: Hoover sign unreliable
trap.note: The Hoover sign has good specificity for functional weakness — it is a clinically validated examination finding that supports a rule-in diagnosis, not an unreliable anecdotal maneuver.

qb_otherdx_005.why: Psychiatric cause required, Full workup before conversion, and Hoover sign unreliable all delay diagnosis or require unnecessary conditions. The page is explicit: 'Conversion/functional neurological disorder is a rule-in diagnosis — Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, non-epileptic seizures. Name conversion by its positive signs — don't make it a diagnosis of exclusion alone.'
qb_otherdx_005.pearl: Functional neurological disorder (conversion) is diagnosed by POSITIVE examination signs (Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness) — not solely by exclusion; DSM-5 removed the psychological precipitant requirement.
qb_otherdx_005.evidence: t_somatic.md — Conversion/functional neurological disorder is a rule-in diagnosis — Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, non-epileptic seizures. Name conversion by its positive signs — don't make it a diagnosis of exclusion alone.

tier2.q: Why did DSM-5 remove the requirement for an identified psychological stressor from the diagnosis of functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion)?

options.t: To make the diagnosis easier to code — the removal was an administrative convenience rather than a clinical improvement.

Because a psychological precipitant is not reliably identifiable in all cases, and requiring it was clinician-attributed (confabulated) rather than patient-reported; the diagnosis now rests on the neurological examination finding, which is objective.
Because DSM-5 de-medicalized all psychiatric diagnoses — the psychological stressor requirement was removed from all diagnoses in the somatic section.
To increase the sensitivity of the diagnosis — more patients qualify without requiring documentation of a precipitant.

tier2.why: The pre-DSM-5 requirement for an identified psychological stressor was criticized because (1) clinicians often attributed stress confabulatorily rather than patients actually reporting a clear precipitant, (2) it was unreliable across clinicians, and (3) it implied that the absence of an identified stressor could falsely reassure about the diagnosis. DSM-5 shifted the criteria to rest on the positive neurological examination finding — an objective, replicable observation — which better separates functional from structural neurological disease and removes the subjective psychological stressor requirement.
