qb_otherdx_006.stem: A 42-year-old woman has been hospitalized multiple times for recurrent infections. Staff have noted that her central line infections always follow nursing shifts during which she is left alone with the IV port. A camera reveals that she is injecting herself with contaminated fluid. She appears distressed when confronted and says, 'I just need doctors to take care of me.' There is no evidence of secondary gain (no pending disability, no legal issue). Which diagnosis is most consistent?

options.t: Malingering — the deliberate production of symptoms for secondary gain is the defining feature.

trap.name: Deliberate = malingering
trap.note: Deliberate production of symptoms is present in BOTH factitious disorder and malingering; the critical distinction is motivation — malingering requires an external incentive (financial, legal, drug-seeking), which is absent here.

options.t: Somatic symptom disorder — the recurrent hospitalizations and the distress of the patient indicate a pattern of disproportionate health concern.

trap.name: Recurrent admissions = SSD
trap.note: SSD is characterized by excessive worry about symptoms — not by deliberate production of illness; the conscious self-injection places this in a different diagnostic category entirely.

options.t: Conversion disorder — the pattern of self-limited infections with resolution suggests a functional mechanism.

trap.name: Episodic = functional
trap.note: Conversion disorder is unconscious and produces neurological symptoms; deliberate self-injection with contaminated fluid is a conscious act in a medically serious, not functional, illness category.

options.t: Factitious disorder imposed on self — conscious falsification or induction of illness motivated by assuming the sick role, without external incentive; 'I need doctors to take care of me' is the factitious driver.

qb_otherdx_006.why: Deliberate = malingering, Recurrent admissions = SSD, and Episodic = functional all apply the wrong framework. The page's diagnostic table: 'Factitious disorder — conscious falsification or induction of illness (self or another) motivated by assuming the sick role, without external reward.' The two-axis rule: 'Separate on two axes: conscious? and external incentive? Factitious = internal motive (sick role); malingering = external incentive (and is not a disorder).'
qb_otherdx_006.pearl: Factitious = conscious, internal motive (sick role); malingering = conscious, external incentive (money/drugs/legal); neither has unconscious somatic symptoms.
qb_otherdx_006.evidence: t_somatic.md — Factitious = internal motive (sick role); malingering = external incentive (and is not a disorder). Separate on the two axes: conscious? and external incentive?

tier2.q: A caregiver is suspected of intentionally inducing illness in her 6-year-old child to maintain hospital access and medical attention. Which specific diagnosis and clinical obligation apply?

options.t: Malingering by proxy — the external incentive (social support, housing) makes this malingering rather than factitious disorder; no mandatory reporting obligation applies.
Factitious disorder imposed on another (medical child abuse) — this is a form of child abuse and a mandatory reporting obligation; protecting the child takes priority over confronting the caregiver.
Munchausen syndrome by proxy — this is a historical term; no specific mandatory reporting obligation exists because psychiatric diagnosis does not create reporting duties.
Somatic symptom disorder imposed by parent — the parent's excessive health preoccupation shapes the child's medical utilization; no reporting duty applies.

tier2.why: The current DSM-5-TR term is 'factitious disorder imposed on another' (formerly Munchausen by proxy). The page explicitly states it is a form of abuse: 'Factitious disorder imposed on another (medical child abuse) is reportable.' The clinical obligation is to protect the dependent (the child) and file a mandatory report — this takes precedence over psychiatric consultation, confrontation, or treatment of the caregiver. The page cross-references the ethics and law teaching: 'Imposed on another (formerly Munchausen by proxy) is a form of abuse — report it.'

qb_otherdx_007.stem: A 55-year-old Puerto Rican woman is brought to the emergency department by her family. She is hyperventilating, trembling, shouting uncontrollably, and has fallen to the floor. Her family says this has happened before after a stressful family argument. Her vitals are normal and she recovers fully within 30 minutes. Which culturally informed interpretation is most accurate?

options.t: This is a panic disorder episode — the hyperventilation and trembling meet the physiological criteria for a panic attack.

trap.name: Symptoms match panic
trap.note: While the symptoms overlap with panic, applying a Western diagnostic label before exploring cultural context risks misdiagnosis; the episodic, stress-triggered, interpersonally mediated presentation with full recovery is classic for ataque de nervios, a culturally recognized pattern.

options.t: This is a functional neurological disorder — the shouting and falling indicate a non-epileptic seizure.

trap.name: Motor symptoms = functional seizure
trap.note: Functional neurological disorder requires positive examination signs and an individual assessment; without those, attributing a culturally patterned episode to conversion is premature and bypasses cultural context.

options.t: This may be ataque de nervios — a Latino cultural concept of distress characterized by trembling, shouting, hyperventilation, and sometimes falling, typically precipitated by family stress; cultural inquiry is essential before applying a Western diagnostic label.
This is malingering — the rapid recovery and interpersonal context suggest the episode served a social function.

trap.name: Socially embedded = malingering
trap.note: Cultural idioms of distress may serve interpersonal functions within their cultural context without constituting malingering — applying malingering to a culturally recognized pattern without adequate assessment is both inaccurate and harmful.

qb_otherdx_007.why: Symptoms match panic, Motor symptoms = functional seizure, and Socially embedded = malingering all bypass cultural inquiry. The page: 'Cultural concepts of distress (e.g., ataque de nervios) can mimic panic or psychosis — ask before you label.' Using Kleinman's explanatory-model questions would surface the patient's interpretation and cultural meaning before assigning a diagnosis.
qb_otherdx_007.pearl: Ataque de nervios: culturally patterned distress in Latino communities — trembling, shouting, hyperventilation, falling, stress-triggered — can be misread as panic, seizure, or psychosis without cultural inquiry.
qb_otherdx_007.evidence: cultural_psychiatry.md — Cultural concepts of distress (e.g., ataque de nervios, susto) can be mistaken for panic, psychosis, or malingering. Ask before you label.

tier2.q: What is the purpose of Kleinman's explanatory-model questions in cross-cultural clinical encounters?

options.t: To confirm that the patient's illness understanding matches the biomedical diagnosis — explaining any discrepancy corrects cultural misunderstanding.

To elicit the patient's own framework for what the illness means, what caused it, what they fear, and what treatment they expect — surfacing beliefs and expectations that shape adherence and therapeutic relationship.
To determine whether the patient requires a medical interpreter — the questions reveal whether language is the primary communication barrier.
To screen for psychosis — patients who attribute illness to supernatural causes are flagged for psychiatric assessment.

tier2.why: Kleinman's explanatory-model questions ('What do you call this problem? What do you think caused it? How does it affect you? What are you most afraid of? What treatment do you expect?') are not about correcting the patient's beliefs or screening for pathology. They are about surfacing the patient's illness framework so the clinician understands what the illness means to the patient — beliefs about cause, significance, and expected treatment that directly influence adherence, trust, and therapeutic planning. Cultural concepts of distress may emerge through these questions that would otherwise be mislabeled as panic or psychosis.

qb_otherdx_008.stem: A 34-year-old Black man presents with paranoid ideation, disorganized thinking, and social withdrawal that began 3 months ago. A student suggests schizophrenia. The attending asks the student to consider a documented cultural bias. Which statement reflects the clinical evidence?

options.t: Black patients present with more severe schizophrenia symptoms on average, which explains the higher diagnostic rate.

trap.name: Severity explains disparity
trap.note: The higher rate of schizophrenia diagnoses in Black patients is not explained by symptom severity — clinician diagnostic bias is a documented contributor; the same presentations in Black patients are more often labeled schizophrenia and less often labeled mood disorder.

options.t: The diagnostic difference reflects differential rates of schizophrenia across demographic groups — epidemiological data confirm higher prevalence in this population, so no allowance for clinician bias is needed.

trap.name: Epidemiology explains disparity
trap.note: Prevalence alone does not explain the gap: comparable presentations are diagnosed differently by race, and clinician diagnostic bias is a documented contributor — so the difference cannot be read as confirmed higher prevalence.

options.t: Cultural mistrust in the clinical encounter leads Black patients to endorse more psychotic symptoms on screening, creating a false-positive signal.

trap.name: Patient behavior explains disparity
trap.note: The documented contributor is clinician diagnostic behavior (over-applying schizophrenia, under-applying mood disorders), not a false-positive signal from patient reporting.

options.t: Black patients are over-diagnosed with schizophrenia and under-diagnosed with mood disorders relative to comparable presentations — a robust disparity to which clinician bias is a documented contributor.

qb_otherdx_008.why: Severity explains disparity, Epidemiology explains disparity, and Patient behavior explains disparity each explain the gap away with a single cause the evidence does not support. The page is explicit: 'Black (and some other minority) patients are disproportionately over-diagnosed with schizophrenia and under-diagnosed with mood disorders relative to comparable presentations.' The evidence shows a robust disparity that persists even with structured interviews, to which clinician bias (e.g., under-weighting affective symptoms) is a documented contributor — guard against it. This is a patient-safety issue that requires active self-monitoring.
qb_otherdx_008.pearl: Documented bias: Black patients are over-diagnosed with schizophrenia and under-diagnosed with mood disorders — a disparity that persists after accounting for symptom profile, with clinician bias a documented contributor; guard against it.
qb_otherdx_008.evidence: cultural_psychiatry.md — Black (and some other minority) patients are disproportionately over-diagnosed with schizophrenia and under-diagnosed with mood disorders relative to comparable presentations.

qb_otherdx_009.stem: A 30-year-old mother, 3 weeks postpartum, scores a 14 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). She is distressed and anxious. The student says, 'She screened positive for postpartum depression — start sertraline.' The attending asks what the student may have missed. Which is most accurate?

options.t: The EPDS is not validated for postpartum use — use the PHQ-9 instead.

trap.name: EPDS not validated postpartum
trap.note: The EPDS is specifically designed and validated for postpartum screening; this is factually incorrect.

options.t: A score of 14 on the EPDS requires hospitalization — outpatient sertraline is below the level of care indicated.

trap.name: EPDS score mandates hospitalization
trap.note: EPDS scores guide clinical decisions but do not directly mandate a specific level of care; the clinical picture (function, safety, psychotic features) determines disposition.

options.t: The EPDS screens for depression and anxiety but does NOT detect psychotic or manic symptoms — explicitly ask about hallucinations, delusions, and manic symptoms before assuming postpartum depression rather than psychosis or bipolar relapse.
Sertraline is contraindicated in the first 4 weeks postpartum — the student should recommend a different SSRI.

trap.name: Sertraline contraindicated postpartum
trap.note: Sertraline and escitalopram are specifically mentioned in the page as usual first-line SSRIs for perinatal depression; there is no 4-week postpartum contraindication.

qb_otherdx_009.why: EPDS not validated, EPDS score mandates hospitalization, and Sertraline contraindicated all misstate the evidence. The page's explicit pearl: 'The EPDS screens depression, not psychosis — ask about delusions and perceptual disturbance directly.' The student's error is treating a positive depression screen as a complete psychiatric assessment — the EPDS misses psychosis and mania by design.
qb_otherdx_009.pearl: EPDS screens for depression and anxiety — it does NOT detect psychosis or mania; always ask explicitly about delusions, hallucinations, and manic symptoms in every postpartum patient.
qb_otherdx_009.evidence: t_perinatal.md — The EPDS screens depression, not psychosis — ask about delusions and perceptual disturbance directly.

tier2.q: A postpartum patient describes recurring intrusive thoughts of accidentally dropping her baby, which she finds horrifying. She does not act on these thoughts and goes out of her way to avoid holding the baby near stairs. What is the correct interpretation, and how does it differ from a concerning psychotic feature?

options.t: This is a command hallucination instructing her to harm the baby — she requires emergency admission and a safety plan for infant protection.

This is postpartum OCD — the intrusive thoughts are ego-dystonic (horrifying to her), and she avoids situations that could lead to the feared outcome; this differs from psychotic phenomena — voices experienced as external or beliefs about the infant held with delusional conviction, which are an emergency regardless of how distressed the mother is by them — and the correct response is clinical support and reassurance, not emergency separation from the baby.
This is a normal postpartum anxiety response — new mothers universally have intrusive thoughts about infant safety, which resolves without treatment.
This is a delusion of persecution — the belief that she might harm her child is a paranoid misinterpretation that requires antipsychotic treatment.

tier2.why: Postpartum OCD intrusive thoughts are a critically important differential. The page states: 'Postpartum OCD intrusive thoughts are ego-dystonic and not command hallucinations — distinguish them to avoid both over- and under-reaction.' Key discrimination: (1) Ego-dystonic: the patient is horrified by the thoughts and does not want to act on them. (2) She avoids, not approaches, situations that could lead to the feared outcome. (3) Psychotic phenomena are experienced as external perceptions (voices) or held with delusional conviction; the mother's distress does not rule them out, and risk tracks conviction and appraisal of the experience, not ego-syntonicity. Mislabeling postpartum OCD as command hallucinations leads to emergency separation and antipsychotic treatment of a patient who needs reassurance and OCD-specific treatment.

qb_cdev_005.stem: A 9-year-old is referred for inattention and hyperactivity. Which is required to diagnose ADHD?

options.t: Symptoms limited to the classroom

trap.name: Single-setting error
trap.note: ADHD requires impairment in at least two settings; one setting suggests a situational cause.

options.t: New onset after age 12 with normal early childhood

trap.name: Late-onset error
trap.note: Several symptoms must be present before age 12.

options.t: A confirmatory brain MRI or EEG

trap.name: Test-confirmation trap
trap.note: ADHD is a clinical diagnosis; no scan confirms it.

options.t: Onset before age 12 and impairment in 2+ settings

qb_cdev_005.why: ADHD requires several symptoms before age 12, ≥6 months, with impairment in ≥2 settings; it is a clinical diagnosis.
qb_cdev_005.pearl: ADHD: symptoms before age 12, ≥2 settings, clinical diagnosis.
qb_cdev_005.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: ADHD criteria.

qb_cdev_006.stem: A 10-year-old has ADHD with significant impairment despite behavioral supports. First-line pharmacologic treatment?

options.t: A stimulant
An antipsychotic

trap.name: Off-target trap
trap.note: Not first-line for ADHD; metabolic and movement risks.

options.t: A benzodiazepine

trap.name: Sedative trap
trap.note: No role in ADHD; can worsen disinhibition.

options.t: An SSRI

trap.name: Wrong-class trap
trap.note: SSRIs treat depression/anxiety, not core ADHD.

qb_cdev_006.why: Stimulants are first-line and most effective for core ADHD symptoms when not contraindicated; non-stimulants such as atomoxetine, viloxazine, and alpha-2 agonists are alternatives when risk-benefit concerns point away from stimulants.
qb_cdev_006.pearl: ADHD: stimulants first-line; non-stimulants are alternatives when risk or tolerability changes the plan.
qb_cdev_006.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: ADHD medication.

qb_cdev_008.stem: A 4-year-old has marked deficits in social communication and reciprocity plus restricted, repetitive behaviors and insistence on sameness, present since early development. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Social (pragmatic) communication disorder

trap.name: Missing-the-RRBs trap
trap.note: That disorder lacks restricted/repetitive behaviors, which are present here.

options.t: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder

trap.name: Wrong-domain trap
trap.note: ADHD is inattention/hyperactivity, not the ASD pattern.

options.t: Autism spectrum disorder
Childhood-onset schizophrenia

trap.name: Psychosis mislabel
trap.note: ASD lacks hallucinations/delusions.

qb_cdev_008.why: ASD requires BOTH social-communication deficits AND restricted, repetitive behaviors with early onset; the restricted/repetitive domain separates it from social communication disorder.
qb_cdev_008.pearl: Autism = social-communication deficits PLUS restricted/repetitive behaviors, early onset.
qb_cdev_008.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: autism spectrum disorder.

qb_cdev_009.stem: A 12-year-old has had multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, waxing and waning for 18 months, onset at age 9. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Persistent (chronic) motor OR vocal tic disorder

trap.name: Single-modality error
trap.note: Chronic tic disorder is motor OR vocal; Tourette requires both.

options.t: Provisional tic disorder

trap.name: Duration error
trap.note: Provisional = tics <1 year; these have lasted 18 months.

options.t: Functional movement disorder

trap.name: Wrong-category trap
trap.note: The chronic multi-tic pattern fits Tourette.

options.t: Tourette disorder with motor and vocal tics

qb_cdev_009.why: Tourette requires BOTH multiple motor tics AND ≥1 vocal tic, >1 year, onset before age 18.
qb_cdev_009.pearl: Tourette: multiple motor tics AND ≥1 vocal tic, >1 year, onset before 18.
qb_cdev_009.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: tic disorders.

qb_cdev_010.stem: A 7-year-old has primary nocturnal enuresis with normal daytime continence and a normal exam. Most appropriate first-line management?

options.t: Behavioral measures plus an enuresis alarm
Open-ended desmopressin as first-line therapy

trap.name: Med-first trap
trap.note: Desmopressin helps short-term control but relapse is common; the alarm has better long-term cure.

options.t: Imipramine as first-line therapy

trap.name: Outdated/risk trap
trap.note: TCAs are later-line because overdose cardiotoxicity matters.

options.t: Fluid restriction and punishment for wet nights

trap.name: Harm trap
trap.note: Punitive approaches are ineffective and harmful.

qb_cdev_010.why: For primary nocturnal enuresis with normal daytime continence and a normal exam, reassurance and behavioral measures are first-line; the enuresis alarm has the best long-term cure. Desmopressin is useful for short-term control, and TCAs are later-line because of toxicity.
qb_cdev_010.pearl: Enuresis: alarm for long-term cure; desmopressin for short-term control; never punish wet nights.
qb_cdev_010.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: nocturnal enuresis.

qb_cdev_011.stem: A child is evaluated for intellectual disability. What determines the severity level (mild, moderate, severe, profound)?

options.t: Full-scale IQ score alone

trap.name: IQ-only trap
trap.note: DSM-5-TR grades severity by adaptive functioning, not IQ cutoffs alone.

options.t: Adaptive-functioning impairment
Chronological age at testing

trap.name: Age error
trap.note: Age does not set intellectual-disability severity.

options.t: Presence of a known genetic syndrome

trap.name: Etiology error
trap.note: Etiology may explain the disorder but does not set severity.

qb_cdev_011.why: Intellectual disability requires deficits in intellectual and adaptive functioning with developmental-period onset; severity is graded by adaptive functioning, not IQ alone.
qb_cdev_011.pearl: Intellectual disability severity = adaptive functioning, not IQ alone.
qb_cdev_011.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: intellectual disability.

link.label: Open the Ethics & the Law page

qb_eth_009.stem: A patient with untreated mania insists on leaving; the team considers an involuntary hold. Which criterion must generally be met?

options.t: The team simply believes admission would be beneficial

trap.name: Paternalism trap
trap.note: Perceived benefit alone is not a legal basis for a hold.

options.t: The patient disagrees with the diagnosis

trap.name: Disagreement trap
trap.note: Disagreement is not grounds for commitment.

options.t: Mental illness plus dangerousness or grave disability
Family request for admission

trap.name: Third-party trap
trap.note: A family request alone does not satisfy criteria.

qb_eth_009.why: Involuntary hospitalization generally requires mental illness plus danger to self, danger to others, or grave disability; statutes vary by jurisdiction and local policy.
qb_eth_009.pearl: Involuntary hold = mental illness + (danger to self / others / grave disability).

link.label: Open the Ethics & the Law page

qb_eth_010.stem: A resident asks whether a delirious patient is 'competent' to refuse a lumbar puncture. Most accurate framing?

options.t: Capacity and competence are identical bedside labels

trap.name: Conflation trap
trap.note: Capacity is clinical and decision-specific; competence is a legal status.

options.t: Judicial review for every medical decision

trap.name: Over-legalization
trap.note: Clinicians assess capacity at the bedside; courts determine competence.

options.t: Lost capacity is permanent once documented

trap.name: Permanence error
trap.note: Capacity can fluctuate and is decision-specific.

options.t: Capacity is clinical; competence is a legal finding

qb_eth_010.why: Capacity is clinical, decision-specific, and can fluctuate; competence is a legal status decided by a court. The four abilities frame the bedside capacity assessment.
qb_eth_010.pearl: Capacity = clinical, decision-specific, fluctuates; competence = legal, court-determined.

link.label: Open the Ethics & the Law page

qb_eth_011.stem: An unconscious patient arrives after an overdose, no surrogate reachable, needing immediate life-saving treatment. Which principle applies?

options.t: Emergency exception with implied consent
Wait for a court-appointed guardian before treating

trap.name: Delay-harm trap
trap.note: Waiting in a life-threatening emergency causes avoidable harm.

options.t: Require written consent before any intervention

trap.name: Consent-absolutism
trap.note: Written consent is not required for emergency life-saving care when consent cannot be obtained.

options.t: Treat an unrelated prior refusal as binding

trap.name: Irrelevant-refusal trap
trap.note: An unrelated prior refusal does not govern emergency overdose care.

qb_eth_011.why: The emergency exception allows necessary treatment to prevent death or serious harm when the patient lacks capacity and no surrogate or applicable advance directive is available.
qb_eth_011.pearl: Emergency exception: implied consent covers necessary urgent care when consent cannot be obtained.
qb_eth_011.evidence: ethics_legal.md — Consent and the emergency exception.

qb_otherdx_011.stem: Fourteen months after her spouse's death, a woman has persistent intense yearning and preoccupation with the deceased, difficulty accepting the death, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbness, and a feeling that life is meaningless. Symptoms impair function and exceed her cultural norms. Which DSM-5-TR diagnosis best fits?

options.t: Prolonged grief disorder
Normal bereavement

trap.name: Under-call trap
trap.note: Grief this intense and impairing beyond ~12 months, exceeding cultural norms, is prolonged grief disorder.

options.t: Major depressive disorder

trap.name: Overlap trap
trap.note: Grief centers on yearning/preoccupation with the deceased; they can co-occur but are distinguishable.

options.t: Adjustment disorder

trap.name: Duration/threshold trap
trap.note: Adjustment disorder is shorter-term; the persistent ≥12-month grief syndrome is prolonged grief disorder.

qb_otherdx_011.why: Prolonged grief disorder is grief-specific: at least 12 months after the death of a close person in adults, intense yearning or preoccupation plus additional grief symptoms causes impairment and exceeds cultural norms. MDD can co-occur, but grief centers on yearning and preoccupation with the deceased.
qb_otherdx_011.pearl: Prolonged grief disorder: persistent yearning/preoccupation plus grief-specific symptoms beyond 12 months in adults, with impairment beyond cultural norms.
qb_otherdx_011.evidence: t_mood.md — Grief vs depression anchor: prolonged grief disorder vs normal bereavement vs MDD.

link.label: Open the Family Therapy Modalities page

qb_rel_016.stem: A patient's adult son calls the unit asking for details of his mother's diagnosis and medications. The patient has not authorized this. What is the most appropriate response?

options.t: Share diagnosis and medications because he is family

trap.name: Family-exception myth
trap.note: Family status alone does not authorize protected clinical disclosure.

options.t: Refuse any conversation and hang up

trap.name: Over-restriction trap
trap.note: You can listen and provide general education without disclosing protected specifics.

options.t: Verify identity, then disclose the full record

trap.name: Identity-only trap
trap.note: Identity verification does not substitute for the patient's authorization to disclose.

options.t: No specifics without consent; offer general support

qb_rel_016.why: Without the patient's consent, do not confirm or share specific diagnosis or medication information. You can still listen, offer general support and education, and coordinate a consented family meeting; safety exceptions are separate.
qb_rel_016.pearl: No consent means no specific disclosure; general support and education are still allowed.
qb_rel_016.evidence: family_modalities.md — Confidentiality and families; ethics_legal.md — disclosure.

qb_anx_015.stem: A veteran with PTSD has nightmares, hypervigilance, and avoidance. Which approach is first-line, and what should generally be avoided?

options.t: Scheduled benzodiazepines as the mainstay; avoid exposure therapy

trap.name: Harm trap
trap.note: Benzodiazepines are generally avoided in PTSD because they do not treat core symptoms and carry risk.

options.t: Antipsychotic monotherapy for core symptoms; avoid SSRIs

trap.name: Off-target trap
trap.note: Antipsychotics are not first-line monotherapy for core PTSD.

options.t: Trauma-focused therapy and/or SSRI/SNRI; avoid benzodiazepines
Watchful waiting without treatment

trap.name: Nihilism trap
trap.note: Effective trauma-focused therapies and medication options exist.

qb_anx_015.why: First-line PTSD care prioritizes trauma-focused psychotherapy such as CPT or prolonged exposure, with sertraline, paroxetine, or venlafaxine as medication options when medication is chosen. Routine benzodiazepines are generally avoided.
qb_anx_015.pearl: PTSD: trauma-focused therapy first; SSRI/SNRI when medication is chosen; avoid routine benzodiazepines.
qb_anx_015.evidence: t_anxiety.md — Exam treatment anchors: PTSD treatment and benzodiazepine avoidance.

qb_anx_016.stem: A student develops intense anxiety only when performing music in public but is comfortable in other social situations. Which best describes the condition and a reasonable option?

options.t: Social anxiety disorder, Performance type requiring PRN medication
Generalized anxiety disorder requiring daily long-term medication

trap.name: Overgeneralization trap
trap.note: Anxiety limited to performance is not pervasive GAD; the performance-only subtype can be managed PRN.

options.t: Panic disorder requiring PRN medication

trap.name: Wrong-dx trap
trap.note: There are no recurrent unexpected panic attacks with persistent worry about attacks; this is performance-limited social anxiety.

options.t: A normal reaction requiring no discussion

trap.name: Dismissal trap
trap.note: Impairing performance anxiety is a recognized, treatable condition.

qb_anx_016.why: Anxiety confined to discrete public performances is performance-only social anxiety. When medically appropriate, a PRN beta-blocker can reduce tremor, tachycardia, and sweating for those events; generalized social anxiety is treated with CBT/exposure and SSRI/SNRI when medication is needed.
qb_anx_016.pearl: Performance-only social anxiety: PRN beta-blocker for physical performance symptoms; generalized social anxiety needs CBT/exposure ± SSRI/SNRI.
qb_anx_016.evidence: t_anxiety.md — Exam treatment anchors: performance-only social anxiety.

qb_per_014.stem: A 40-year-old executive expects constant admiration, believes he is uniquely special and entitled to the best of everything, and dismisses colleagues as beneath him; he becomes enraged by mild criticism. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Narcissistic personality disorder
Antisocial personality disorder

trap.name: Rights-violation trap
trap.note: ASPD centers on disregard for and violation of others' rights; NPD centers on grandiosity, entitlement, and need for admiration.

options.t: Histrionic personality disorder

trap.name: Attention-mechanism trap
trap.note: Histrionic patients seek attention through emotionality/seductiveness, not grandiosity and entitlement.

options.t: Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic

trap.name: State-vs-trait trap
trap.note: Mania is an episodic mood state; this is an enduring characterological pattern.

qb_per_014.why: Grandiosity, need for admiration, entitlement, and lack of empathy define narcissistic personality disorder — distinct from antisocial (rights violations) and histrionic (attention through emotionality).
qb_per_014.pearl: NPD = grandiosity + need for admiration + entitlement + lack of empathy.
qb_per_014.evidence: t_personality.md — Exam diagnostic anchors: narcissistic personality disorder.

qb_per_015.stem: A 33-year-old woman cannot make everyday decisions without excessive reassurance, feels helpless when alone, and urgently seeks a new relationship for care whenever one ends. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Avoidant personality disorder

trap.name: Cluster-C mix-up
trap.note: Avoidant patients want relationships but avoid them from fear of criticism/rejection; dependent patients cling and urgently seek care.

options.t: Dependent personality disorder
Borderline personality disorder

trap.name: BPD conflation
trap.note: BPD features identity disturbance, self-harm, and unstable intense relationships, not the pure submissive/clinging dependence described.

options.t: Histrionic personality disorder

trap.name: Attention-seeking trap
trap.note: Histrionic is attention-seeking emotionality, not the need to be cared for described here.

qb_per_015.why: A pervasive, excessive need to be taken care of — submissiveness, difficulty making decisions without reassurance, and urgently seeking a replacement relationship for care — defines dependent personality disorder (Cluster C).
qb_per_015.pearl: Dependent PD = excessive need to be cared for, submissive/clinging, urgently replaces lost relationships.
qb_per_015.evidence: t_personality.md — Exam diagnostic anchors: dependent personality disorder.

qb_per_016.stem: A 29-year-old is uncomfortable when not the center of attention, is dramatic and seductive with staff, shows rapidly shifting shallow emotions, and considers acquaintances closer than they are. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Borderline personality disorder

trap.name: BPD conflation
trap.note: BPD features abandonment fears, identity disturbance, and self-harm; histrionic centers on attention-seeking emotionality and seductiveness.

options.t: Narcissistic personality disorder

trap.name: Grandiosity trap
trap.note: Narcissistic patients seek admiration for specialness; histrionic patients seek attention through emotionality.

options.t: Histrionic personality disorder
Dependent personality disorder

trap.name: Cluster-C mix-up
trap.note: Dependent patients seek care and reassurance, not attention through dramatic emotionality.

qb_per_016.why: Excessive attention-seeking, dramatic and seductive behavior, shallow shifting emotions, and overestimating intimacy define histrionic personality disorder (Cluster B).
qb_per_016.pearl: Histrionic PD = attention-seeking, dramatic/seductive, shallow shifting emotions.
qb_per_016.evidence: t_personality.md — Exam diagnostic anchors: histrionic personality disorder.

qb_cdev_012.stem: A 7-year-old refuses school, complains of stomachaches on school mornings that resolve on weekends, and is terrified that something will happen to his mother while apart. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Generalized anxiety disorder

trap.name: Over-broad trap
trap.note: GAD is pervasive worry across domains; here the fear is specifically about separation from an attachment figure.

options.t: Oppositional defiant disorder

trap.name: Defiance mislabel
trap.note: This is fear-driven school refusal, not an angry/defiant pattern.

options.t: Malingering for external gain

trap.name: Intent trap
trap.note: The somatic complaints are anxiety-driven, not consciously feigned for external gain.

options.t: Separation anxiety disorder

qb_cdev_012.why: Developmentally inappropriate, excessive fear of separation from attachment figures — with somatic complaints and school refusal, lasting ≥4 weeks in a child — is separation anxiety disorder.
qb_cdev_012.pearl: Separation anxiety disorder: excessive separation fear, somatic complaints, school refusal (≥4 weeks in children).
qb_cdev_012.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: separation anxiety disorder.

qb_cdev_013.stem: A 6-year-old repeatedly soils his underwear; exam reveals a large stool mass and history of painful, infrequent bowel movements. Best diagnosis and initial management?

options.t: Retentive encopresis from constipation
Conduct disorder with deliberate defiance

trap.name: Intent trap
trap.note: Retentive encopresis with overflow is not willful defiance; it stems from constipation.

options.t: Primary psychotic process

trap.name: Overpathologizing
trap.note: Soiling from constipation is not a psychotic symptom.

options.t: Normal age-appropriate behavior

trap.name: Under-call trap
trap.note: Encopresis is diagnosed at chronological age 4 or older and warrants treatment.

qb_cdev_013.why: Encopresis at age 4 or older is often retentive with overflow incontinence. Treat the constipation with disimpaction and maintenance, add toileting routine and behavioral support, and avoid punishment.
qb_cdev_013.pearl: Encopresis: usually retentive overflow — treat the constipation first, add behavioral measures.
qb_cdev_013.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: encopresis.

qb_cdev_014.stem: A 6-year-old speaks normally at home but consistently fails to speak at school, where she is otherwise engaged; this has lasted the school year and impairs learning. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Autism spectrum disorder

trap.name: Social-communication trap
trap.note: ASD involves pervasive social-communication deficits and restricted/repetitive behaviors; selective mutism is situation-specific with normal speech elsewhere.

options.t: Selective mutism
A language (communication) disorder

trap.name: Capacity trap
trap.note: The child can speak normally at home; the failure is situational, pointing to an anxiety disorder, not a language deficit.

options.t: Oppositional defiant disorder

trap.name: Defiance mislabel
trap.note: The mutism is anxiety-driven, not willful defiance.

qb_cdev_014.why: Selective mutism is a consistent failure to speak in specific social situations (e.g., school) despite speaking normally elsewhere, interfering with functioning — an anxiety-spectrum disorder, not a language or defiance problem.
qb_cdev_014.pearl: Selective mutism: won't speak in specific settings but speaks normally elsewhere — an anxiety disorder.
qb_cdev_014.evidence: t_neurodev.md — Child and adolescent exam anchors: selective mutism.

link.label: Open the Ethics & the Law page

qb_eth_014.stem: During an interview, a child discloses details strongly suggesting physical abuse at home. The parent asks you to keep it confidential. What must you do?

options.t: Keep it confidential because the parent requested it

trap.name: Confidentiality-override trap
trap.note: Confidentiality yields to mandatory reporting of suspected child abuse; a parent cannot waive that duty.

options.t: Wait until you have definitive proof before reporting

trap.name: Proof trap
trap.note: Reporting requires reasonable suspicion, not proof.

options.t: Report to CPS based on reasonable suspicion
Wait for the child to request a report

trap.name: Assent trap
trap.note: The duty to report does not depend on the child's request.

qb_eth_014.why: Suspected child abuse is a mandatory report based on reasonable suspicion — you do not need proof, and confidentiality (including a parent's request) does not override the duty. Elder/dependent-adult abuse carries similar duties.
qb_eth_014.pearl: Suspected child abuse = mandatory report on reasonable suspicion; confidentiality does not override it.

link.label: Open the Ethics & the Law page

qb_eth_015.stem: A 15-year-old comes alone requesting evaluation. Which statement about consent for a minor is most accurate?

options.t: Parental consent is required for every non-emergency service

trap.name: Absolutism trap
trap.note: Emancipated-minor, confidential-service, and emergency exceptions vary by jurisdiction.

options.t: A minor has broad adult authority for routine care

trap.name: Over-broad trap
trap.note: Minors do not have blanket adult authority; parental consent is the general rule.

options.t: Emergency care waits while staff reach a parent

trap.name: Emergency trap
trap.note: Emergency care proceeds under implied consent when delay would cause harm.

options.t: Parental consent is usual, with defined exceptions

qb_eth_015.why: Parental consent is the general rule for minors, but important exceptions exist: emancipated or mature minors, certain confidential services depending on jurisdiction, and the emergency exception. Local law matters.
qb_eth_015.pearl: Minors usually need parental consent, with jurisdiction-dependent confidential-service, emancipated-minor, and emergency exceptions.

qb_otherdx_012.stem: A 20-year-old has months of overwhelming daytime sleepiness with sudden, brief episodes of bilateral leg weakness triggered by laughter, plus vivid hallucinations while falling asleep and episodes of waking paralysis. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Obstructive sleep apnea

trap.name: Mechanism trap
trap.note: OSA causes fragmented sleep and sleepiness but not cataplexy, the emotion-triggered muscle-tone loss described.

options.t: Narcolepsy with cataplexy
A primary psychotic disorder

trap.name: Hallucination trap
trap.note: Hypnagogic hallucinations at sleep onset are a narcolepsy feature, not a primary psychosis.

options.t: Generalized anxiety disorder

trap.name: Wrong-domain trap
trap.note: The tetrad points to narcolepsy, not anxiety.

qb_otherdx_012.why: The narcolepsy tetrad — excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy (emotion-triggered muscle-tone loss), sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations — with low CSF orexin/hypocretin defines narcolepsy type 1; MSLT shows short REM latency.
qb_otherdx_012.pearl: Narcolepsy: sleepiness + cataplexy + sleep paralysis + hypnagogic hallucinations; low orexin.

qb_otherdx_014.stem: A woman with a severe childhood trauma history has recurrent gaps in memory for everyday events and describes two distinct identity states with different names and behaviors that others have witnessed. Best diagnosis?

options.t: Borderline personality disorder

trap.name: Identity-disturbance trap
trap.note: BPD identity disturbance is an unstable self-image, not distinct alternating identity states with amnesia.

options.t: Malingering for external gain

trap.name: Intent trap
trap.note: The presentation, corroborated by others and tied to severe trauma, is not simply feigned for gain.

options.t: Schizophrenia with primary psychosis

trap.name: Psychosis conflation
trap.note: 'Split personality' is not schizophrenia; DID involves identity states and amnesia, not primary psychosis.

options.t: Dissociative identity disorder

qb_otherdx_014.why: Two or more distinct personality states plus recurrent amnesia beyond ordinary forgetting, strongly associated with severe early trauma, defines dissociative identity disorder — commonly confused with (but distinct from) schizophrenia.
qb_otherdx_014.pearl: DID = ≥2 distinct identity states + amnesia, linked to severe early trauma; not schizophrenia.

[Drug Safety and Availability](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability "Drug Safety and Availability") [In this section](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/drug-safety-communications#section-nav) [Español](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/comunicaciones-de-la-fda-sobre-la-seguridad-de-los-medicamentos-en-espanol) [药物安全通讯](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/yaowuanquantongxun) [Drug Safety Podcasts](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-drug-safety-podcasts) FDA Drug Safety Communications are intended to provide important information to patients and health care professionals about new safety issues with the medicines they are taking or prescribing so they can make more informed decisions about treatment. Widespread or long-term use of drugs by patients may uncover side effects not discovered during the clinical trials a drug company did to get FDA approval of the medicine. As a result, FDA physicians and scientists continue to monitor the safety of drugs after they are approved. When we learn information about a potential new safety issue, we review the data from available clinical trials or other studies, case reports, and medical literature. Based on what we find, we may require changes to the prescribing information or the patient Medication Guide. We may also release a Drug Safety Communication to alert patients and health care professionals about the issue. [Read more](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/surveillance-post-drug-approval-activities/postmarketing-surveillance-programs "Postmarketing Surveillance Programs"). You can get new safety information on medicines you’re prescribing or taking by signing up for [email alerts](https://public.govdelivery.com/accounts/USFDA/subscriber/new) [External Link questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability who lives in a group home is admitted for acute behavioral escalation — he became agitated and hit a staff member after a change in his daily routine. A nurse says, 'He has ASD — this is probably just how he behaves.' Which response reflects the correct clinical approach?

An 18-year-old with autism spectrum disorder is admitted for aggressive behavior. His parents ask if medication can 'help with his autism.' The team considers starting risperidone. Which statement about the pharmacological target of risperidone in ASD is most accurate?

A 16-year-old boy with a childhood diagnosis of ADHD is admitted following his first episode of several days of markedly decreased sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech, and impulsive behavior. His parents report that his ADHD has 'always been there' but this episode is 'completely different.' His Vanderbilt score from 3 years ago documented inattention and hyperactivity across home and school settings. Which interpretation is most accurate?

A 26-year-old man with autism spectrum disorder is admitted by his group home for a change in behavior. Over the past 10 days he has become mute, stopped eating, and is found in fixed postures for hours at a time. He previously spoke in simple sentences and was active in daily activities. Which diagnosis must be actively evaluated?
A 9-year-old is referred for inattention and hyperactivity. Which is required to diagnose ADHD?
A 10-year-old has ADHD with significant impairment despite behavioral supports. First-line pharmacologic treatment?
An 8-year-old is argumentative, loses his temper, and defies adults, but has never been physically aggressive, destroyed property, stolen, or seriously violated others' rights. Best diagnosis?
A 4-year-old has marked deficits in social communication and reciprocity plus restricted, repetitive behaviors and insistence on sameness, present since early development. Best diagnosis?
A 12-year-old has had multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, waxing and waning for 18 months, onset at age 9. Best diagnosis?
A 7-year-old has primary nocturnal enuresis with normal daytime continence and a normal exam. Most appropriate first-line management?
A child is evaluated for intellectual disability. What determines the severity level (mild, moderate, severe, profound)?
A 7-year-old refuses school, complains of stomachaches on school mornings that resolve on weekends, and is terrified that something will happen to his mother while apart. Best diagnosis?
A 6-year-old repeatedly soils his underwear; exam reveals a large stool mass and history of painful, infrequent bowel movements. Best diagnosis and initial management?
A 6-year-old speaks normally at home but consistently fails to speak at school, where she is otherwise engaged; this has lasted the school year and impairs learning. Best diagnosis?

A 19-year-old college student is brought to the inpatient unit by his parents after three weeks of dramatically decreased need for sleep (sleeping two to three hours and feeling rested), expansive and grandiose mood, pressured speech, and impulsive spending. His parents note he has always been 'a little hyper' in school but never like this. He takes no medications and denies substance use. Most likely diagnosis?

An autistic adult admitted after aggression at his group home is increasingly distressed on the inpatient unit — covering his ears, rocking, and repeatedly asking when it will be quiet. He is not in imminent danger. No PRN medication has been given. The most appropriate first step is which of the following?

A 76-year-old woman on hospital day 3 after hip-fracture repair is referred to psychiatry for 'depression.' She is quiet, slow to respond, and sleeps much of the day; her nurse notes she was conversational yesterday evening but is 'flat' this morning. She cannot recite the months of the year backward. Most likely explanation?

An 82-year-old man on postoperative day 2 after hip arthroplasty is confused and agitated. The Confusion Assessment Method is positive for delirium. He has no history of dementia. Which is the most appropriate initial management step?

A 78-year-old woman with mild Alzheimer disease is admitted from her nursing home after 2 days of worsening confusion. A CAM is positive. She is agitated and picking at her IV. The team asks the student to help select an appropriate PRN medication for dangerous agitation. Which of the following is correct?

A 74-year-old man presents with an 18-month history of vivid recurrent visual hallucinations (small animals in the room), episodes of staring with fluctuating cognition, mild rigidity and slowness, and his wife's report that he 'acts out his dreams' and has struck her while asleep. Which dementia subtype does this constellation most strongly suggest?

A patient with known Lewy body dementia is admitted with agitation and paranoid delusions. A nurse asks whether the team should start haloperidol. The most appropriate response is which of the following?

A 69-year-old man is referred for evaluation of progressive cognitive decline, urinary incontinence that preceded the cognitive changes by several months, and a gait his wife describes as 'shuffling and magnetic — like his feet are stuck to the floor.' MRI is pending. Which diagnosis should be considered first because of its potential reversibility?

Psychiatry is consulted on an 82-year-old man in the surgical ICU on postoperative day 3. He is quiet, slow to respond, and sleeping between nursing checks — his nurse reports he was interactive at yesterday's evening assessment. His CAM is positive. The covering team wonders why this presentation is more concerning than a 'hyperactive' delirious patient. Which statement best explains the clinical risk?

A 68-year-old woman is admitted after 4 months of progressive cognitive decline and withdrawal. Neuropsychological testing suggests a moderate amnestic syndrome. She has no known prior psychiatric or neurological history. Which is the most appropriate first-line laboratory workup before assigning a neurodegenerative diagnosis?

A 78-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment is admitted for worsening confusion and agitation over the past week. She recently started diphenhydramine nightly for insomnia and oxybutynin for urge incontinence. The student reviews her medication list. Which is the most appropriate next step?

A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife, who reports an 18-month history of increasingly disinhibited behavior — making inappropriate sexual comments to strangers, hoarding food, and neglecting hygiene. He has no memory complaints, names and recognizes objects normally, and denies mood symptoms. Neuropsychological testing shows prominent executive dysfunction with intact episodic memory. Most likely diagnosis?

A 74-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history is brought to the emergency department by her family. She has developed, over the past month, a fixed belief that her neighbors are poisoning her food and has stopped eating. She is alert, coherent, and oriented. There is no mood disturbance. Which is the most important next step?

An 82-year-old man with moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease is currently on donepezil 10 mg daily. His neurologist asks the student to identify what pharmacotherapy optimization is supported by evidence for this stage of disease.

A 73-year-old woman with recurrent major depression (last treated 5 years ago) is referred for cognitive evaluation after 3 months of 'memory problems.' On formal cognitive testing she scores in the impaired range on delayed recall but consistently answers 'I don't know' rather than confabulating; she is slow to initiate answers and appears effortfully disengaged. She remains alert and attentive, and scores 22 on the PHQ-9. Most appropriate next step?

A 31-year-old woman is admitted for a severe depressive episode with passive suicidal ideation. The intern plans to start sertraline today. Before initiating an antidepressant, the most important step is which of the following?

A 38-year-old man with bipolar I disorder, stable on lithium maintenance for two years, presents with a 2-day course of worsening tremor, confusion, and vomiting. Five days ago he began ibuprofen for back pain. Which of the following best explains his presentation?

A 31-year-old woman with two prior depressive episodes was started on escitalopram without a bipolar screen. Two weeks later she is brought to the emergency department with 4 days of markedly decreased sleep, racing thoughts, and grandiosity. What does this presentation most likely represent?

A 38-year-old man presents for admission with a current depressive episode. He reports no prior manic episodes. His wife, who accompanied him, states that 3 years ago he 'went weeks without sleeping, gave away his car, and was fired for erratic behavior.' He does not recall this period as abnormal. Which diagnostic move has the highest yield in clarifying the bipolar question?

A 29-year-old man is admitted with depressed mood, anhedonia, and feelings of worthlessness. On detailed MSE, he also has racing thoughts, psychomotor agitation, and is sleeping only 3 hours per night despite feeling exhausted. He endorses passive suicidal ideation. Which statement about his presentation is most clinically important?

A 71-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history presents with 2 weeks of elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, and grandiosity. Her family calls it her 'first manic episode.' She is on prednisone 40 mg daily for a recent flare of rheumatoid arthritis. Which step is most important before proceeding with a bipolar diagnosis?

A 44-year-old man with bipolar I disorder and two prior suicide attempts is starting maintenance therapy. The team is choosing between lithium and lamotrigine. Which argument most strongly favors lithium?

A 67-year-old woman with treatment-resistant MDD is hospitalized. She has failed two adequate antidepressant trials, has active suicidal ideation, refuses all oral intake, and expresses the nihilistic delusion that her intestines have rotted. The team debates a third antidepressant versus ECT. Which framing is most accurate?

A 45-year-old man with MDD was started on sertraline 50 mg outpatient 4 weeks ago. His PHQ-9 improved from 22 to 18. His outpatient clinician says, 'No response — time to add lithium augmentation.' A student asks what should be verified before changing the plan. Which element of measurement-based, sequential treatment (in the spirit of STAR*D) is most relevant here?

A patient with bipolar I disorder, admitted during a depressive episode, tells the student: 'I don't see why the staff keeps bothering me about sleep — it doesn't affect my moods.' Which response best reflects the clinical evidence?

A 28-year-old man with bipolar I disorder is admitted for his first acute manic episode. He has no prior mood stabilizer exposure. Which is the most appropriate pharmacological framework for acute mania management?

A 58-year-old man with bipolar I disorder is stable on lithium 900 mg daily, level 0.8 mEq/L. He recently started ibuprofen for knee pain and reports new-onset hand tremor and mild mental fogginess for the past week. Most appropriate next step?

A 70-year-old woman is admitted with severe depression. She is convinced her children have died in a car accident — despite video calls with her healthy children — and that her body is 'empty inside.' She is oriented, alert, and attentive. No confusion on exam. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this presentation?

A 36-year-old man with 'recurrent unipolar depression' has been on sertraline 100 mg for 8 months. His current episode resolved well, but over the past 2 weeks he has developed markedly decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, and impulsive spending. He is not using substances. Which is the most accurate interpretation?

A 49-year-old man admitted for severe bipolar depression requests discharge on day 6. His mood has partially improved (PHQ-9 from 24 to 17), but he is still sleeping only 4 hours per night, his safety plan is not yet completed, and he does not have an outpatient appointment scheduled. The attending asks the student to frame the clinical decision. Which is most accurate?

A 24-year-old woman in her 14th week of pregnancy presents with severe MDD: active suicidal ideation with a plan, refusal to eat, psychomotor retardation, and a prior excellent response to ECT 4 years ago. The team debates continuing the current antidepressant versus offering ECT. Which statement best reflects the clinical standard?

A 27-year-old mother, 9 days postpartum, arrives with acute confusion and delusions that her infant 'was sent to test her faith.' Her husband reports hours of apparent lucidity followed by rapid deterioration. The diagnosis of postpartum psychosis is made. Which management priority is most immediately critical?

A 28-year-old woman who delivered 6 days ago is brought by her husband with confusion, talking to people who aren't there, and expressing beliefs that her baby 'was sent to test her faith.' She had been laughing and crying alternately. She was seen yesterday and appeared fine for two hours. What is the most critical diagnosis to consider?

A 30-year-old mother, 3 weeks postpartum, scores a 14 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). She is distressed and anxious. The student says, 'She screened positive for postpartum depression — start sertraline.' The attending asks what the student may have missed. Which is most accurate?

Fourteen months after her spouse's death, a woman has persistent intense yearning and preoccupation with the deceased, difficulty accepting the death, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbness, and a feeling that life is meaningless. Symptoms impair function and exceed her cultural norms. Which DSM-5-TR diagnosis best fits?

A 23-year-old man with a history of depression on high-dose sertraline is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after a second serotonergic medication was added to his regimen. Examination shows agitation, diarrhea, diaphoresis, and clonus; reflexes are brisk and symmetrically hyperactive throughout. Temperature is 38.3°C. Which of the following best explains this presentation?

A 34-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has just been started on clozapine. He reports feeling better than he has in years. Which ongoing monitoring is most critical for this medication?

A student argues that quetiapine should be chosen over haloperidol for a patient with psychosis because 'it's a second-generation agent and therefore more effective.' An attending asks what the CATIE trial established about this reasoning. Which response is most accurate?

A 23-year-old man is starting risperidone for his first psychotic episode. The student is asked to set up his monitoring schedule. What does the standard require for ALL patients starting any antipsychotic?

A 49-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has had three prior hospitalizations and two suicide attempts. The team is weighing lithium versus valproate for maintenance. Which statement about lithium's unique clinical profile is most accurate?

The team plans to start valproate for a 27-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder admitted for acute mania. The student reviews her chart and finds no documentation of pregnancy status or contraception. Which action must occur before the first dose is given?

A 29-year-old man presents with a 3-week first depressive episode. His maternal grandmother and aunt both have bipolar disorder. The team is ready to prescribe sertraline. The student asks whether a bipolar screen should be done first. What is the most appropriate response?

A 24-year-old woman started sertraline 3 days ago for major depression. She calls the unit and says, 'I don't feel any better — maybe this medication isn't right for me.' What is the most accurate and helpful response?

A 21-year-old man is starting escitalopram for his first major depressive episode. His parents ask: 'We've heard there's a black box warning on these medications — what does it mean?' Which response best reflects the FDA warning?

A 71-year-old woman with generalized anxiety disorder has been prescribed lorazepam 0.5 mg TID continuously for 18 months by her primary care physician. She is now admitted for a fall and mild confusion. The student is asked to comment on her lorazepam use. Which is the most accurate framing?

A 39-year-old man with schizophrenia has failed two adequate antipsychotic trials (olanzapine, then risperidone) at adequate doses and durations. The team discusses clozapine. What is the non-negotiable safety requirement before clozapine can be initiated?

A 65-year-old man with bipolar I disorder maintained on lithium 900 mg daily presents with intention tremor, unsteady gait, and mild confusion over 5 days. His lithium level was 0.75 mEq/L two months ago. He recently started lisinopril for newly diagnosed hypertension. Most likely explanation?

A 72-year-old woman with treatment-resistant MDD has active suicidal ideation, has stopped eating and drinking, and expresses a fixed belief that her body is rotting. She has failed two adequate antidepressant trials. The team is choosing between a third antidepressant plus antipsychotic versus ECT. Which response best reflects the evidence?

A patient with severe depression is scheduled for ECT tomorrow. Her current medications include clonazepam 1 mg BID, gabapentin 300 mg TID, and escitalopram 20 mg daily. Her ECT team asks the student to identify which medication adjustment is most critical before the procedure.

A 48-year-old man with treatment-resistant depression (two adequate antidepressant trials, no psychotic features, no active suicidality) strongly prefers to avoid general anesthesia. He asks the team about neuromodulation options. Which correctly characterizes what is available?

A 27-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history is admitted for new-onset paranoid ideation, disorganized behavior, and auditory hallucinations. Her chart notes she was started on high-dose prednisone three weeks ago for an autoimmune flare. Before establishing a primary psychiatric diagnosis, the most important step is which of the following?

A 37-year-old man with schizophrenia has been stable on haloperidol 5 mg/day and sertraline 100 mg/day for a comorbid depressive episode. His sertraline was increased to 150 mg two days ago. He now presents with fever (38.9°C), agitation, diaphoresis, and muscle rigidity. CK is mildly elevated at 680 U/L. The differential includes serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Which finding, if present on examination, would most strongly support serotonin syndrome over neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

A 22-year-old man presents with 3 weeks of auditory hallucinations, paranoid delusions, and disorganized behavior. The team is ready to diagnose schizophrenia and start an antipsychotic. The student asks whether anything should be done first. Which step is most critical?

A 19-year-old man presents with his first psychotic episode — 4 weeks of auditory hallucinations, paranoid delusions, and social withdrawal with no prior psychiatric history. Laboratory workup is sent. The team is discussing imaging. When is neuroimaging warranted in first-episode psychosis?

A student argues that lurasidone should be prescribed for a first-episode patient because 'it is one of the newest second-generation agents and therefore most effective.' Which framing from CATIE is most relevant here?

A 24-year-old man with schizophrenia is brought to the inpatient unit by his parents. He insists there is nothing wrong with him and refuses to engage with the treatment plan. His parents ask: 'Why won't he just accept that he's sick?' Which response best reflects the clinical approach?

A 37-year-old man with schizophrenia has had an inadequate response to olanzapine (adequate dose and duration) and then risperidone (adequate dose and duration). Residual negative symptoms (flat affect, avolition, alogia) have persisted on both trials. The team is now choosing a next step. Which is the evidence-based recommendation?

A 32-year-old woman with schizophrenia started haloperidol 5 days ago. She is now febrile to 39.9°C, diaphoretic, and rigid. Nursing staff describe her muscle tone as 'like a pipe.' Her CK is 5,400. What is the most important immediate action?

A 21-year-old woman develops subacute psychosis, behavioral changes, and seizures over 4 weeks. She also has involuntary mouth movements and facial grimacing, and her family reports fluctuating states of agitation and relative unresponsiveness. Which diagnosis should be actively considered in this presentation?

A 20-year-old man is diagnosed with first-episode schizophrenia. His family asks, 'What kind of treatment should we expect — just medication?' Which response best reflects the evidence-based approach for first-episode psychosis?

A 78-year-old man with no prior psychiatric history is noted to be 'psychotic' — he is making nonsensical statements, appears to be responding to internal stimuli, and is alternating between agitation and somnolence. He was admitted 2 days ago for a hip fracture repair. Which diagnosis should be considered first?

A 41-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia on clozapine for 6 months presents with 3 days of fever, severe constipation, and abdominal distension. His ANC is within the monitored range. Which clozapine adverse effect must be immediately considered?

A 28-year-old woman presents with 2 weeks of auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions coinciding with a severe depressive episode. Between prior mood episodes she has no psychotic symptoms. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this pattern?

A 33-year-old man with schizophrenia has had a modest response to risperidone 4 mg/day for 6 weeks. His attending considers this a non-response and wants to proceed to clozapine. The student questions whether the treatment resistance threshold has been met. What must be true before clozapine is indicated for treatment-resistant schizophrenia?
A 22-year-old has had delusions, hallucinations, and disorganized speech for the past 3 months with functional decline and no mood episode or substance cause. Which diagnosis best fits at this point?

A patient has had auditory hallucinations and delusions for two weeks with no significant mood symptoms during that period, but has also had major depressive episodes during most of the illness. Best diagnosis?

A 34-year-old man admitted last night for opioid use disorder asks to start buprenorphine right away — 'I don't want to get sick.' His last heroin use was about 6 hours ago. He is anxious but has no yawning, rhinorrhea, mydriasis, or piloerection; his COWS score is 4. Best next step?

A 52-year-old man with a history of heavy daily alcohol use is admitted in early withdrawal — tremulous and tachycardic. A nurse is about to start an IV dextrose infusion for a fingerstick glucose in the low-normal range. The most important step before administering the glucose is which of the following?

A 57-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder is admitted through the ED with altered mental status. The nurse establishes IV access and is preparing to infuse D5W. He appears malnourished and confused. Which step must occur before the glucose infusion is started?

A 46-year-old woman is admitted for alcohol detoxification. Her CIWA-Ar score is 16 on admission. A nurse asks how benzodiazepines should be dosed for alcohol withdrawal management on this unit. Which approach is correct?

A 28-year-old man with opioid use disorder requests buprenorphine. He last used heroin 5 hours ago and reports mild cramping but looks comfortable. His COWS score is 5. He says, 'I'm ready to start — please give it now.' What is the most appropriate response?

A 34-year-old woman with cocaine use disorder presents with elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, and grandiosity beginning 2 days after she used cocaine heavily. The team wants to document a diagnosis of bipolar I disorder. Which statement best characterizes the diagnostic approach?

A 61-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder is admitted for detoxification. On day 2, a nurse pages: he is increasingly confused, stumbling when ambulated, and his eyes appear to be 'moving strangely.' He was ambulatory on admission. Which diagnosis must be excluded immediately?

A 31-year-old man with opioid use disorder is being discharged after a brief admission for opioid intoxication. He declines to start buprenorphine during the admission. Which discharge intervention has the strongest direct evidence for preventing death in the weeks following discharge?

A 52-year-old woman completes medically supervised alcohol detoxification and wants pharmacotherapy to support sobriety. She has normal renal and hepatic function and no contraindications. Which agents are FDA-approved, evidence-based first-line options for alcohol use disorder maintenance?

A patient with opioid use disorder says: 'I'm not an addict. I can stop whenever I want — it hasn't caused me any real problems.' You are the student conducting the initial interview using a motivational interviewing approach. Which response is best?

A 19-year-old man is admitted for heroin withdrawal. He is visibly distressed, diaphoretic, tachycardic, and requesting immediate medication. A colleague asks, 'Is this patient in danger?' Which response most accurately conveys the clinical urgency?

A 56-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is brought in by EMS after being found unresponsive. Blood alcohol level is 0.22. He remains obtunded 45 minutes after arrival despite being stable. A colleague says, 'He's just drunk — let's monitor and wait.' Which response is most accurate?

A 64-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder and documented Child-Pugh B cirrhosis is admitted for alcohol withdrawal. CIWA-Ar is 14. The team considers using chlordiazepoxide for symptom-triggered dosing. A student identifies a safety concern. Which response is most accurate?

A 49-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder is admitted after a tonic-clonic seizure at home. He has a documented prior alcohol withdrawal seizure from two years ago. CIWA-Ar on arrival is 12. Which statement best characterizes his risk and clinical priority?
